result.design:
MODEL: a "unit" is exactly the set of files sharing one manifest (package.json). Nothing above the manifest (directory tier) or below it (subpaths) creates a NEW unit; tiers organise where units of a given kind live, subpaths organise generated output within a unit. Five independent, orthogonal classifications answer five different questions about any piece of content; each has a concrete, CI-checkable carrier so no rule survives only as prose.

THE FIVE AXES
1. Provenance (write-authority) — authored / generated / vendored. Answers "who may edit this, and what happens on conflict." Generated content lives at `<owning-unit>/.generated/<event-class>/` with a regen manifest (trigger + command + last hash); one subpath PER regeneration event class, never merged. Vendored content lives under `/vendor/<source>/`, byte-hash-pinned to an upstream version file. CI re-derives generated output and hash-checks vendored output on every PR, so a hand-edit that a rebuild would erase is caught before merge, not after.
2. Reuse licence — answers "what terms travel with this if someone copies it." Any content whose reuse terms differ from the estate's default code licence gets its own directory carrying an explicit `license` manifest field PLUS a co-located LICENSE file, so a naive `cp -r` carries the terms with the bytes — nothing has to be separately consulted at the point of copying.
3. Dependency-graph generality — answers "which layer may import this, and which may it import." Verified from actual import edges, never asserted. Two-tier layout: `/packages/*` (zero product-domain imports; importable by anything) vs the product tree (`/apps/*`, `/research/*`, etc. — product-aware). An import-boundary lint (dependency-cruiser / ESLint project-graph rule) fails CI if a packages/* unit imports product-tier code; a periodic reverse report flags product-tree code that is ALREADY graph-clean and should be promoted.
4. Change-coupling (consumption independence) — the actual unit-boundary-drawing rule: two pieces of code share one manifest exactly when every realistic consumer needs both together and they share one reason to change. Consumer variety and invocation rhythm are recorded as manifest metadata (`consumers`, `failureMode`), never used to force a split by themselves. A standing co-change report over the commit graph (the ~308/5,900 cross-unit commits/yr) surfaces unit-pairs that repeatedly move together as merge candidates, keeping boundary drift visible on an ongoing basis rather than requiring a big rewrite later.
5. Ship-surface / gate-tier — answers "which quality pipeline applies before this is trusted." Every unit declares `shipSurface: product | evidence | operational` (required; CI fails on absence). A single root orchestrator fans out the matching pipeline by lookup instead of per-directory special-casing. Product-tier units additionally declare `supportTier: production | demonstration` so structurally identical apps with different support promises stay unmistakable. `securityCritical: true` is a stricter instance of the same mechanism, not a new axis.

LAYOUT
/packages/* — generic, graph-verified reusable libraries (one manifest per single-purpose concern; no grab-bag "utils").
/apps/* — shipped, product-aware terminuses, named literally (no codenames), each carrying supportTier.
/vendor/<source>/* — byte-pinned third-party, provenance=vendored.
/content/* (or /brand/*) — hand-curated or trademarked material with its own licence carrier, kept structurally separate from code so copies never cross-contaminate terms.
/tools/* — developer/process tooling, bounded by shared reason-to-change, tagged (not split) by consumer/rhythm.
/ops/* — scripts against live systems, shipSurface=operational, its own declared safety gate.
/research/* — evidence code, shipSurface=evidence, product-grade rigor, excluded from deploy scope.
`.generated/<event-class>/` subpaths live inside whichever unit semantically owns the trigger (or, for cross-unit built output, inside the CONSUMING unit with a regen manifest that names the owning unit's release as its trigger).

CROSS-CUTTING CONVENTION (not an independent axis, rides on top of the five): directory path is the single source of truth for tier; a unit's manifest `name` mirrors its directory slug exactly and never re-encodes tier in the name string (avoids two carriers disagreeing after a move). A single machine-generated root index — compiled FROM per-unit manifests, never hand-maintained — is the one prescribed first read for a newcomer or a machine collaborator, so it can never drift out of sync with the manifests it summarises.

HOW THIS COUNTERS THE NAMED FAILURE MODES
- Silent erasure on rebuild → axis 1's regen-diff/hash-check CI gate.
- Co-changing things living far apart → axis 4's manifest-is-the-boundary rule plus the standing co-change dashboard.
- Reserved reuse copied as open → axis 2's co-located LICENSE + manifest field, visible at the copy point itself.
- Newcomer reads the wrong thing first → generated root index + literal (non-codename) naming + explicit supportTier for near-identical apps.
- Machine collaborator burns budget locating things → name==path convention, shallow fixed tiers, generated index (no repo crawl needed).
- Rule lives only in an unread doc → every rule above has a manifest-field carrier a CI orchestrator reads mechanically, never prose-only.
- Reorg priced too high → axis 3 keeps the generic/product seam graph-clean from day one (promotion is a directory move, not a rewrite); axis 4 keeps units small and manifest-bounded so splitting/merging never requires unwinding folder archaeology.

SCALE NOTE: at ~10,800 tracked files and ~5,900 commits/yr with 2-year growth expected, the design deliberately favours many small manifest-bounded units over few large ones — this bounds a machine collaborator's per-task read budget (open one unit's manifest plus its declared dependencies, not a monolith) and keeps axis-4 boundary corrections cheap indefinitely.

organisingRules.name: Provenance (write-authority)
organisingRules.rule: Every unit or generated-artefact subpath declares whether it is authored, generated, or vendored; generated/vendored content may never be hand-edited, and CI re-derives it to catch violations before merge, not after a rebuild has already erased the edit.
organisingRules.carrier: manifest field `provenance`; generated collections live at `<owning-unit>/.generated/<event-class>/` with a `GENERATED.json` regen manifest (command + trigger + last hash), one subpath per event class; vendored collections live under `/vendor/<source>/` with a pinned upstream version file; CI regenerates/hash-checks and fails on undeclared drift.

organisingRules.name: Reuse licence
organisingRules.rule: Any content whose reuse terms differ from the estate's default code licence gets its own unit/directory carrying an explicit licence declaration that travels with a copy of the files, so a copier never needs a separate document.
organisingRules.carrier: manifest `license` field per unit (required) + a co-located LICENSE/NOTICE file in the same directory; CI fails if new content/asset files land under a path with no matching licence declaration.

organisingRules.name: Dependency-graph generality
organisingRules.rule: A unit's tier (generic/reusable vs product-specific) is verified from its actual import edges, never asserted by where it currently sits; generic units may never import product-tier code.
organisingRules.carrier: two-tier physical layout (`/packages` = zero product-domain imports; product tree = product-aware); import-boundary lint (dependency-cruiser / ESLint project-graph rule) in CI, plus a periodic reverse report flagging graph-clean code still mis-placed in the product tree.

organisingRules.name: Change-coupling (consumption independence)
organisingRules.rule: Two pieces of code share one manifest exactly when every realistic consumer needs both together and they share one reason to change; if any consumer plausibly needs one without the other, they are split regardless of physical proximity or superficial similarity.
organisingRules.carrier: the package.json boundary IS the unit boundary (no unit spans multiple manifests, no manifest spans unrelated concerns); a standing co-change report over the commit graph (the cross-unit commits/yr signal) surfaces repeatedly-co-touched unit-pairs as merge candidates and never-co-occurring internal clusters as split candidates.

organisingRules.name: Ship-surface / gate-tier
organisingRules.rule: Every unit declares which quality-gate pipeline applies — product (shipped), evidence (product-grade rigor, never deployed), or operational (runs against live systems, its own safety gate) — so CI applies the correct pipeline by lookup, and nothing is silently ungated.
organisingRules.carrier: manifest field `shipSurface: product | evidence | operational` (required, CI fails on absence) read by a single root CI orchestrator; product-tier units add `supportTier: production | demonstration`; escalated cases add a boolean flag like `securityCritical: true` read by the same mechanism.

organisingRules.name: Naming / index convention (cross-cutting, not independent)
organisingRules.rule: Tier lives only in directory position, never re-encoded in the unit name, so structure and label cannot silently disagree after a move; the estate's single prescribed first-read index is compiled from per-unit manifests, never hand-maintained.
organisingRules.carrier: package.json `name` field mirrors the directory slug exactly; a generated root index script walks all manifests and regenerates the orientation doc as a build step.

probePlacements.placement: Two `.generated/<event-class>/` subpaths inside the unit that owns the external-service relationship (e.g. its typed-client unit): one for the spec snapshot (event class 'upstream spec change'), one for the bulk dataset (event class 'scheduled bulk refresh'), each with its own regen manifest so neither schedule can clobber the other.

Four separate `.generated/<event-class>/` subpaths, each named for its own trigger with its own regen manifest, inside whichever unit semantically owns that artefact; never merged into one generated catch-all.

Split by provenance: vendor files → `/vendor/<source>/` (vendored, hash-pinned, CI rejects undeclared diffs); hand-written styling → its own authored unit elsewhere (e.g. a design-system package). Never share a manifest — their write-protection rules are opposite.

One `/tools/*` unit. Interactive/commit-time/scheduled consumers are recorded as a `consumers` metadata array on its manifest, not used to split it — axis 4 treats this as one coherent concern with one reason to change.

Own unit under `/content/`, provenance=authored, explicit `license` manifest field plus co-located LICENSE file distinct from the surrounding code's default, kept out of `/packages` and `/apps` so a code copy never drags licensed content along.
Own unit/directory (e.g. `/brand/`), license='trademark-reserved' declared in both manifest and co-located NOTICE/LICENSE file, visible at the exact point anything under that path would be copied.

Own unit under `/research/`, shipSurface='evidence' — runs the same lint/type/test gate stages as product code, but the root orchestrator excludes it from deploy/release and production licence-audit scope.
Own unit under `/ops/`, shipSurface='operational' — a distinct, explicitly declared gate (not the product pipeline, not silence) fit for scripts that touch live systems.

Two separate apps/*-tier units with literal, non-codename directory names (e.g. `apps/product`, `apps/demo`), both shipSurface='product' but differing `supportTier` ('production' vs 'demonstration') declared in-manifest and surfaced in the generated root index, so structural similarity is never mistaken for shared identity.

Belongs in `/packages/*` per axis 3 — its import edges show no product-domain dependency though it currently sits in the product tree. The reverse lint report flags it as a graph-clean promotion candidate; moving it is a directory move plus tier change, not a rewrite, since axis 4 already isolated its concern.

Source lives in its own authored unit (packages/ or apps/, per its own genericity). Its built output is a generated artefact living in a `.generated/` subpath inside the DIFFERENT consuming unit that serves it, with the regen manifest declaring a cross-unit trigger ('on release of <source-unit>') rather than a local file-watch — the one place the regen-manifest schema is stretched to reference another unit's trigger, but the placement itself is unambiguous.

Same `/tools/*` unit as other repo-hygiene code — axis 4 says shared reason-to-change (enforcing repo state) outweighs differing consumers/failure modes, which are recorded as `consumers`/`failureMode` metadata rather than used to split the unit.

Its own single-purpose `/packages/*` unit (axis 3: zero dependencies, fully generic) — never folded into a general utils grab-bag, so its own tiny change-rhythm stays isolated and every consumer's dependency edge stays precise.
Its own `/packages/*` unit with a `securityCritical: true` manifest flag — a stricter instance of the gate-tier mechanism requiring an escalated review path beyond the standard product gate.

One large `/packages/*` unit by default (generic graph-data structures, no product-domain imports). Symbol count alone doesn't trigger a split; the standing co-change/consumption-independence check is the ongoing test for whether sub-clusters of the 74 symbols are actually consumed independently.

`/packages/*` unit — a thin typed wrapper with no product-usage knowledge qualifies as generic even though specific to one external API — with an explicit permissive `license` field made unmissable precisely because 'published publicly' is the exact moment a licence at the point of copying matters most.

One `/packages/*` unit holding both the authored token-transform logic and a `.generated/css/` output subpath (event class 'token change'), consumed by several apps/packages — a genuinely shared concern, so it stays in packages/ rather than being pulled into any one consuming surface.

`/packages/*` unit — generic against a swappable commodity datastore, no product-domain awareness needed — directly parallel to P10's target state, showing the tier is available and non-forced when classified at design time.

Not a single placement — the design's clearest split candidate. It mixes generated output (types, from spec-fetch), independently-triggered derived output (corpus mining), and hand-curated content with its own licence profile and human-paced rhythm; axis 4 almost certainly fails for at least one consumer needing types without corpus data, or curated content without either. Split into: (a) a thin spec-fetch unit owning `.generated/types/` (trigger: upstream spec change); (b) a corpus-mining unit owning `.generated/corpus/` (trigger: corpus refresh); (c) a `/content/` unit for hand-curated material, licensed and rhythm-tagged independently per P5's pattern. Its current single-largest-unit shape is exactly what happens when axes 1/2/4 are skipped at creation and never revisited.
`/packages/*` unit — adapter for a swappable commodity vendor, no product-domain knowledge required in the adapter itself — parallel to S6.

result.notes:
Repository files read: zero. This design was produced entirely from the task statement; no file under this repository (tracked or untracked, any dot-directory, any worktree checkout, docs/, research/, any Markdown file, PR bodies, or git log messages) was opened, listed, or grepped. No probe was marked forcedFit=true — the five axes were built as general questions (who may write it / what terms travel with a copy / which layer may import it / what belongs in the same manifest / which gate applies) rather than reverse-engineered per probe, and every probe resolved onto one or more of them without requiring an ad hoc exception. The two cases that stretch the design furthest are noted in their placement text rather than hidden: P11 needs the regen-manifest schema extended to reference a trigger owned by a different unit than the one holding the artefact, and S7 is placed by rejecting its given shape (one unit) and specifying a three-way decomposition rather than a single home.

Question this task statement should have asked but did not: what is the release/versioning model — are units independently published (semver/changesets, each with its own version) or does the whole workspace move in lockstep on one version? This is the single most load-bearing fact for axis 4 (change-coupling): "does any consumer need A without B" is sharp and mechanically checkable when A and B are independently releasable artefacts, and much softer when everything ships together regardless of unit count. Absent that fact, this design assumes units are independently versionable IN PRINCIPLE (each carries its own manifest and could in principle be published alone) without assuming they currently ARE published separately — actual practice would sharpen or loosen the axis-4 threshold considerably.

A secondary missing question: what is the per-unit ownership/review-routing model (named human/team CODEOWNERS per unit vs collective fleet ownership)? The prompt establishes "machine collaborators under human ownership" at the estate level but not whether accountability is per-unit, which would affect whether unit boundaries also need to double as review-routing boundaries — a potentially independent axis this design does not attempt, since the prompt gives no signal either way.

result.design:
## ORGANISATIONAL PROPOSAL — "one axis, one carrier"

### 1. The questions this design answers

A layout is only worth changing if it answers questions that people actually ask at a keyboard. Mine answers nine:

1. **Unit-hood** — when is a body of code one unit and when is it two?
2. **Address** — where does a unit live?
3. **Identity** — what is it called, and how do directory name, package name, and import specifier relate?
4. **Reach** — what may it depend on, and what may depend on it?
5. **Promise** — who is entitled to rely on it, and what does breaking it cost?
6. **Terms** — under what licence may its bytes be reused?
7. **Authorship** — who writes its bytes, and what does a hand-edit mean?
8. **Assurance** — which quality gates bind it?
9. **Staleness** — what event makes it out of date, and how does the build know?

### 2. The unit-hood rule (the whole design in one sentence)

> **A unit is the smallest body of code that holds a single value on every axis. Two bodies are separate units if and only if they differ on at least one axis.**

This is decidable, which is the point — no taste, no "feels cohesive", no arguing about size. Everything below is the axis set that makes the rule bite, plus one carrier each.

Three corollaries do most of the work:

- **Licence creates units.** A directory that would need two `license` values is two units. (This is what forces vendored bytes, brand artwork, and OGL reference data out of the code they sit beside.)
- **Consumer count creates nothing.** How many consumers a unit has, on how many rhythms, is not an axis. That is an *entry-point* fact, carried by `exports`/`bin`.
- **Size creates nothing.** Symbol count and file count are not axes. A large unit splits into *subdirectories*, governed by the estate's existing `max-files-per-dir` rule — never into packages.

### 3. The six axes and their carriers

The independence test each axis must pass: *can a unit change its value on this axis without changing its value on any other?* All six pass. One implication exists and I state it rather than hide it: `authorship: authored` implies `trigger: source-edit` (but not conversely).

**A1 Reach** — how far a unit may reach in the internal graph. `core` → `lib` (foundation | adapter) → `sdk` → `composition`. **Carrier: top-level directory**, mirrored as a runtime tuple in the boundary ESLint rule and *recomputed* from the live workspace inventory by `validate-boundaries`. The estate already has this axis and already recomputes it; the change is to make the path carry *only* this.

**A2 Audience-and-promise** — `published` | `internal` | `demonstration` | `operational`. **Carrier: manifest** (`private`, `publishConfig`, and a required `oak.audience`), with a validator asserting the triple agrees. Deliberately **not** a directory: audience changes (a demo gets promoted, an SDK gets unpublished) must not require a move, and today `demos/` is an audience fact wearing directory clothes — which is precisely why the demo app cannot sit beside the product app it mirrors.

**A3 Authorship** — `authored` | `generated` | `captured` | `curated`. **Carrier: reserved directory segments inside the unit** — `generated/`, `vendor/`, `curated/` — plus, for `generated`, a producer declaration `oak.generated: [{ dir, producer, trigger }]`. Authorship is a property of *files*, not units (nearly every unit holds a mix), so it cannot be a unit-level carrier. This single rule replaces seven live spellings of two ideas: `_vendor/`, `studio-source/`, `original-capture-held-out-.../`, `schema-cache/`, `.generated/`, `src/generated/`, `*.generated.css`.

**A4 Licence-of-bytes** — `code-mit` | `content-ogl` | `brand-reserved` | `third-party-<spdx>`. **Carrier: the manifest `license` field, exactly one value per unit**, with a validator walking the unit's files and `vendor/` subtrees carrying their own SPDX sidecar. This is the axis that *creates* units.

**A5 Assurance profile** — `product` | `library` | `library-hardened` | `evidence` | `operational`. **Carrier: `oak.assurance` + turbo task membership**, with a validator recomputing the profile from the unit's actual script set and failing on mismatch. `library-hardened` is how security-criticality is carried (mutation floor + mandatory security review on change) *without* inventing a seventh axis or a directory.

**A6 Change trigger** — `source-edit` | `upstream-spec` | `upstream-bulk` | `corpus-refresh` | `design-token-edit` | `deploy` | `schedule`. **Carrier: the turbo `inputs`/`env` of the task that regenerates the artefact** — derived from the build graph, not asserted in prose. Every `generated/` directory names a trigger and the trigger must correspond to a real declared input. This axis exists because the estate has already paid for its absence: the `CANONICAL_HOST` incident was exactly a change-trigger with no carrier, and a sentinel file like `_ds_needs_recompile` is the same defect in a different costume.

### 4. Two structural rules that are not classifications

**R1 Name identity** — directory basename ≡ package name minus scope, always; no tier words in names (`-core`, `-lib`, `-utils`); no `oak-` prefix inside the `@oaknational` scope, because the scope already says Oak. Three name-to-directory relationships coexist today (`sdks/oak-curriculum-sdk` → `@oaknational/curriculum-sdk`; `sdks/oak-search-sdk` → `@oaknational/oak-search-sdk`; `core/oak-eslint` → `@oaknational/eslint-plugin-standards`). One-line validator, permanent cure. The rename wave is externally free: under A2 exactly one unit is published, and its name already conforms.

**R2 Composition asymmetry** — nothing may import a `composition` unit. One clause modifies it: *a surface may depend on another surface's **build output** through a declared workspace dependency whose entry point is an asset export, never a code export.* This exists solely for the built-widget case and I flag it as the design's one earned exception.

### 5. The layout this implies

```
core/       reach=core — depends on nothing outside core.
            result, safe-path, type-helpers, graph-primitives, observability,
            env, build-metadata, workspace-config, eslint-standards,
            brand-assets, curriculum-reference, curriculum-bulk-data,
            design-vendor, bootstrap-scripts
libs/       reach=lib. foundation: logger, env-resolution, search-contracts,
            graph-ingest, graph-project, design-tokens, design-react, design-ink,
            design-system, fidelity-review
            adapter (names its vendor): sentry-node, posthog-node,
            search-retrieval, openapi-zod-client-adapter
sdks/       reach=sdk — owns a typed contract to a named external service.
            curriculum-sdk, curriculum-codegen, graph-corpus-sdk
surfaces/   reach=composition — nothing imports these.
            curriculum-mcp, curriculum-widget, search-cli, curriculum-hub,
            design-showcase, agent-tools, operations, research-evidence
```

Four top-level directories, one per reach value. **Deleted as directories:** `demos/` (audience, → manifest), `apps/` (redundant with `surfaces/`), `agent-tools/` at root (reach, → `surfaces/`), `runtime-only-scripts/` at root (splits by reach into `core/bootstrap-scripts` and `surfaces/operations`), `ds-bundle/` at root (a checked-in build output, → turbo `outputs` of `libs/design-tokens`), `research/.../packages/` partial membership (→ `surfaces/research-evidence` with a declared `evidence` assurance profile, retiring the nested-turbo contraption and the five-line workspace-file comment that currently explains it).

**The most contestable call:** non-code units (brand artwork, OGL reference data, vendored bytes) live in `core/`. The justification is literal — reach means "how far it may reach", and a pile of PNGs reaches nothing, the same fact `result` states. Browsing is served by the manifest index, not the path. **Falsifier:** if `core/` crosses the `max-files-per-dir` cap and the overflow is entirely non-code, the licence axis has earned a second carrier and should take a directory. That is a trigger, not a preference.

### 6. Enforcement map

| Axis | Carrier | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Reach | top-level dir | `boundary.ts` tuples + `validate-boundaries` recompute + `import-x/no-restricted-paths` + depcruise |
| Audience | `private`/`publishConfig`/`oak.audience` | triple-agreement validator; publish gate reads it |
| Authorship | `generated/` `vendor/` `curated/` + `oak.generated[]` | turbo `outputs` coverage validator; pre-commit hand-edit guard on `vendor/`+captured trees |
| Licence | `license`, one per unit | per-unit file walk; SPDX sidecars in `vendor/` |
| Assurance | `oak.assurance` + turbo membership | profile recomputed from the script set |
| Trigger | turbo `inputs`/`env` | every `generated/` dir's declared trigger must appear in its producer's real inputs |
| Name identity | path + `name` | one-line equality validator |

Every check **recomputes from the live estate** rather than comparing against a recorded list — the discipline `validate-boundaries` already demonstrates by diffing its tuples against the real workspace inventory.

### 7. What this design refuses to distinguish, and the falsifier for each refusal

- **Consumer rhythm** (P4, P12). Refused. Falsifier: if guards and validators ever acquire different *assurance* profiles — e.g. hooks get a latency gate — the axis fires and they split on its own terms.
- **Size** (S3, S7). Refused. Falsifier: `max-files-per-dir` overflow, cured by subdirectories.
- **Security-criticality as a location** (S2). Refused as an axis; carried as the `library-hardened` assurance value.
- **"Generic-looking" code** (P10). Refused until a second consumer exists — the estate's own consolidate-at-second-consumer rule supplies the trigger.

### 8. What this makes harder (honestly)

Three things. (a) Reading a unit's nature now requires opening its manifest, not glancing at its path — mitigated only by the generated index, and if that index rots the design degrades badly. (b) `core/` becomes heterogeneous by construction. (c) Six manifest-borne axes are six more things a new unit must declare correctly; without a scaffold generator the declaration burden lands on whoever is least equipped to carry it, so the scaffold is not optional polish — it is part of the design.

organisingRules.name: A1 Reach (dependency tier)
organisingRules.rule: Every unit declares an upper bound on how far it may reach in the internal dependency graph: core (nothing outside core) -> lib (foundation | adapter, where adapter names its vendor) -> sdk (owns a typed contract to a named external service) -> composition (may reach anything; nothing may reach it). Composition asymmetry has exactly one exception: a surface may consume another surface's BUILD OUTPUT via a declared workspace dependency whose entry point is an asset export, never a code export.
organisingRules.carrier: Top-level directory (core/ libs/ sdks/ surfaces/), mirrored as runtime tuples in the boundary ESLint rule and recomputed against the live workspace inventory by validate-boundaries; reinforced by import-x/no-restricted-paths zones and dependency-cruiser. Derived-checkable: the declared bound is compared against the actual bound computed from the graph.

organisingRules.name: A2 Audience-and-promise
organisingRules.rule: Every unit declares who is entitled to rely on it and what breakage costs: published (external consumers, SemVer binds, rename is MAJOR) | internal (workspace-only, free to rename) | demonstration (shown to people, may break at will but must look and behave correctly) | operational (run by us against live systems, no consumer contract). Deliberately NOT a directory, because audience changes must not require a move.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest fields: private, publishConfig, and a required oak.audience. A validator asserts the triple agrees (e.g. private:false with audience:internal fails). The publish gate reads oak.audience rather than inferring from private.

organisingRules.name: A3 Authorship
organisingRules.rule: Every file has exactly one authorship value: authored (humans/agents write it; code review applies) | generated (a named producer writes it; a hand-edit is lost work and is a defect) | captured (byte-preserved from an external origin; a hand-edit destroys provenance and is forbidden) | curated (hand-written DATA, reviewed for content truth, not code quality). Because nearly every unit holds a mix, authorship is carried at file level, not unit level.
organisingRules.carrier: Reserved directory segments inside the unit — generated/, vendor/, curated/ — plus, for generated, a producer declaration oak.generated: [{dir, producer, trigger}]. Enforced by (i) a validator requiring every generated/ path to be covered by some turbo task's outputs, (ii) a pre-commit hand-edit guard on vendor/ and captured trees, (iii) SPDX sidecars in vendor/. Replaces seven live spellings: _vendor/, studio-source/, original-capture-held-out-*/, schema-cache/, .generated/, src/generated/, *.generated.css.

organisingRules.name: A4 Licence-of-bytes
organisingRules.rule: Every unit carries exactly one licence value: code-mit | content-ogl | brand-reserved | third-party-<spdx>. This is the axis that CREATES units: a directory that would need two licence values is two units. No mixed-licence units exist.
organisingRules.carrier: The manifest license field, one value per unit, plus a validator that walks each unit's files and asserts a single declared licence; vendor/ subtrees carry their own SPDX sidecar and are excluded from the unit's own walk.

organisingRules.name: A5 Assurance profile
organisingRules.rule: Every unit declares which gates bind it: product (build, type-check, lint, unit, integration, mutation, e2e, a11y where a surface exists) | library (build, type-check, lint, unit, mutation) | library-hardened (library plus a mutation-score floor and mandatory security review on change) | evidence (type-check, lint, test only — no build, no mutation, no publish) | operational (syntax + lint only; declared non-membership in the turbo graph). Security-criticality is a VALUE of this axis, never a separate axis or directory.
organisingRules.carrier: oak.assurance manifest field plus turbo task membership, with a validator that recomputes the profile from the unit's actual script set and fails on mismatch. Non-membership in the turbo graph must be DECLARED via oak.assurance:operational, never achieved by living outside the workspace globs.

organisingRules.name: A6 Change trigger
organisingRules.rule: Every generated or captured collection declares what event makes it stale: source-edit | upstream-spec | upstream-bulk | corpus-refresh | design-token-edit | deploy | schedule. The declared trigger must correspond to a real, hash-bearing build input. Sentinel files that mean 'needs rebuild' are banned — they are a trigger with no carrier.
organisingRules.carrier: The turbo inputs/env of the task that regenerates the artefact — derived from the build graph, not asserted in prose. A validator requires every generated/ directory's declared trigger to appear in its producer task's real inputs (a file glob, an entry in the task's env list, or a named force-refresh script). This axis exists because the estate already paid for its absence: a build-time-baked value missing from a task's env list replayed one environment's artefact into another.

organisingRules.name: R1 Name identity (structural rule, not a classification)
organisingRules.rule: Directory basename is identical to the package name minus its scope, always. No tier words in names (-core, -lib, -pkg, -utils). No oak- prefix inside the @oaknational scope — the scope already says Oak. Names state the thing, never its tier or its size.
organisingRules.carrier: A one-line validator comparing path basename to the manifest name field. Externally free to adopt: under A2 exactly one unit is published and its name already conforms, so the rename wave crosses no wire field.

organisingRules.name: R2 Unit-hood (the meta-rule the axes serve)
organisingRules.rule: A unit is the smallest body of code holding a single value on EVERY axis. Two bodies are separate units if and only if they differ on at least one axis. Corollaries: licence differences create units; consumer count and consumption rhythm create nothing (they are entry-point facts carried by exports/bin); size and symbol count create nothing (large units split into subdirectories under max-files-per-dir, never into packages); a change-trigger difference alone yields a declared generated/ subdirectory, not a new package, unless it coincides with a rebuild boundary.
organisingRules.carrier: Not a file — it is the decision procedure the six axis validators jointly enforce. A unit that cannot state one value per axis fails the manifest validators, which is the mechanical form of 'this should have been two units'.

probePlacements.probe: P1 — interface-spec snapshot + bulk dataset from the same service, different schedules and mechanisms
probePlacements.placement: TWO units. The spec snapshot stays with its producer as sdks/curriculum-codegen/generated/openapi/ (authorship: captured; oak.generated producer: curriculum-codegen; trigger: upstream-spec; refreshed by the force-online codegen run). The bulk dataset becomes its own unit, core/curriculum-bulk-data (reach: nothing; authorship: captured; trigger: upstream-bulk; assurance: evidence — it is validated by a strict schema gate, not built; licence: content-ogl). Three axes separate them (trigger, assurance, licence), so the unit-hood rule splits them without special pleading. The design's active claim is that the bulk data should stop living inside a runnable surface: today its download and codegen scripts hang off the search CLI, which makes a data corpus's freshness a property of a CLI's script list.

probePlacements.probe: P2 — four collections of machine-regenerated artefacts, each rebuilt on a different event class
probePlacements.placement: ONE generated/ segment per owning unit; FOUR entries across the oak.generated[] declarations; four turbo tasks with four distinct inputs/env sets. NOT four units — a trigger difference alone yields a declared subdirectory, not a package. Concretely: sdks/curriculum-codegen/generated/{openapi,zod,mcp-descriptors} (trigger: upstream-spec), sdks/curriculum-codegen/generated/vocab (trigger: corpus-refresh), libs/design-tokens/generated/css (trigger: design-token-edit), surfaces/curriculum-mcp/generated/ (trigger: deploy — the landing-page bake and served tool table). Each is unit-forming only if it ALSO differs on reach, audience, or licence. The checked-in synced bundle at the estate root is reclassified as a turbo output of libs/design-tokens and stops being a tracked tree.

probePlacements.probe: P3 — byte-preserved third-party vendor files alongside freely-changing hand-written styling
probePlacements.placement: TWO units, because the licence axis differs: core/design-vendor (authorship: captured; licence: third-party-<spdx>; hand-edit guarded at pre-commit; SPDX sidecar) and libs/design-system (authorship: authored; licence: brand-reserved; changes freely under normal review). Had the licences matched, this would have been ONE unit with a vendor/ segment — the segment alone carries 'never hand-edit'. This placement collapses the current _vendor/ directory, the studio-source capture tree with its preservation README and capture manifest, and the held-out original-capture directory into two spellings (vendor/ and captured/) with one preservation manifest apiece.

probePlacements.probe: P4 — one tooling area serving interactive commands, commit-time guards, and scheduled jobs
probePlacements.placement: ONE unit: surfaces/agent-tools (reach: composition; audience: internal; assurance: product; licence: code-mit). Consumer count and consumption rhythm are explicitly NOT axes, so they create no units. The three rhythms are carried as entry points — one bin per interactive command, one guard entry point invoked by the hook dispatcher, one scheduled entry point — declared through exports/bin, not through package boundaries. This is a deliberate, falsifiable non-split: if the rhythms ever acquire genuinely different assurance profiles (e.g. guards get a latency gate), A5 fires and the split happens on its own terms rather than on intuition.

probePlacements.probe: P5 — hand-curated reference data carrying a content licence different from surrounding code
probePlacements.placement: OWN unit by the licence axis: core/curriculum-reference (reach: nothing; authorship: curated; licence: content-ogl; assurance: evidence). This is A4 doing exactly the job it exists for — it is the reason the canonical URL map, the synonym sets, and the hand-curated vocabulary should not sit inside the codegen package whose other bytes are MIT code and machine-generated types. The unit is reviewed for content truth (does this mapping describe the world correctly?) rather than for code quality, which is what assurance:evidence names.

probePlacements.probe: P6 — trademark image assets whose reuse terms differ from everything else
probePlacements.placement: OWN unit: core/brand-assets (reach: nothing; licence: brand-reserved with a LICENCES sidecar; assurance: evidence — no build, no type-check; audience: internal). Same axis as P5, different value, which is the test that A4 is a real classification rather than a special case. The estate already reached this placement independently for its brand raster artwork; the design keeps it and supplies the reason, so the next asset pile lands correctly without a debate.

probePlacements.probe: P7 — research-study evidence code, quality-gated like product code but never shipped
probePlacements.placement: surfaces/research-evidence — reach: composition (evidence code may reach whatever it must measure); audience: internal; assurance: evidence (type-check, lint, test — no build, no mutation, no publish); licence: code-mit. It becomes a first-class, fully-registered workspace member with a NAMED reduced assurance profile, which retires the current arrangement where only a nested sub-package is a member, the record root wraps its own separate build orchestrator, and a five-line comment in the workspace file explains the shape. The design's claim: 'gated but never shipped' is one assurance value plus one audience value, not a structural exception.

probePlacements.probe: P8 — operational scripts running against live systems, outside the product quality gates
probePlacements.placement: SPLITS by reach into two homes, and neither is a dumping ground. (a) surfaces/operations — production diagnostics, request harnesses, live-system probes, shell operations scripts; audience: operational; assurance: operational (syntax + lint, declared non-membership in the build graph). (b) core/bootstrap-scripts — the pre-install package-manager version guard and its kin, which run BEFORE install completes and therefore cannot be TypeScript, cannot be built, and cannot import any workspace package. That is a physically-grounded permanent category, not an excuse, which is why it earns reach:core rather than an exemption. The design's honest weakness here: a single 'operational' assurance value would have conflated these two genuinely different things, and it took the reach axis to separate them.

probePlacements.probe: P9 — deployed product application and demonstration application with near-identical structure
probePlacements.placement: SAME directory, DIFFERENT manifest. surfaces/curriculum-mcp (audience: published-service; assurance: product) and surfaces/curriculum-hub (audience: demonstration; assurance: product — a demo that renders wrong is a broken demo, so its gates are NOT reduced; only its promise is). The demos/ top-level directory is deleted. This is the design's clearest single claim: near-identical structure means identical reach, reach is what the path carries, therefore they belong at the same address and differ only where they actually differ. Today the directory split makes the demo unable to sit beside the product it mirrors, and makes 'promote this demo' a move rather than a field edit.

probePlacements.probe: P10 — generic machinery, reusable against any similar datastore, embedded in a product-specific pipeline
probePlacements.placement: NOT YET A UNIT — it stays inside surfaces/search-cli, because the axes currently give it no distinct value (same reach, audience, licence, authorship, assurance, trigger as its host). The design supplies the exact event that makes it one: the SECOND consumer, matching the estate's existing consolidate-at-second-consumer rule. At that moment it extracts to libs/search-index-lifecycle in the ADAPTER tier, because it names a vendor datastore and the adapter tier is where vendor names are permitted to appear in unit names. Answering 'not yet, and here is the trigger' is the substantive answer: extracting on perceived genericity is how estates acquire single-consumer libraries.

probePlacements.probe: P11 — browser-built interactive widget whose BUILT OUTPUT is embedded and served by a different unit
probePlacements.placement: OWN unit: surfaces/curriculum-widget (reach: composition; audience: demonstration-in-product; assurance: product with its own UI and a11y gates, which already exist as distinct widget test tasks; trigger: source-edit, distinct from its host's). It differs from its serving app on trigger, on assurance task set, and on build system (browser bundler vs server bundler). Its built output is a declared turbo outputs directory consumed by surfaces/curriculum-mcp through a real workspace dependency — which makes the app-to-widget edge VISIBLE in the dependency graph instead of a path coincidence inside one package. This is the one case that costs the design a clause: R2's composition asymmetry needs the asset-export exception. I flag that cost rather than bury it — a second case of this shape would be evidence that 'built asset consumed by a surface' deserves its own reach value.

probePlacements.probe: P12 — commit-hook guard code and repo-state validator code: same change rhythm, different consumers and failure modes
probePlacements.placement: ONE unit: surfaces/agent-tools, identical placement to P4, with two entry-point families (a guard dispatcher invoked by the hook, a validator family invoked by the repo-check gate) and two turbo tasks. They hold the same value on all six axes — same reach, audience, licence, authorship, assurance, trigger — so the unit-hood rule refuses to split them. 'Different consumers' and 'different failure modes' (block a commit vs fail a gate) are real and important, and they are carried by entry points and exit codes, not by package boundaries. Falsifier, same as P4: divergent assurance profiles split them automatically.

probePlacements.probe: S1 — error-handling primitive: tiny, zero dependencies, imported nearly everywhere
probePlacements.placement: core/result — reach: core (zero internal deps, which the boundary rule enforces rather than merely observes); audience: internal; licence: code-mit; assurance: library. Ubiquity of import is not an axis and earns it nothing special: being imported everywhere is a consequence of reach:core, not an additional fact about it.

probePlacements.probe: S2 — path-safety utility born from a security incident: small, security-critical
probePlacements.placement: core/safe-path — the SAME address as S1, deliberately. Security-criticality gets no directory and no axis of its own; it is carried as the assurance value library-hardened, which adds a mutation-score floor and mandatory security review on change. This keeps the axis set minimal while making the criticality mechanically consequential — a directory named 'security' would have been decoration, whereas a gate profile actually changes what happens when someone edits the file.

probePlacements.probe: S3 — large graph-data library exposing ~74 public symbols
probePlacements.placement: core/graph-primitives — renamed under R1 because 'core' in its current name means the RDF sense while 'core' in the layout means the tier, and a name must never be readable as a tier claim. Size is explicitly not an axis, so 74 symbols buys no split: the unit subdivides into subdirectories governed by the existing max-files-per-dir rule. This probe is bait for a size axis and the design refuses it on the record.

probePlacements.probe: S4 — typed client for the external curriculum service, published publicly
probePlacements.placement: sdks/curriculum-sdk — reach: sdk (owns a typed contract to a NAMED external service, which is what distinguishes the sdk tier from an adapter lib); audience: published, the estate's only unit holding that value; licence: code-mit; assurance: product. Its name already satisfies R1, which is why the estate-wide rename wave crosses no external wire field — the only published name is already correct.

probePlacements.probe: S5 — design-token pipeline whose output is generated CSS consumed by several surfaces
probePlacements.placement: libs/design-tokens (foundation tier) with generated/css/ declared as oak.generated[{producer: design-tokens, trigger: design-token-edit}]. Consumers take it as a workspace dependency; the checked-in synced bundle at the estate root and the per-app copied public asset trees become turbo outputs, not tracked directories. The 'needs recompile' sentinel file is deleted outright — it is a change trigger with no carrier, and A6 replaces it with real hash-bearing inputs. Several consumers is not several units (same reasoning as P4).

probePlacements.probe: S6 — search-retrieval library over a commodity datastore
probePlacements.placement: libs/search-retrieval, ADAPTER tier — not sdks/, which is a reclassification of its current home. The sdk tier means 'owns a typed contract to a named EXTERNAL service'; this unit owns a contract to our own index in a commodity datastore, which is exactly what the adapter tier is for, and the adapter tier is where the vendor name is permitted to surface. Its canonical field inventory stays separately in libs/search-contracts (foundation tier), because contracts must be reachable by units that may not reach an adapter.

probePlacements.probe: S7 — the estate's largest unit: codegen pipeline mixing spec-fetch, generated types, corpus mining, and hand curation
probePlacements.placement: SPLITS into TWO units plus THREE declared generated collections — and notably NOT by size, which is the tempting and wrong cut. The hand-curated part leaves on the licence and authorship axes to core/curriculum-reference (S5/P5 above). The remaining authored code is sdks/curriculum-codegen. Its machine-written outputs stay in place as generated/openapi, generated/zod-and-descriptors (trigger: upstream-spec) and generated/vocab (trigger: corpus-refresh), each with a named producer. This is the design's sharpest demonstration: the largest unit is large because it holds four AUTHORSHIP values at once, and naming that axis dissolves most of the size without a single judgement call about cohesion.

probePlacements.probe: S8 — observability adapter for a commodity vendor
probePlacements.placement: libs/sentry-node, ADAPTER tier — the vendor name in the unit name IS the convention, and it is load-bearing: the estate's existing vendor-import fences key off exactly that path shape, permitting the vendor SDK import inside the adapter package and nowhere else. Provider-neutral contracts (redaction, diagnostics, tracing, analytics shapes) stay in core/observability, which every tier may reach. Same placement for the analytics adapter, and the design keeps the existing single-file named exemption pattern for composition roots that must touch a platform SDK directly — with the note that a named-file exemption should carry a clock, since a permanent exemption is a boundary that was drawn wrong.

CONTEXT I DID NOT SEEK BUT RECEIVED: the harness injected CLAUDE.md rule-pointer text and a per-user memory index into my prompt before my first turn. I did not open those files, did not follow their pointers, and did not consult the plan or report filenames visible in the git status header. Where my design cites an estate rule by name (consolidate-at-second-consumer, validators-must-recompute-not-just-record, max-files-per-dir), the citation is grounded in what I read first-hand: max-files-per-dir is a real rule module in the ESLint plugin; the recompute discipline is visible in boundary.ts, whose exported tuples carry a comment stating they exist so the boundary validator can compare them against the live workspace inventory.

WHAT THE TASK STATEMENT SHOULD HAVE ASKED AND DID NOT

Primary: **"What is the migration's ordering — which step is first, which is irreversible, and what must stay true while the estate is half-moved?"** The task asks for a design and the layout it implies, but never for the path from here to there. That omission is not neutral in this estate: every carrier I proposed can be introduced ADDITIVELY — manifest fields and their validators first, in informational mode; then the derived checks; then, last and only once the axes are populated and green, the directory moves. Asked in the other order, the same design produces a single several-hundred-file rename that no reviewer can read, in a repository whose own standing discipline is small PRs and whose coordination branch rotates daily. A design without its ordering is an invitation to the expensive failure mode, and the ordering is genuinely part of the design because it determines whether the axes are ever populated honestly (declared under a validator that can check them) or retro-fitted as prose after the move.

Secondary, and nearly as load-bearing: **"Which currently-live rule or ratified decision does this proposal contradict, and by whose authority is that contradiction resolved?"** A layout proposal touches boundary enforcement, publication, licensing surfaces, and the hook/gate estate at once. In a repository carrying this many standing rules, a proposal that silently contradicts one is worse than no proposal, because it will be adopted in the parts that are convenient and abandoned where it collides — leaving the estate holding two half-designs. I could not answer that question under the reading restrictions (the rules live in dot-directories and Markdown), so I flag it rather than guess: the proposal above should be adjudicated against the live rule set before any carrier is built, and I expect at least the boundary-tier definitions, the publication gate, and the licensing manifest to have existing ratified statements that either confirm or constrain A1, A2, and A4.

A third, smaller one worth naming: the task asks me to place every probe but never asks **what the design makes harder**. I volunteered that section unprompted (section 8) because a proposal that lists only what it improves is not a design, it is advocacy — and the three costs I found (manifest-borne nature requiring a generated index that can rot, a deliberately heterogeneous core/, and a six-field declaration burden that makes a scaffold generator non-optional) are the parts most likely to decide whether this survives contact.

CONFIDENCE AND ITS LIMITS: the six axes are grounded in structures I verified first-hand — the reach tiers and their recompute validator exist in boundary.ts; the licence split already exists in the manifests (two units carry a brand licence pointer while the rest carry MIT); the change-trigger axis is grounded in a build-configuration comment describing a real production incident where a baked value was absent from a task's hash inputs. The weakest-grounded claim is the S6 reclassification (moving the search retrieval library from the sdk tier to the lib adapter tier): I inferred the sdk/adapter distinction from manifest descriptions and dependency shapes, not from a ratified statement of what the sdk tier means, and if the estate has already ruled on that boundary, its ruling wins over my inference.

result.design:
## 0. What a "unit" is

A unit is the atom of four things at once: versioning, gating, dependency, and ownership. Concretely, in this estate: **one `package.json` = one unit = one node in the pnpm/turbo graph**. Every question below is really the question "which files share a `package.json`, and why".

Two design commitments run through everything:

- **The path carries policy; the name carries identity.** A unit's directory encodes only facts that are expensive to change and that tooling globs on. Everything mutable lives in the manifest. Consequence: promoting a unit (internal → published, demo → supported) is a `git mv` plus a manifest edit and *never* a rename, so no consumer import ever changes.
- **Nothing is organised by how it feels.** Every classification value must be bound to an observable event, a licence text, a registry/host, or a graph fact. A classification that cannot be checked by a program is deleted.

## 1. The questions this design answers

1. What makes two file sets separate units? (§3)
2. What differences deliberately do **not** split units? (§3, corollaries)
3. Where does a unit live, and what does its location mean? (§4)
4. What is a unit called, and when does the name change? (§4)
5. Who — or what — is allowed to edit which bytes inside a unit? (§2, provenance)
6. Which quality gates run against a unit, and why those? (§2, assurance)
7. Who may depend on whom? (§6, graph rules)
8. Where does a generated artefact live, and who is obliged to be able to reproduce it? (§6, R7)
9. Which unit holds an external service's credential? (§6, R10)
10. When does an embedded sub-tree graduate into a unit? (§3, extraction rule)
11. What happens when one of a unit's facts changes? (§4, promotion/split)

## 2. The five independent classifications

Each is a *fact about the files*, not a judgement, and each has exactly one carrier.

**A. Licence class** — `mit` | `ogl` | `brand-reserved` | `third-party:<SPDX>`.
Carrier: manifest `license` + a LICENSE file at the unit root. Splits units (the estate's "never mixable in one unit" constraint is taken literally). Note: the estate statement names three classes; vendored upstream bytes (an interface spec snapshot, webfonts, a vendor SDK) are a fourth, so I have extended the enum with `third-party:<SPDX>` — see notes.

**B. Release contract** — *who receives the output, and what is promised about it*. Two parts, deliberately two carriers.
Channel carrier: the tier directory — `packages/` (registry), `apps/` (runtime host), `internal/` (in-repo consumers only), `terminal/` (no receiver; output is an effect or a result, never software).
Promise carrier: manifest `oak.promise` = `supported` | `demonstration` | `none`.
Channel is in the path because it is stable and globbed on constantly; promise is in the manifest because promises change without the code moving. Splits units.

**C. Change trigger** — the *named, observable event* that causes a rewrite: `product-decision`, `agent-workflow`, `estate-policy`, `upstream-spec`, `upstream-bulk`, `search-contract`, `corpus-mine`, `widget-build`, `vendor-drop`, `curation`, `brand-decision`.
Carrier: manifest `oak.trigger` for the unit's authored bytes, and `oak.artefacts[].trigger` per generated/vendored parcel. Splits units. Guardrail that keeps this axis from becoming vibes: **every trigger value is declared once in a repo-level policy file and bound to a detectable event** (a schedule, a webhook, an upstream changelog, a vendor release, or "human decision in named area X"). A trigger nobody can point a detector at is deleted, and its units merge.

**D. Provenance** — `authored` | `generated` | `vendored` | `curated`.
Carrier: reserved directory names *inside* a unit — `src/`, `gen/`, `vendor/`, `data/` — plus `oak.artefacts[]` giving each non-`src` parcel a producer command (generated), a content digest (vendored), or a schema + licence marker (curated). **Does not split units.** It governs who may edit the bytes and what proves them correct.

**E. Assurance profile** — `critical` | `product` | `operational`.
Carrier: manifest `oak.assurance`; the gate runner selects a closed, named profile from it. **Does not split units.** Enforced additionally by a graph monotonicity rule (R6).

*Why these five are independent (dissociation, one pair each):* licence × contract — brand-reserved+internal (P6) coexists with mit+published (S4) and ogl+published; contract × assurance — terminal+product (P7) vs terminal+operational (P8) vs published+critical (S2); trigger × provenance — authored+`product-decision` (S3), generated+`upstream-spec` (P1), vendored+`vendor-drop` (P3), curated+`curation` (P5), and authored+`upstream-spec` (a hand-written correction layer) all occur; provenance × licence — vendored bytes may be `third-party` (fonts) or `ogl` (bulk curriculum data), generated bytes may be `mit` (types) or `ogl` (mined corpus).

## 3. The unit rule

> **Two file sets are separate units if and only if they differ in licence class, release contract, or change trigger. Otherwise they are one unit with several entry points.**

Explicitly **not** splitting criteria: file count or byte size; number of public symbols; fan-in ("imported everywhere"); consumer identity; execution rhythm (interactive vs commit-time vs scheduled); language or file type; "this part looks generic".

Corollaries:

- **Entry points absorb consumer differences.** Distinct consumers get distinct `exports`/`bin` entries with their own transitive-closure budget (R8), not distinct packages. Splitting on consumers multiplies release trains and directly inflates the multi-unit-commit rate.
- **Extraction rule.** An embedded sub-tree becomes a unit at the *second consumer*, or the moment it acquires a different licence, contract, or trigger — never on the argument that it is reusable in principle. Until then it must already be imported through a self-referencing specifier (`#store`, or the package's own name), so extraction is a directory move with no call-site rewrites.
- **Surface size triggers an entry-point partition, not a split.** A unit exporting a large symbol surface from `.` must partition its exports so consumers' dependency closures stay honest.
- **Two axes agreeing is the strongest split signal.** Where licence *and* trigger both say split (vendored fonts vs authored styles; upstream spec bytes vs generated types), the split is not negotiable. Where only one says split, it still splits, but it is the first place to look if the multi-unit-commit rate rises.

## 4. Carriers, layout, naming

**Manifest block** (strict schema, validated; the only place mutable policy lives):

```json
{
  "name": "@oak/curriculum-corpus",
  "license": "OGL-UK-3.0",
  "private": true,
  "oak": {
    "channel": "internal",
    "promise": "none",
    "trigger": "corpus-mine",
    "assurance": "product",
    "services": [],
    "artefacts": [
      { "path": "data/corpus", "provenance": "generated",
        "producer": "pnpm run mine", "trigger": "corpus-mine", "verify": "reproduce" }
    ],
    "entrypoints": [{ "export": ".", "closureBudget": 40 }]
  }
}
```

**Naming.** `@oak/<area>-<role>`; the directory basename equals the name suffix; the tier never appears in the name. Imports are always by package name or `#`-specifier — no relative path may cross a unit root, and no consumer may reach past a declared export.

**Layout.**

```
packages/                      channel: registry (self-contained tarballs)
  kernel/                      S1 + S2 — mit, critical, zero out-degree
  graph/                       S3 — entry points ./model ./traverse ./serialise
  curriculum-client/           S4 — sole holder of the curriculum credential
  curriculum-types/            generated from the spec snapshot, gen/ committed
  design-tokens/               S5 — src/ tokens + gen/ CSS
  search/                      S6
  obs-<vendor>/                S8
apps/                          channel: host; in-degree must be zero
  <product-app>/               promise: supported          P9a
  <demo-a>/  <demo-b>/         promise: demonstration      P9b
  mcp-curriculum/              promise: supported; embeds the widget build via dependency
internal/                      channel: none; in-repo consumers only
  curriculum-spec-snapshot/    vendor/, third-party, trigger upstream-spec     P1a
  curriculum-bulk/             vendor/+gen/, trigger upstream-bulk             P1b
  curriculum-corpus/           data/, ogl, trigger corpus-mine                 S7
  curriculum-curation/         data/, ogl, trigger curation                    P5
  search-contracts/            gen/, trigger search-contract                   P2
  widget/                      src/+gen/, trigger widget-build                 P11
  brand-assets/                brand-reserved, trigger brand-decision          P6
  webfonts-vendor/             vendor/, third-party, trigger vendor-drop       P3a
  ui-styles/                   mit, authored                                   P3b
  agent-tooling/               entry points ./cli ./hooks ./jobs               P4
  estate-checks/               trigger estate-policy                           P12
  build-config/                shared tsconfig/eslint presets
terminal/                      channel: none; in-degree must be zero
  study-<name>/                assurance: product                              P7
  ops-<name>/                  assurance: operational                          P8
```

Every tracked file maps to exactly one unit root; the only exceptions are a short, explicitly declared repo-root allow-list (`pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `turbo.json`, the policy file).

## 5. Enforcement

One unit, `internal/estate-checks`, owns all of it and exposes two entry points — `./hooks` (cheap subset, commit-time) and `./validators` (full set, CI). The rules, each a named module with its own failure message, are listed in `organisingRules`. Three read the manifest schema, four are computed from the resolved pnpm/turbo graph, three re-derive bytes (reproduce generated parcels, match vendor digests, validate curated data against its schema).

## 6. What this predicts, and how to falsify it

- The largest unit (S7) becomes five units, split by trigger and licence, not by size.
- **Falsifier 1:** today's multi-unit commit rate is 308/5900 ≈ 5.2%. If, a quarter after the trigger splits, it exceeds ~7%, or if any single trigger event routinely lands in two units, the trigger axis has been mis-valued and those units merge.
- **Falsifier 2:** any trigger value that cannot be bound to a detector within one quarter is deleted, and its units merge.
- **Falsifier 3:** if a real decision needs a sixth manifest field to explain it, an axis is missing. P12 already fires this (see its placement).
- **Falsifier 4:** if the one-licence-per-unit validator ever needs an exemption, the rule is wrong — not the unit.

**Migration order:** manifest block + validators in report-only mode first (visibility before enforcement), then the licence-forced splits, then the S7 trigger splits, then tier moves last (they are pure `git mv` and are the cheapest step, so they go last, not first).

organisingRules.name: Licence class
organisingRules.rule: Every unit declares exactly one licence class (mit | ogl | brand-reserved | third-party:<SPDX>). Files of two licence classes never share a unit; cross-class material is reached by dependency, never by copied bytes.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest `license` field + a LICENSE file at the unit root; validator R1 maps every tracked file to its unit and asserts a single class.

organisingRules.name: Release contract (channel)
organisingRules.rule: Who receives the unit's output: registry (packages/), runtime host (apps/), in-repo consumers only (internal/), or no-one — output is an effect or a result (terminal/). Differing channel splits units.
organisingRules.carrier: Tier directory — the ONLY axis the directory level encodes. Channel is in the path because it is stable and globbed on by every tool.

organisingRules.name: Release contract (promise)
organisingRules.rule: What is promised about the output: supported | demonstration | none. Differing promise splits units even at the same channel; a supported unit may never depend on a demonstration unit.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest `oak.promise`, plus graph rule R4. In the manifest, not the path, because a promise changes without the code moving (a demo gets promoted).

organisingRules.name: Change trigger
organisingRules.rule: The single named, observable event that causes a rewrite. Differing trigger splits units, because co-locating a 29x/yr refresh with a 7x/yr one drags every consumer of one through the other's release churn.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest `oak.trigger` (unit) and `oak.artefacts[].trigger` (parcel); the enum is declared once in a repo-level policy file, and each value is bound to a detector (schedule, webhook, upstream changelog, vendor release, named decision area). Unbindable values are deleted and their units merged.

organisingRules.name: Provenance
organisingRules.rule: Who writes the bytes: authored | generated | vendored | curated. Never splits a unit; it governs who may edit what and what proves it correct.
organisingRules.carrier: Reserved directory names INSIDE a unit — src/ gen/ vendor/ data/ — plus oak.artefacts[] carrying a producer command (generated), a content digest (vendored), or a schema + licence marker (curated).

organisingRules.name: Assurance profile
organisingRules.rule: Which closed, named gate profile runs: critical | product | operational. Never splits a unit; decoupled from channel so a non-shipping unit can carry product gates and a shipping-adjacent one cannot silently weaken.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest `oak.assurance` selects the gate profile in the turbo task graph.

organisingRules.name: R0 unit identity
organisingRules.rule: Two file sets are separate units iff licence, release contract, or trigger differs. Size, public-symbol count, fan-in, consumer identity, execution rhythm, language, and apparent genericness never split a unit.
organisingRules.carrier: One package.json per unit; validator asserts every tracked file resolves to exactly one unit root against a declared repo-root allow-list.

organisingRules.name: R1 name/path separation
organisingRules.rule: The path carries policy, the name carries identity. Directory basename equals the package name suffix; the tier never appears in the name, so promotion is a move plus a manifest edit and never touches a consumer import.
organisingRules.carrier: Name convention `@oak/<area>-<role>` + validator comparing basename to manifest name.

organisingRules.name: R2 entry points absorb consumers
organisingRules.rule: Distinct consumers get distinct exports/bin entries within one unit, not distinct units. No relative import may cross a unit root; no consumer may reach past a declared export.
organisingRules.carrier: package.json `exports`/`bin` + `oak.entrypoints[]`; deep-import ban enforced over resolved specifiers from the pnpm graph.

organisingRules.name: R3 extraction threshold
organisingRules.rule: An embedded sub-tree becomes a unit at the second consumer, or when it acquires a different licence, contract, or trigger — never on reusability in principle. Until then it is imported through a self-referencing specifier so extraction rewrites no call sites.
organisingRules.carrier: Enforced by an intra-unit import-direction check declared in `oak.entrypoints[]`, plus a graph check that fires when a second consumer appears.

organisingRules.name: R4 dependency direction
organisingRules.rule: apps/ and terminal/ units must have in-degree zero. A supported unit may not depend on a demonstration unit. A published unit may have no runtime or types dependency on an unpublished unit (devDependencies are permitted, and generated parcels are committed so the tarball is self-contained).
organisingRules.carrier: Derived from the resolved pnpm/turbo dependency graph.

organisingRules.name: R5 licence-crossing bytes
organisingRules.rule: Brand-reserved bytes may never be embedded in a published tarball; ogl content may never be embedded in an mit unit's published output. Cross-class material travels by dependency and is resolved at deploy time.
organisingRules.carrier: Graph rule keyed on licence class × channel, plus a pack-time file manifest check.

organisingRules.name: R6 assurance monotonicity
organisingRules.rule: No unit may declare a weaker assurance profile than any unit that depends on it. Operational assurance is therefore only reachable at in-degree zero.
organisingRules.carrier: Computed over the dependency graph from `oak.assurance` values.

organisingRules.name: R7 parcel locality and reproducibility
organisingRules.rule: A generated parcel lives in the unit whose script produces it, never in the unit that consumes it; the consumer depends on the producing unit and reads the output through its exports map. Every gen/ parcel must be byte-reproducible by its declared producer; every vendor/ parcel must match its recorded digest.
organisingRules.carrier: `oak.artefacts[].producer` / `.digest` + turbo `verify:gen` and `verify:vendor` tasks that re-run the producer and diff the tree.

organisingRules.name: R8 entry-point closure budget
organisingRules.rule: Each entry point declares a transitive-dependency budget, checked from the resolved graph — this is how a commit-time guard stays fast while sharing a unit with heavier code.
organisingRules.carrier: `oak.entrypoints[].closureBudget` evaluated against the per-export closure computed from the pnpm graph.

organisingRules.name: R9 one service per unit
organisingRules.rule: A unit declares at most one external service (terminal/ units may declare several but must declare all). Each service's refresh cadence and failure modes are then owned by exactly one unit.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest `oak.services[]`, validated against the policy file's service registry.

organisingRules.name: R10 single credential owner
organisingRules.rule: For each external service, exactly one unit — its client/adapter — may read the credential. Every other unit declares the service and obtains access through that adapter.
organisingRules.carrier: Static check that the service's credential env-var identifier appears only in the declaring adapter unit's src/.

probePlacements.placement: Two units, both declaring the same service and both depending on the credential-owning client (S4): `internal/curriculum-spec-snapshot` (vendor/ bytes, licence third-party:<upstream SPDX>, trigger upstream-spec, producer = the fetch script in-unit, digest-verified) and `internal/curriculum-bulk` (vendor/ payload + gen/ schemas, licence ogl, trigger upstream-bulk). Decided by the trigger axis (29/yr vs 7/yr — co-location would force 36 version bumps a year on consumers who care about one of them) with the licence axis agreeing. The shared credential is not a unit fact: it is `oak.services[]` on both plus R10 naming the client as sole reader.

Four units, one per event class, each in `internal/` with a gen/ parcel, an in-unit producer script, and a distinct `oak.trigger` (upstream-spec, search-contract, upstream-bulk, corpus-mine). Each carries a `verify:gen` task that re-runs the producer and asserts a clean tree. Decided purely by the trigger axis; provenance (all generated) is identical and splits nothing.

Two units: `internal/webfonts-vendor` (vendor/ only, licence third-party:<OFL or equivalent>, trigger vendor-drop, digest-verified, hand-edit rejected at commit time) and `internal/ui-styles` (src/, mit, trigger product-decision), the latter depending on the former. Both the licence axis and the trigger axis independently demand the split, which is the strongest signal the design produces.

One unit, `internal/agent-tooling`, with three entry points: `./cli` (bin), `./hooks` (commit-time guards), `./jobs` (scheduled). Licence, contract, and trigger are identical across the three, so R0 keeps them together; R2 gives each consumer its own export and R8 gives the hooks entry point a tight closure budget so the interactive and scheduled surfaces cannot slow the commit path. Execution rhythm is explicitly not a splitting criterion.

Own unit, `internal/curriculum-curation`: content in data/, provenance curated, licence ogl, trigger curation, assurance product (a schema validates the data at build). Decided by the licence axis alone — hand-curation would otherwise sit happily beside the code it feeds. Consumers depend on the package; no consumer copies the bytes (R5).

Own unit, `internal/brand-assets`: a manifest plus a data/ parcel, no src/. Licence brand-reserved, trigger brand-decision, promise none. R5 is the operative rule: no published tarball may embed these bytes, so packages/ units may not depend on it at all and apps/ resolve it at deploy time.

`terminal/study-<name>`: channel terminal (in-degree zero enforced by R4, so nothing shipped can ever come to depend on study code), `oak.assurance: product` (the same gate profile as product code), promise none. This is the case that proves channel and assurance must be separate axes.

`terminal/ops-<name>`: channel terminal, `oak.assurance: operational`, `oak.services[]` listing every live system touched, plus an `oak.effects` marker distinguishing live-read from live-write. R6 (assurance monotonicity) means operational assurance is only legal at in-degree zero, so relaxed gates can never leak into anything shipped. Same tier as P7, different assurance — the dissociation pair.

Two units in `apps/`, identical on licence, channel, provenance and trigger, split solely on `oak.promise`: `supported` vs `demonstration`. R4 then forbids the supported app depending on anything demonstration-classed, and the promise value selects the release gate (changelog, deprecation policy and rollback path for supported; none for the demo, which must be marked as such in-product). Shared structure is shared by depending on the same packages/ units, never by merging the apps.

Not yet a unit. It stays inside its host pipeline as its own entry point (`#store`, or an export on the host package), with an import-direction check forbidding it from importing the product-specific modules, so extraction later is a directory move with no call-site rewrites. R3 fires the extraction the moment a second consumer appears or the machinery acquires a different contract or trigger — and if S6's retrieval library is the consumer that needs it, that is the second consumer and extraction fires now. 'Reusable in principle' is explicitly not a reason to extract.

Two units. `internal/widget` owns both src/ (authored, trigger product-decision) and gen/ (the built bundle, trigger widget-build, ~18x/yr, reproducible from the in-unit producer). The serving unit (`apps/mcp-curriculum`) depends on the widget package and reads the bundle through its `./embed` export, wired by turbo `dependsOn: ["^build"]`. R7 is the operative rule and it kills the classic failure here — a build output checked into the consumer's public/ directory, where nobody can prove which source produced it.

One unit, `internal/estate-checks`, with two entry points — `./hooks` (commit-time) and `./validators` (CI) — separated from `internal/agent-tooling` by trigger (`estate-policy` vs `agent-workflow`), never by consumer. R8 gives the hooks export a tight closure budget so the heavy validator dependencies cannot reach the commit path. FORCED: 'different failure modes' — a local guard that must fail open under a missing toolchain versus a CI validator that must fail closed — has no carrier among the five axes. I attach it as an entry-point-level `failure: open|closed` field, which is an admitted patch, not a classification. Falsifier 3 fires here: either failure semantics earns a sixth axis, or this field must be shown to be derivable from assurance × channel of the consumer.

Not its own unit. It lives in `packages/kernel` alongside S2 as the `.` export: mit, authored, trigger product-decision, `oak.assurance: critical`, out-degree zero. Fan-in is explicitly not a splitting criterion — a package per 100-line primitive buys a release train and a version-churn amplifier across every consumer, and buys nothing else. Published because published units may not expose types from unpublished ones (R4) and this error type appears in S4's public surface.

`packages/kernel`, `./path` export. Same licence, contract and trigger as S1, so R0 says one unit. Its security criticality is carried by `oak.assurance: critical` on the unit (cheap, because the unit is tiny) plus a required regression test named to the originating incident — not by a directory and not by a package boundary. Security criticality is a gate fact, not a boundary fact.

`packages/graph`, one unit. Size and a ~74-symbol surface split nothing; instead the surface triggers an entry-point partition (`./model`, `./traverse`, `./serialise`) under R2 and R8, so a consumer that only reads the model does not drag the serialiser's closure. If a partition later acquires its own trigger or contract, R3 promotes it to a unit at that point and not before.

`packages/curriculum-client`: mit, promise supported, `oak.services: [curriculum-platform]`, and under R10 the sole reader of that service's credential in the estate. It depends on `packages/curriculum-types` (published, gen/ committed so the tarball is self-contained) which in turn has a devDependency on `internal/curriculum-spec-snapshot` — permitted by R4 because it is build-time only. Its trigger is upstream-spec, which is simply true: a typed client for an external service changes when that service's spec changes.

One unit, `packages/design-tokens`: src/ token sources (authored, trigger product-decision) plus gen/ CSS (generated, same trigger, producer in-unit, reproduced in CI).
