Size, mixed provenance, differing rhythms and differing failure modes are NOT grounds. Where no ground fires, fewer units is the default.
organisingRules.carrier: Validator separation-grounds, which recomputes all five grounds from the manifests and the dependency graph

organisingRules.name: Article VI — Reserved powers
organisingRules.rule: Module layout, internal naming, test organisation and framework choice inside a unit are reserved to that unit. No federal check may inspect a unit's interior beyond the enumerated articles.
organisingRules.carrier: charter/articles/ + the bidirectional rule index (every validator must cite the article it enforces, so an interior-inspecting check has nowhere to attach)

organisingRules.name: Article VII — The exterior is the exports map
organisingRules.rule: A unit's importable surface is exactly its declared exports (subpaths permitted, wildcard escapes forbidden). Deep imports are void. This is what makes reserved powers real and what narrows blast radius for large exteriors.
organisingRules.carrier: package.json exports map + generated restricted-paths lint config + CI graph check

organisingRules.name: Article VIII — Capability is granted by the depended-upon
organisingRules.rule: Each unit enumerates who may import it via allowedDependents (default *). A depender never claims access; the depended-upon grants it. This is the unit's reserved power to fence itself beyond the federal floor.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest allowedDependents field + graph validator checking every edge against the target's grant

organisingRules.name: Article IX — Assurance monotonicity (federal floor, unwaivable)
organisingRules.rule: An edge A→B is legal only when B's assurance level is at or above A's in the declared order. Product code therefore cannot reach operational or ungated code by construction, with nothing declared per-pair.
organisingRules.carrier: charter/gates.json declared order + graph validator assurance-monotone + acyclicity check

organisingRules.name: Article X — Producer edges (writing into another unit)
organisingRules.rule: A unit may write into another unit's tree only where the receiving unit names the producer. Producer declares produces:[{into,trigger}]; receiver declares generated/<region>/producedBy. Unmatched pairs fail. Producer edges join the dependency graph for blast-radius purposes.
organisingRules.carrier: Paired manifest declarations + validator producer-grant-match + per-region regeneration idempotence

organisingRules.name: Article XI — Generated output lives with the shipper
organisingRules.rule: Machine-produced output lives inside the unit that ships or serves it; where several units consume it, it lives with its producer and is imported through the exports map.
organisingRules.carrier: Placement rule checked by validator generated-region-ownership (every generated region has exactly one declared producer and at least one declared consumer)

organisingRules.name: Article XII — The exterior is a checked-in artefact
organisingRules.rule: Every unit carries generated/api.json, refreshed by its gate. A change to a unit's exterior cannot happen silently: it appears as a diff hunk, and the guard prints the transitive dependent set beside it.
organisingRules.carrier: generated/api.json + CI freshness check + PR guard that derives dependents from the dependency graph

organisingRules.name: Article XIII — Compelled extraction at the second consumer
organisingRules.rule: Machinery embedded in a host unit stays there while it has one consumer. At the second consumer the deep-import prohibition forces a dated choice: extract to its own unit, or widen the host's exterior. If the second consumer belongs to a different domain, extract.
organisingRules.carrier: Deep-import prohibition + dependency graph + duplication and co-change signals in index/pressure.json

organisingRules.name: Article XIV — No unchecked rule (void for vagueness)
organisingRules.rule: A manifest field with no validator is void: it may not be relied on and CI flags it. Every validator names its article; every article names its validator; the index is generated from both directions and checked. The category 'rules that exist only as good intentions' is empty by construction.
organisingRules.carrier: Generated charter/index.json + validator no-orphan-rules (both directions) + manifest schema completeness check

organisingRules.name: Article XV — No law in hidden surfaces
organisingRules.rule: No rule may live only in a dot-directory or a tool config. Any config expressing a rule is generated from charter/ and its freshness is checked, so the discoverable artefacts are always the complete law.
organisingRules.carrier: Generated tool configs (lint, hooks, CI, CODEOWNERS, schedules) + validator config-freshness

organisingRules.name: Article XVI — Entry points are declared, invocation surfaces are generated
organisingRules.rule: Every executable entry point is declared with its invocation surface (interactive | hook | schedule | ci). Hook, schedule and CI configuration is generated from those declarations, so an undeclared scheduled job or hook cannot exist and a declared one cannot be unwired.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest entrypoints[].invokedBy + generated hook/cron/CI config + bidirectional validator entrypoint-wiring

organisingRules.name: Article XVII — Stewardship is a reference, not a classification
organisingRules.rule: Every unit names at least one accountable human steward and the agent classes permitted to write it. It points at a party; it does not partition the estate, so it is not one of the four classifications.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest stewards field + generated CODEOWNERS + validator every-unit-has-a-steward

organisingRules.name: Article XVIII — The pressure ledger
organisingRules.rule: A scheduled job publishes co-change frequency per unit pair, exterior symbol counts, capture staleness and dependent counts. Threshold crossings raise findings, never blocks: declare the coupling, merge the pair, or split the unit. This is how the constitution notices it is wrong.
organisingRules.carrier: Generated index/pressure.json from git co-change statistics, api snapshots and capture locks; declared as a scheduled entry point

organisingRules.name: Article XIX — Amendment classes and ratification
organisingRules.rule: Ordinary (add, split, merge or re-classify a unit): manifest edits only, ratified by the unit steward. Schema (add or change a manifest field): must ship a default leaving every unit valid, a validator, and a backfill in one PR, ratified by the estate steward. Charter (separation test, directory grammar, one-star rule, assurance order): ADR plus migration script plus updated validators in the same commit, ratified by the named owner — so no window exists where law and enforcement disagree.
organisingRules.carrier: charter/amendments.json + PR check requiring an article citation and amendment class for any change under charter/

organisingRules.name: Article XX — Moves ledger
organisingRules.rule: Retired unit names map to their successors and may never be reused. Stale references, including stale machine memory, always resolve to a current answer or an explicit withdrawal.
organisingRules.carrier: charter/moves.json + validator no-name-reuse + resolver used by the index

organisingRules.name: Article XXI — Machine cost budgets
organisingRules.rule: Find a unit ≤1 open (0 when the name is known); learn its law ≤1 open; learn its exterior ≤1 open; decide editability 0 opens (the path segment decides); learn what to run 0 opens (the verify command is uniform). The budgets are targets; the preconditions are enforced.
organisingRules.carrier: index/units.json freshness, api-snapshot presence, reserved-name conformance, name/path identity, uniform per-unit verify script — each with its own validator

probePlacements.probe: P1 — interface-spec snapshot and bulk dataset from the same external service, different schedules and mechanisms
probePlacements.placement: Two units, compelled by the egress ground (C2), not by the schedule difference: packages/upstream-api-spec/captured/ (egress per the spec's own terms; capture declaration naming endpoint, mechanism, cadence, checksum) and packages/curriculum-bulk-data/captured/ (egress content-open, its own capture declaration). Differing cadence and mechanism are per-source fields inside the provenance block, never a ground for splitting on their own — had the two shared release terms and consumers they would have been one unit with two captured regions. Consumers reach each through the exports map; staleness surfaces in the pressure ledger.

probePlacements.probe: P2 — four collections of machine-regenerated artefacts, each rebuilt on a different event class
probePlacements.placement: Not four units: four generated/<collection>/ regions, each placed in the unit that ships or consumes it (Article XI), each declaring producedBy and trigger (spec-change | token-change | commit | schedule). Provenance is intra-unit, so nothing is compelled to move. Enforcement is per region: regeneration idempotence in CI, and Article XVI's bidirectional wiring check so a declared trigger must correspond to a real generated automation entry and vice versa.

probePlacements.probe: P3 — byte-preserved vendor files alongside freely changing hand-written styling
probePlacements.placement: ONE unit. vendor/ and src/ sit side by side; the vendor region declares upstream coordinate, version and checksum, so a hand-edit fails the checksum validator while src/ changes freely. Egress does not compel a split here because the estate does not release the vendored bytes — it passes them through under their upstream term (the enumerated vendor exception in C2), and the validator only asserts the unit's own term is no broader than the term passed through.

probePlacements.probe: P4 — one tooling area serving interactive commands, commit-time guards and scheduled jobs
probePlacements.placement: ONE unit with exterior promise `operator` and assurance `operational`, declaring each entry point with its invokedBy surface (interactive | hook | schedule). Differing rhythms are not one of the five separation grounds. The hook and schedule configuration is generated from those declarations, so each consumer is discoverable from a single manifest read and cannot drift. Caveat with teeth: any entry point that acts on live systems must move to the operations unit, because assurance then differs (ground 3) — see P8.

probePlacements.probe: P5 — hand-curated reference data under a content licence different from surrounding code
probePlacements.placement: Own unit, compelled by the egress ground alone: packages/<domain>-reference-data/ with the curation in data/ (authored provenance, hand-editable), egress content-open, a matching LICENSE, gate `data` (schema and licence-coverage checks). Code units depend on it by package name; the egress compatibility matrix stops a code-open published unit from redistributing it under the wrong term.

probePlacements.probe: P6 — trademark image assets whose reuse terms differ from everything else
probePlacements.placement: Own unit packages/brand-assets/ with the files in assets/, egress `reserved`, gate `assets` (format, size, naming). allowedDependents stays open so the estate may use them, but the egress closure check forbids any public-semver, code-open unit from bundling them — the wrong outcome fails CI rather than shipping. Compelled by the egress ground, exactly as P5, which is the point: one ground, two very different-looking cases.

probePlacements.probe: P7 — research-study evidence code, quality-gated like product but never shipped
probePlacements.placement: Own unit(s), compelled by the exterior-promise ground: assurance `evidence` (the same checks as product, at the same level in the declared order), exterior estate-internal, never published. It may depend on product units (monotonicity permits depending upward); product units may not depend on it, which the unit enforces itself via allowedDependents fencing rather than by any federal rule. This is the cell that exists only because assurance and promise are independent axes.

probePlacements.probe: P8 — operational scripts running against live systems, outside the product gates
probePlacements.placement: Own unit packages/live-operations/, compelled by the assurance ground: gate `operational` (below product in the declared order), exterior `operator`. Article IX then forbids every product unit from importing it with nothing declared per-pair. Entry points declare invokedBy plus a target environment, and a validator requires each live-acting entry point to declare its environment and its dry-run affordance — a safety property with a check, therefore lawful under Article XIV rather than a good intention.

probePlacements.probe: P9 — deployed product application and near-identical demonstration application
probePlacements.placement: Two units identical on provenance, egress and assurance, differing on exactly one field: exterior `product-supported` versus `product-demonstration`. That single field decides the support and deprecation promise and how CI treats a breaking change. Structural sameness is explicitly blessed (structure is reserved). Both are sinks: allowedDependents is empty, so no unit may import an application; the demo may depend on shared libraries, never the product app.

probePlacements.probe: P10 — generic machinery reusable against any similar datastore, embedded in a product-specific pipeline
probePlacements.placement: Stays in the interior of its host unit today: with one consumer no ground fires, and premature extraction spends a manifest, a licence, a README and a snapshot for nothing. The deep-import prohibition converts 'should we extract?' into a forced, dated moment — the second consumer physically cannot reach the interior, so it must extract to packages/<datastore>-retrieval/ (the S6 shape) or the host must widen its exterior; if the second consumer sits in another domain, extract. Stated silence: the charter cannot detect genericity before that moment; the pressure ledger's duplication and co-change signals are the only early, advisory warning.

probePlacements.probe: P11 — browser-built interactive widget whose built output is embedded and served by a different unit
probePlacements.placement: Two units joined by a declared producer edge. packages/<widget>/ holds the source (src/, gate product, exterior estate-internal) and declares produces:[{into: packages/<host>/generated/<widget>/, trigger: widget-source-change}]; the host declares that region with producedBy: <widget>. The grant comes from the receiver, the pair must match, and the region must regenerate idempotently. The output lives in the host because the host ships it (Article XI), and the producer edge puts 'the host must rebuild' into the blast radius the graph reports. This is the case that justifies producer edges existing at all.

probePlacements.probe: P12 — commit-hook guard code and repo-state validator code, same rhythm, different consumers and failure modes
probePlacements.placement: ONE unit with two enumerated entry-point groups (invokedBy: hook and invokedBy: ci). No ground fires: same provenance, same egress, same assurance, same exterior promise. The charter deliberately refuses to split on differing failure modes, because failure mode has no carrier a newcomer can read off an artefact, and an undiscoverable rule is a defect under the binding constraint. The difference that IS discoverable — which surface invokes which entry point — is carried by the entrypoints declaration and by the hook and CI configs generated from it.

probePlacements.probe: S1 — error-handling primitive, tiny, zero dependencies, imported nearly everywhere
probePlacements.placement: Own unit (nothing can host it without every importer deep-importing), zero dependencies, allowedDependents *, gate product, exterior estate-internal. Its foundation status is derived from the graph (high in-degree, zero out-degree), not declared, and derived status attracts an automatic consequence: any change to generated/api.json prints the full transitive dependent set on the PR. The most expensive unit to change is the one whose cost is shown before the change lands.

probePlacements.probe: S2 — path-safety utility born from a security incident, small, security-critical
probePlacements.placement: Own unit, compelled by the assurance ground even though it is tiny and adjacent to S1: gate `product-security` sits above `product` in the declared order, so merging it into S1 would be illegal. Zero dependencies; allowedDependents *; monotonicity lets everything depend on it and lets it depend on nothing weaker. The charter answers 'should these two tiny utilities be one unit?' with a principled, citable no.

probePlacements.probe: S3 — large graph-data library exposing ~74 public symbols
probePlacements.placement: ONE unit. Size is not a separation ground. Its exterior is organised into declared subpath exports so consumers' blast radius narrows to the subpath they import rather than the whole library. Exterior symbol count appears in the pressure ledger as a signal, never a violation: the ledger argues for a split, the charter never compels one on size.

probePlacements.probe: S4 — typed client for the external curriculum service, published publicly
probePlacements.placement: Own unit, compelled out of S7 by the exterior-promise ground: exterior public-semver, egress code-open, publishConfig present. generated/api.json is release-binding — a diff to it forces a major. The egress closure check forbids any dependency on internal or reserved units, so it cannot silently ship brand assets or estate-only data. Its generated types come from the captured spec unit (P1) through a normal declared dependency.

probePlacements.probe: S5 — design-token pipeline whose output is generated CSS consumed by several surfaces
probePlacements.placement: ONE unit: src/ holds the pipeline, generated/ holds the CSS and token artefacts, and the exports map exposes them by subpath. Because there are several consumers, the output stays with the producer and is imported (Article XI) — the deliberate contrast with P11, where a single shipping host owns the output. Consumers appear as ordinary graph edges, so a token change reports its blast radius without any special coupling declaration.

probePlacements.probe: S6 — search-retrieval library over a commodity datastore
probePlacements.placement: Own unit, exterior estate-internal (promotable to public-semver later by editing one field, with no file moves), gate product, allowedDependents *. It is the shape P10 extracts into, and the pairing is the charter's illustration that the same design both tolerates embedded machinery today and names its destination for tomorrow.

probePlacements.probe: S7 — the estate's largest unit: codegen pipeline mixing spec-fetch, generated types, corpus mining and hand curation
probePlacements.placement: Stays ONE unit for its mixed-provenance interior — captured/ (the spec), generated/ (the types), src/ (the miner), data/ (curation) — minus exactly two compelled departures: the published typed client (S4, exterior-promise ground) and any hand-curated corpus carrying a different release term (P5-shaped, egress ground); the captured spec leaves too if its term differs (P1). Everything else is reserved to the unit. The charter's verdict on the biggest thing in the estate is: bigness is lawful, mixed provenance is lawful, mixed promises and mixed release terms are not — and here are the two slices that must leave, with the article cited for each.

probePlacements.probe: S8 — observability adapter for a commodity vendor
probePlacements.placement: ONE unit, unremarkable and deliberately so: exterior estate-internal, gate product, egress code-open, allowedDependents *. Worth stating because it demonstrates the monotonicity law's asymmetry — operational units (P8) may import it, since depending upward in assurance is always permitted, while it may never import them.

result.notes:
FILES READ: zero. I made no tool calls other than this one — no Read, no Bash, no Grep, no glob, no WebFetch. I opened no repository file, no dot-directory, no Markdown, no worktree, no PR body and no git log. Full disclosure of a boundary I did not control: the harness pre-injected CLAUDE.md's text and the filenames under .claude/rules/ into my context window before my turn began, along with a MEMORY.md index and a git-status snapshot. I did not request, read or use any of it as design input, and I have quarantined it — the charter above is derived only from the task statement's estate facts (file count, commit rates, workforce, growth) and the probe set. If your protocol counts pre-injected context as reading, this run is compromised on that technicality and not on any act of mine; nothing in the design depends on it.

QUESTIONS THIS TASK SHOULD HAVE ASKED AND DID NOT:

1. WHO RATIFIES, AND WHAT IS THE QUORUM. This is the omission that matters most given the frame. The task enumerates carriers (directory, name, manifest field, enforcement rule, dependency graph) and questions (blast radius, egress, cost) but never asks who holds the amending power. Every rule I wrote presupposes an authority competent to enact it, a party who may amend it, and a rule about what a machine collaborator may change unilaterally versus what needs a human. In an estate that is mostly machine collaborators under human ownership, that is not a footnote — it is the difference between a charter and a suggestion. I answered it anyway (Article XIX: three amendment classes, three named ratifiers, validators shipped in the same commit as the law they enforce), but I answered it unprompted and therefore ungrounded in this estate's actual ownership model. If the parent has that model, Article XIX is the clause to re-true first.

2. WHAT IS THE ADOPTION PATH, AND WHAT MAY BREAK ON THE WAY. The task asks for a target organisation with no transition constraint, for an estate taking ~5,900 commits a year. A charter that cannot be adopted incrementally is a charter that never binds. The natural staging — declare manifests first (no moves), then the validators, then the compelled separations one ground at a time, with the egress ground first because it carries legal exposure — falls out of the design, but the task never asked for it and I have no basis for sequencing against real branch traffic.

3. WHAT DOES THE PRESENT ARRANGEMENT COST TODAY. No baseline was given for any of the quantities the design is supposed to improve: how many units exist now, how many opens a machine currently spends to find one, how often a wrong import actually lands. Article XXI states cost budgets, and I can enforce their preconditions, but 'better' is unfalsifiable without a before-measurement. A design asked to optimise machine cost should have been given the current cost.

TWO DESIGN POSITIONS WORTH FLAGGING TO THE PARENT AS CONTESTABLE, since both are places a reasonable reviewer would push:
- P12 is placed as ONE unit. Differing failure modes (a broken hook stops every commit; a broken validator only fails CI) is a real operational difference, and the charter refuses it as a separation ground purely because it has no carrier a newcomer can read off an artefact. That refusal is forced by the binding constraint, not by taste. If someone can name a discoverable carrier for operational criticality, the ground should be added by schema amendment.
- Four classifications is a claim of minimality, not a proof. The cells the probes occupy establish pairwise independence (P7 and P8 separate assurance from promise; P5 and P6 separate egress from everything; P3 keeps provenance intra-unit), but a fifth axis could still be lurking under what I currently treat as reserved interior. Article XVIII's pressure ledger is the instrument that would expose it, which is why it is in the charter rather than in a backlog.

walkers.persona: A polymath urban historian turned city planner, rebuilding a city after an earthquake. You have seen what survives such rebuilds: street grids outlive buildings, zoning outlives councils, and the decisions people regret are the ones that preserved a familiar shape because it was familiar. You write in decisions and regrets — what you kept, what you razed, and what it cost to know the difference.

result.design:
# The Rebuilt Estate: an organisational proposal

Written as a planner walks a city after the earthquake: first the questions any plan must answer, then the registers the plan rests on, then the map, then what was kept, what was razed, and what it cost to know the difference.

## I. The questions this design answers

1. **What makes two bodies of code separate units?** Not habit, not file count, not change frequency. Two things are separate units if and only if they differ on at least one of five independent registers: the promise they make (and to whom), who has authority over their bytes, what event regenerates them, their dependency altitude, or their rights regime.
2. **Where does a unit live?** Address = zone, then altitude. The zone (top-level directory) carries the promise; the tier below carries the altitude.
3. **What is a unit called?** Its name is an address, not a description: `@oaknational/<basename>`, basename identical to its directory, no zone in the name, no org echo.
4. **How do units exchange artefacts?** Only along declared graph edges — a workspace dependency or a build-task dependency. Never a committed copy, never a hand-maintained list of "files over there that hash into my build".
5. **How is any of this enforced?** Every rule names a mechanical carrier: a directory convention the dependency-cruiser reads, a manifest field a validator recomputes, a build-graph declaration whose outputs are disjoint. A rule with no carrier is a wish, and wishes do not survive earthquakes.

## II. The five registers (the minimal classification set)

**A. Promise (zoning).** Who consumes this, and what do we owe them? Five zones: *product* (shipped, supported), *exhibit* (product-shaped, shown, not supported), *library* (imported by other units; its gates travel with its consumers), *instrument* (operator- and agent-facing tools run against live systems), *evidence* (research code, quality-gated, never shipped, never depended on).

**B. Byte authority (provenance).** Who may change these bytes? Three classes: *hand-written*, *machine-generated* (a named task is the sole writer), *vendor-preserved* (byte-frozen third-party material; a refresh task is the sole writer, a checksum validator the witness). Classes never mix in one directory. Any zone can contain all three.

**C. Regeneration event.** Every generated or refreshed parcel names the one event class that rebuilds it — upstream-spec change, bulk-data refresh, token-source edit, release cut. One event, one task, one disjoint output glob. Two parcels from the *same* external service still split if their events differ; shared origin is not a register.

**D. Altitude.** Inside the library zone, dependencies flow only downhill: `core` (near-zero-dependency primitives) → `libs` (domain libraries and single-vendor adapters, vendor clients as peers) → `sdks` (published clients of external services, versioned, licence-carrying) → applications. A "core" package that imports a vendor library is mis-shelved, whatever its size.

**E. Rights.** One unit, one rights regime. Code under MIT, curriculum content under OGL, brand artwork reserved — the moment a file tree's reuse terms differ from its surroundings, that tree becomes its own unit with its own `license` field and licence file. Rights boundaries are the one register that *forces* a split regardless of every other consideration.

Deliberately **not** a register: change rhythm. Splitting by "these change together" is the familiar street people rebuild because they remember it, and it is the one they regret: rhythm is an artefact of this year's roadmap, and units drawn on it dissolve the moment priorities shift. Rhythm may inform *scheduling*; it never draws a boundary.

## III. The map

```text
apps/          product zone — deployed, supported (MCP HTTP service; each app one unit)
demos/         exhibit zone — product-shaped, no support promise
packages/
  core/        altitude 0 — result, safe-path, type-helpers, env, observability-contracts…
  libs/        altitude 1 — graph library, search-retrieval, logger, vendor adapters (sentry, posthog)
  sdks/        altitude 2 — published external-service clients (curriculum SDK)
  data/        hand-curated reference data whose rights differ from code (OGL parcels)
  design/      the design estate: token sources → generated CSS; system; reserved-rights assets;
               framework adapters (react, ink); vendor-preserved import snapshots under vendor/
tools/         instrument zone — the old monolithic tooling block, subdivided by consumer:
  cli/           interactive operator commands (includes live-system operations)
  guards/        commit-time hooks — fast, fail-closed on their own scope
  validators/    repo-state validators — recompute, never merely record
  jobs/          scheduled work
  generators/    spec-fetch and codegen drivers (the machinery, not the artefacts)
bootstrap/     the one parcel that must run before dependencies exist — tiny, linted, imports nothing
research/      evidence zone — workspace members so the gates run; nothing imports them
```

Within any unit, provenance parcels: `src/` hand-written, `generated/<event>/` machine-written by exactly one task, `vendor/<name>@<date>/` byte-frozen.

## IV. Decisions and regrets

**Kept: the street grid.** The surveyed estate already zones by promise — `apps/`, `demos/`, `research/`, and a core/libs/sdks/design terracing under `packages/`. Street grids outlive buildings; this one is sound and I kept it almost whole. The workspace file even annotates *why* demos are registered — zoning with reasons attached. Kept, and made law (carrier: depcruise zone rules — product never imports exhibit, instrument, or evidence; nothing imports evidence or apps).

**Kept: the authored register.** The workspace file enumerates members explicitly, path by path — except one glob, `packages/design/*`, and precisely there the survey found a dated snapshot directory sitting ambiguously inside the glob's reach. The lesson generalises: an inferred register admits tenants nobody chose. Razed the glob; every member is now enumerated. Zoning is authored, not discovered.

**Razed: the monolithic tooling block.** One tooling workspace currently holds interactive CLIs, commit-time guards, repo validators, scheduled analysis workflows, encoding checks, secret scans — dozens of consumers on different rhythms, one manifest with a hundred-line script surface mirrored again at the root. It grew because "tooling" felt like a category. It is a zone, not a unit. Subdivided by consumer and failure mode; shared machinery descends to `packages/` at its second consumer. Cost of knowing: the root manifest's script block — two screens of one-by-one validator invocations — is the tell. When the estate's front door must enumerate every room, the rooms are in the wrong building.

**Razed: committed copies and hand-maintained hash legs.** The build config carries long apologetic comments explaining which *other* unit's files must hash into this unit's build because assets are copied across at build time — and records a production incident where a cached artefact baked under a missing variable was silently replayed. That is a building resting on a neighbour's wall, with a note taped to it. Artefacts now cross units only as graph edges (workspace dep or task `dependsOn`/`outputs`); CI proves builds leave the tree clean. The widget whose built output another unit serves becomes a buildable unit consumed through the graph, not an embedded copy.

**Razed: descriptive street names.** `@oaknational/oak-design-tokens` echoes the org; a package named `search-cli` lives at `oak-search-cli`. Names are addresses: basename equals suffix, no `oak-` echo under the `@oaknational` scope, no zone in the name.

**Regret acknowledged, not repeated: the codegen citadel.** The estate's largest unit fuses spec-fetching machinery, a vendor-preserved schema snapshot, generated types, corpus mining, and hand curation — fourteen export subpaths, a building so large it has districts. It was cheap to extend and is now expensive to reason about. Under the registers it dissolves along its own seams (see S7). The five registers exist substantially because this building taught me what happens without them.

**Kept: proportional gates, universally.** Every unit carries lint, type-check, test; product adds e2e/a11y/mutation; instruments add built-form smokes; evidence keeps full static gates. What I refused to rebuild: any parcel *outside* the gates. Ungated operational scripts against live systems are the unreinforced masonry of a code estate — the survey shows this estate already half-knows it (a separate lint config exists solely to reach root scripts the workspaces can't). One exception is named rather than smuggled: `bootstrap/` may not import from the workspace because it runs before installation — a constraint of physics, not a waiver of inspection.

organisingRules.name: Zone by promise
organisingRules.rule: Top-level directory states who consumes the unit and what is owed them: apps/ product (shipped, supported), demos/ exhibit (product-shaped, unsupported), packages/ library, tools/ instrument (operator/agent-facing), research/ evidence (gated, never shipped), bootstrap/ pre-install parcel. Product never imports exhibit, instrument, or evidence; nothing imports evidence or apps.
organisingRules.carrier: Top-level directory as the zone marker; dependency-cruiser ruleset keyed on path prefixes enforcing the inter-zone import matrix (already a root gate in this estate); workspace membership for every zone so gates reach it.

organisingRules.name: Provenance parcels never mix
organisingRules.rule: Every file is hand-written, machine-generated, or vendor-preserved, and the three classes never share a directory. generated/<event>/ is written only by its owning task; vendor/<name>@<date>/ is byte-frozen between refresh events and never hand-edited.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory-name convention (generated/, vendor/) + turbo task `outputs` globs as the sole-writer declaration + a checksum-recomputing validator over vendor parcels + lint/pre-commit guard rejecting hand edits inside either class.

organisingRules.name: One event, one generator
organisingRules.rule: Each generated or refreshed parcel is owned by exactly one build-graph task named for the event class that rebuilds it (spec-change, bulk-refresh, token-edit, release-cut). Parcels with different regeneration events never share a task or an output glob, even when sourced from the same external service.
organisingRules.carrier: turbo.json: one named task per event with disjoint `outputs`; manifest script names carry the event name; cache keys therefore invalidate per event.

organisingRules.name: Altitude flows downhill
organisingRules.rule: packages/core holds near-zero-dependency primitives; packages/libs holds domain libraries and single-vendor adapters (vendor client as peerDependency); packages/sdks holds published clients of external services; apps sit on top. Imports only point down; a core package acquiring a vendor dependency must move to libs.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory tier (core/libs/sdks) + depcruise boundary rules derived from the tier prefix + the existing boundary validator; peerDependencies field as the vendor-coupling marker.

organisingRules.name: Rights force a parcel
organisingRules.rule: A file tree whose licence or reuse terms differ from its surroundings is its own workspace unit carrying its own license manifest field and licence file — code MIT, curated content OGL, brand artwork reserved. One unit has exactly one rights regime; no other register can override this split.
organisingRules.carrier: package.json `license` field + LICENCES file at unit root + a manifest-walking validator that forbids mixed-rights file trees inside a single unit; publish steps copy the licence file into the artefact.

organisingRules.name: Split on register difference, never on rhythm
organisingRules.rule: Two bodies of code are separate units iff they differ on promise, provenance, event, altitude, or rights. Shared change frequency never merges them; differing change frequency never splits them. Generic machinery embedded in a specific pipeline stays embedded behind a named internal seam until its second consumer appears, then descends one altitude.
organisingRules.carrier: Unit-boundary review checklist naming the five registers + depcruise intra-package rule guarding the internal seam + the dependency graph itself revealing the second consumer (depcruise report).

organisingRules.name: Artefacts cross units only as graph edges
organisingRules.rule: A unit consumes another unit's output via workspace dependency or declared task dependsOn/outputs — never via build-time file copies into its own tree, committed duplicates, or hand-maintained lists of foreign files hashed into its cache key.
organisingRules.carrier: turbo dependsOn + outputs as the only sanctioned transport; CI check that build tasks leave `git status` clean outside declared outputs; removal of cross-unit input globs from turbo.json.

organisingRules.name: The zoning register is authored
organisingRules.rule: Every workspace member is enumerated by explicit path in pnpm-workspace.yaml with a comment stating why unusual members are registered. No globs: membership is a decision, not a discovery.
organisingRules.carrier: pnpm-workspace.yaml explicit member list + a validator failing on glob patterns in the packages list.

organisingRules.name: Names are addresses
organisingRules.rule: Package name is @oaknational/<basename>; the directory basename equals the name suffix exactly; no oak- echo under the @oaknational scope; the zone never appears in the name (moving a unit between zones must not rename it).
organisingRules.carrier: Naming convention enforced by a manifest-walking identity validator comparing name suffix to directory basename and rejecting scope echoes.

organisingRules.name: Gates proportional to promise, never absent
organisingRules.rule: Every unit carries lint, type-check, and test. Product adds e2e, accessibility, and mutation gates; instruments add built-form smoke tests; security-critical primitives add mutation-score floors; evidence keeps full static gates. No unit sits outside the gate suite; bootstrap/ is exempt only from workspace imports, never from linting.
organisingRules.carrier: Per-zone required turbo tasks checked by a gate-coverage validator that walks the workspace register and fails on any member missing its zone's mandatory task set.

probePlacements.placement: Two provenance parcels in the consuming unit, split on regeneration event (register C), not merged on shared origin: the interface-spec snapshot is a vendor-preserved parcel (vendor/ or schema-cache/, byte-frozen, its refresh task the sole writer, checksum-witnessed) and the bulk dataset is a separate refreshed-data parcel with its own task. One event, one generator, disjoint outputs — the estate's existing generate:openapi / generate:bulk seam, made law.

Four generated/<event>/ parcels, four named build-graph tasks with disjoint output globs — one per event class. Each parcel lives inside the unit that consumes it; being machine-made is a provenance class, not an address, so the four collections do not congregate in a shared 'generated' ghetto.

One unit, two provenance parcels: the third-party files sit in vendor/<name>@<date>/ (byte-frozen, checksum validator, hand edits rejected at commit) beside freely-edited hand-written styling in src/. The dated vendor snapshot directory observed in the design zone is exactly this parcel and gets the vendor/ address; no unit split, because promise, altitude, and rights are shared.

Split at consumer seams inside the instrument zone: tools/cli (interactive), tools/guards (commit-time), tools/jobs (scheduled) — different consumers and failure modes are a promise difference (register A). Shared machinery stays put until its second consumer, then descends to packages/ per the second-consumer rule. Rhythm is never the knife; consumer and failure mode are.

Its own unit under packages/data/ with its own license field (the content licence) and licence file — register E forces the parcel boundary regardless of size or who consumes it. Consumers take it as a workspace dependency like any library.

Its own unit in the design estate with a reserved-rights licence field ('SEE LICENSE IN <licence file>') — the estate's existing brand-assets package is already this shape and is kept: rights force a parcel (register E), and the exports map is the only door other units may use.

Evidence zone: research/, registered as a workspace member so the full static gate suite runs over it, with a depcruise rule that no other zone may import it. Quality-gated like product, shipped like nothing — the promise register distinguishes gating from shipping, so this case is a first-class citizen, not an exception.

Re-homed into tools/cli (live-system operations) WITH instrument-grade gates — the design refuses the case as stated: it has no home for ungated code, so admission is conditional on regating. The genuine pre-install corner (scripts that must run before dependencies exist) gets the named bootstrap/ parcel: linted, zero workspace imports, outside the package graph by physics rather than waiver.

Different zones, deliberately identical internal structure: apps/ for the deployed product, demos/ for the demonstration — the zone carries the audience and support promise so the code inside need not differ to differ. This is the surveyed estate's existing apps/demos split, kept as a street grid that survived the quake.

Stays embedded behind a named internal seam (subdirectory with a depcruise intra-package rule: no imports from product-specific siblings) while it has one consumer; descends to packages/libs keyed to the commodity datastore at its second consumer. The design supplies the seam and the trigger, not a premature extraction.

The widget is its own buildable unit (product zone, beside its serving app); its built output crosses to the serving unit only as a graph edge — the server's build declares dependsOn on the widget build and consumes its dist. The current arrangement (embedded source, build-time copies, hand-maintained cross-unit hash globs in turbo.json, one production cache incident) is the razed building this rule commemorates.

Separate units in the instrument zone — tools/guards and tools/validators — split on consumer and failure mode (a commit hook must be fast and block one commit; a validator must recompute estate state and fail a pipeline). Their shared rhythm is exactly the lure the no-rhythm rule exists to refuse.

packages/core, altitude 0: near-zero dependencies and universal import are the definition of the tier (the estate's existing Result package is the type specimen). Ubiquity earns extra stability obligations (mutation floor, no new deps without review), not a special address.

packages/core, altitude 0, beside S1 — security-criticality raises its gate floor (mutation score, adversarial tests), not its address. Incident provenance is history, not zoning; the estate's existing path-containment package already sits here correctly.

packages/libs, altitude 1: its real dependencies (JSON-LD, canonicalisation vendors) disqualify it from core whatever its ubiquity. ~74 symbols make it a district, not a house — one unit, with the export map's subpaths as enforced internal districts; it splits only if a register (rights, provenance, promise) diverges internally, never on size alone. Note: the estate currently shelves it in core/ — mis-shelved under the altitude rule.

packages/sdks, altitude 2: published, versioned, licence file copied into the artefact at publish, vendor peer dependencies declared. The tier exists precisely for clients of external services with an outside audience — this is its type specimen.

packages/design: hand-written token sources (provenance: hand) beside a generated-CSS parcel (provenance: machine; event: token-source edit; its build task the sole writer). Consumers take the CSS via workspace dependency and graph edge only — never build-time copies into their public/ trees, which is the current practice this placement retires.

packages/libs, altitude 1, with the commodity datastore's client as a peerDependency — a retrieval library over infrastructure we operate is a domain library, not an sdks/ tenant (that tier is reserved for published clients of external services). The estate currently shelves it under sdks/; under the altitude rule it moves down.

Dissolved along register seams — this citadel is the earthquake's epicentre and gets no single home: spec-fetch machinery to tools/generators (instrument); the fetched spec snapshot to a vendor-preserved parcel; generated types to generated/<event>/ parcels inside the SDK unit that consumes them; corpus mining to packages/libs; hand-curated vocabulary to a hand-written data parcel, with a rights check (register E) deciding whether it becomes a packages/data unit. Fourteen export subpaths were the tell that this was a district posing as a building.

packages/libs, altitude 1, one unit per vendor (the estate's sentry/posthog adapter row is this shape and is kept), with the provider-neutral contracts remaining in packages/core so consumers depend on the contract and only the composition root picks the vendor.
