READ COUNTS AND PATHS. File reads: 20 attempted, 19 returned content, 1 failed (nonexistent file). All paths (repo-root-relative, root <repo-root>): (1) pnpm-workspace.yaml, (2) package.json, (3) turbo.json, (4) packages/sdks/oak-sdk-codegen/package.json, (5) agent-tools/package.json, (6) packages/core/result/package.json, (7) packages/core/safe-path/package.json, (8) packages/core/graph-core/package.json, (9) packages/sdks/oak-curriculum-sdk/package.json, (10) packages/design/oak-design-tokens/package.json, (11) packages/design/oak-design-system/package.json, (12) apps/oak-curriculum-mcp-streamable-http/package.json, (13) research/web-app-deconstruction/packages/research-evidence/package.json, (14) packages/sdks/oak-search-sdk/package.json, (15) packages/core/observability/package.json, (16) apps/oak-search-cli/package.json, (17) demos/oak-curriculum-hub/package.json, (18) packages/design/oak-design-assets/package.json, (19) packages/design/design-import/package.json (attempted — file does not exist, no content returned), (20) tsconfig.base.json. Directory listings/searches: 1 of 5 — `ls packages/design` (the only workspace glob; needed to resolve its members). No full-repository listing or glob was run.

FORBIDDEN-SURFACE DISCLOSURE. I opened no forbidden file. Three contaminating surfaces were INJECTED into my context by the harness without my requesting them, and I state them for the validity judgement: (a) the session system prompt carried the repo CLAUDE.md stub, a long list of .claude/rules file names, and a user memory index summarising estate history; (b) reading packages/design/oak-design-system/package.json triggered automatic injection of that directory's CLAUDE.md contents; (c) task-list reminders named an in-flight survey/census lane. I did not open any of these as files and did not use their content as grounding — every claim in the design traces to the 19 allowlisted reads — but a strict reading of 'reading any Markdown invalidates the run' may count the injected (b) as contact, since its full text entered my context. Flagging rather than concealing; the arbiter should decide. The probe set itself obviously describes this estate; I matched probes to allowlisted evidence only.

QUESTIONS THE TASK SHOULD HAVE ASKED. (1) Migration order: the task asks for the target layout but not the sequencing of moves on a live estate — which walls are load-bearing while inhabitants keep working is half of any real rebuild plan (e.g., dissolving the codegen citadel before rewiring artefact transport would break the product's build twice). (2) Who navigates the estate: the root manifest shows this city is operated substantially by agents; whether organisation should optimise for agent legibility (context budgets, discoverable-over-enumerated script surfaces) changes several carriers — my 'authored register' and per-zone task discovery lean agent-ward without the question being posed. (3) Rezoning procedure: what happens when a unit's register values change mid-life — a demo hardening into a product, an instrument becoming publishable — the design fixes addresses at a moment in time but a real estate needs the change-of-use permit process. (4) The city limits: which units are meant to leave the city (publication boundary, external consumers, semver promises) and what obligations attach at the gate — I inferred it from publishConfig and version fields, but it deserved to be asked.

CALIBRATION. One forced fit declared (P8): the design refuses 'outside the quality gates' as a property any unit may hold, so the case is admitted only by regating — that is the design overruling the case, not housing it. Two placements knowingly contradict the current estate (S3 core→libs, S6 sdks→libs); both follow from the altitude rule rather than taste, and I flag them as the two places my proposal would generate migration argument.

walkers.persona: A theatrical production manager running a repertory house: the same stage hosts different shows nightly. Your world is turnover cost, labelling, and who may touch which props — and above all the difference between the house's permanent fabric and each production's transient assets. You have struck too many sets at 2am to trust any scheme that confuses the two.

result.design:
## The frame

A repertory house survives because everyone can tell the permanent fabric from the show that closes on Sunday. The stage, the fly tower, the dimmer racks are maintained on their own schedule and touched only by house crew; each production's flats and props arrive labelled, live in their own dock, and are struck without touching the building. Sets are never repaired by hand at 2am — they are re-made from the shop drawings. Everything below is that discipline applied to a TypeScript monorepo.

## The questions this design answers

For any file in the estate, five questions must have mechanical answers:

1. Who may write this, and how is an illegitimate write caught? (provenance)
2. If this changed, what event caused the change? (trigger)
3. Under what terms may this be reused? (licence)
4. Whose show is this — what promise does it make, and which gates prove it? (audience/assurance)
5. What may this lean on, and what leans on it? (stratum)

And one meta-question: what makes two things separate units at all?

## The unit boundary law

A unit is one pnpm workspace package: a directory with a manifest, a single licence, a single audience, and (if machine-made) a single regeneration trigger. **Two files belong to different units when they differ in trigger, licence class, or audience.** Differences in write-authority alone do NOT split a unit — they split zones inside one (a package may carry a `vendor/` subtree beside its `src/`). Differences in change rhythm alone also never split a unit, and shared rhythm never merges one: rhythm is an observation, not an axis. This keeps the common case — one change, one unit, one commit — honest against the estate's economics (~5,900 commits/yr, only 308 multi-unit: roughly 5% of commits may legitimately cross a boundary, and most of those should be S0 API changes or refresh cascades).

## The five classifications (details in the rules list)

- **Provenance zones** — reserved intra-unit directories: `src/` (hand), `gen/` (machine, provenance-stamped), `vendor/` (byte-locked), `data/` (curated, schema-gated).
- **Regeneration trigger** — the transient-asset law: a machine-made artefact is a committed unit of its own iff its regeneration event is decoupled from the commits that consume it (external release, scheduled mining, cross-toolchain build). One trigger, one unit — even when two artefacts come from the same vendor. Artefacts rebuilt by the same commit that edits their source (token CSS) are turbo build products and are never committed.
- **Licence class** — MIT code, OGL content, reserved brand: one per unit, decided at file creation, visible in the path.
- **Audience/assurance** — the top-level directory IS the support promise, and the gate runner keys off it.
- **Dependency stratum** — S0 generic (no vendor, no estate knowledge), S1 domain/adapter libraries (estate-aware; at most one named external vendor each; vendor SDKs importable only inside the adapter that names them), S2 surfaces and tools. Imports point strictly downward; committed artefact units are leaves that import nothing.

## The layout

```text
packages/                    house fabric, S0/S1, MIT
  errors/                    S0  (S1 probe)
  path-safety/               S0, security gate profile (S2 probe)
  graph/                     S0  (S3 probe)
  datastore-machinery/       S0  (P10 extraction target)
  curriculum-client/         S1 adapter, published (S4 probe)
  search-retrieval/          S1 adapter (S6 probe)
  observability-adapter/     S1 adapter (S8 probe)
design/
  tokens/                    S1, CSS emitted via turbo, not committed (S5)
apps/                        productions with a support promise
  mcp-server/  search-cli/  widget/
demos/                       productions without one (P9)
artefacts/                   committed transient assets, one per trigger
  spec-snapshot/   ~29x/yr   (P1a)
  search-contracts/ ~16x/yr
  bulk-data/        ~7x/yr   (P1b)
  corpus/           ~19x/yr, 24MB
  widget-dist/      ~18x/yr  (P11)
content/                     OGL, hand-curated data/ zones (P5)
brand/                       reserved licence, owner-gated (P6)
tools/                       split by consumer and failure mode
  cli/  guards/  jobs/  validators/     (P4, P12)
studies/                     evidence: full gates, never shipped, never imported (P7)
ops/                         live-system scripts, operational gate profile (P8)
```

## Enforcement summary

Every unit manifest carries: `license` (SPDX), `audience`, `stratum`, and for artefact units `trigger` + `regeneratedBy` (a runnable command). CI enforces: (a) regenerate-and-diff on any `gen/`/artefact diff — a hand-edit fails the build, it is not a review comment; (b) checksum verification on every `vendor/` zone; (c) schema validation on `data/` zones; (d) licence-mix scan — no unit contains two licence classes; (e) path/manifest agreement — the gate profile comes from the top-level directory and refuses a mismatched manifest; (f) a graph lint recomputed from the pnpm lockfile each run — downward-only imports, vendor SDKs confined to their adapters, nothing imports `studies/`, artefact units import nothing.

## Why the artefact dock earns its keep

The measured refresh rates (29, 19, 18, 16, 7 per year) are five independent get-ins. Housing each in its own unit means a refresh is one commit touching one unit with machine provenance — reviewable as "did the named command produce this?", never as code review. Mixing two triggers in one unit makes every refresh diff unreadable and every 2am strike dangerous; mixing generated with hand-written makes both untrustworthy. The single upstream credential lives behind the S1 curriculum-client contract; the refresh jobs in `tools/jobs/` call through it, so credential handling has exactly one home.

organisingRules.name: Provenance zones — who may write
organisingRules.rule: Every file sits in exactly one write-authority zone: src/ (hand-written, edited freely), gen/ (machine-produced, written only by the unit's named regenerator), vendor/ (byte-preserved third-party, written by nobody), data/ (hand-curated records, edited only through the unit's declared curation gate). Zones are intra-unit and never a unit boundary by themselves. A hand-edit in gen/, a byte drift in vendor/, or an unvalidated data/ change is a CI failure, not a review comment.
organisingRules.carrier: Reserved directory names inside every unit, plus per-zone CI enforcement: gen/ diffs must reproduce under the manifest's regeneratedBy command (regenerate-and-diff), vendor/ zones carry a checksum manifest verified on every commit, data/ changes must pass the unit's declared schema validator.

organisingRules.name: Regeneration trigger — one strike, one set
organisingRules.rule: A machine-made artefact is a committed unit of its own if and only if its regeneration event is decoupled from the commits that consume it: an external release, a scheduled mining run, or a cross-toolchain build handoff. One trigger event class = one unit, even when two artefacts come from the same external service. Artefacts regenerated by the very commit that edits their in-repo source are turbo build products and are never committed. A refresh commit touches exactly one artefact unit.
organisingRules.carrier: artefacts/<name>/ directory per trigger; manifest fields trigger (the event class) and regeneratedBy (a runnable command); CI rejects any artefact-unit diff the named command does not reproduce; everything below the committed line belongs to the turbo build graph.

organisingRules.name: Licence class — one insurance policy per unit
organisingRules.rule: MIT code, OGL curriculum content, and reserved brand assets never share a unit. Licence is decided when a file is created, not audited afterwards, and the licence boundary is visible in the path: OGL lives under content/, reserved assets under brand/, everything importable is MIT.
organisingRules.carrier: SPDX license field in every unit manifest; dedicated top-level homes content/ (OGL) and brand/ (reserved); a CI licence-mix scan that fails any unit containing files of two licence classes, and blocks reserved-licence files from entering any published or deployable unit.

organisingRules.name: Audience and assurance — whose show, what promise
organisingRules.rule: Every unit declares who it serves and which gate profile proves its promise: product (full gates + deploy + support), demo (full gates, no support promise), library (full gates, consumed not deployed), tooling (profile per consumer: interactive, commit-time, scheduled), evidence (full gates, never shipped, never imported), operational (live-system safety gates — dry-run proof and credential review — outside the product profile but never gateless). Shared change rhythm never merges units across an audience or failure-mode boundary; structural similarity never does either.
organisingRules.carrier: The top-level directory is the audience: packages/, design/, apps/, demos/, artefacts/, content/, brand/, tools/{cli,guards,jobs,validators}/, studies/, ops/. The manifest audience field must match the path, and the gate runner selects its profile from the path, failing on mismatch.

organisingRules.name: Dependency stratum — what may lean on what
organisingRules.rule: Three strata for importable code: S0 generic (no vendor names, no estate knowledge; must survive extraction to any other estate unchanged), S1 domain and adapter libraries (estate-aware, consumed by surfaces; each names at most one external vendor, and that vendor's SDK may be imported nowhere else), S2 surfaces and tools. Imports point strictly downward; committed artefact units are leaves that import nothing; nothing imports studies/. A unit that sheds its estate knowledge graduates from S1 to S0.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest stratum field plus a graph lint recomputed in CI from the pnpm workspace dependency graph and lockfile (never from a hand-maintained list); violations block merge.

probePlacements.probe: P1 — spec snapshot + bulk dataset, same service, different schedules/mechanisms
probePlacements.placement: Two artefact units: artefacts/spec-snapshot (trigger: upstream spec release, ~29x/yr) and artefacts/bulk-data (trigger: bulk release, ~7x/yr). Shared vendor is not an axis; trigger is. Both regenerators live in tools/jobs and call through the single S1 curriculum-client, which owns the shared credential contract.

probePlacements.probe: P2 — four machine-regenerated collections, four event classes
probePlacements.placement: Four units under artefacts/, one per trigger, each with its own trigger + regeneratedBy manifest. A refresh commit touches exactly one; CI regenerate-and-diff makes each refresh reviewable as provenance, not as code.

probePlacements.probe: P3 — byte-preserved vendor files beside hand-written styling
probePlacements.placement: One unit, two zones: vendor/ (checksum-locked, CI verifies bytes every commit) beside src/ (free). Write-authority differences are zones, not unit boundaries — same trigger, licence, and audience means same unit.

probePlacements.probe: P4 — one tooling area, several consumers on different rhythms
probePlacements.placement: Split by consumer and failure mode: tools/cli (interactive), tools/guards (commit-time), tools/jobs (scheduled). Shared logic is demoted to a packages/ unit the moment a second consumer appears, keeping each tool unit's gate profile honest to its failure mode.

probePlacements.probe: P5 — hand-curated reference data under a different content licence
probePlacements.placement: content/<collection>: its own unit because licence is a unit axis. OGL in the manifest, records in a data/ curated zone behind the unit's schema validator; the licence-mix scan keeps it out of every MIT package.

probePlacements.probe: P6 — trademark image assets with unique reuse terms
probePlacements.placement: brand/: a reserved-licence unit, owner-gated writes, visible in the path. The licence-mix scan blocks brand files from entering any published or deployable unit, so reuse terms are enforced structurally rather than remembered.

probePlacements.probe: P7 — research-study evidence code, gated like product, never shipped
probePlacements.placement: studies/<study>: audience class 'evidence' — full quality gates, no deploy target, and a graph-lint rule that nothing may import it. The gates prove the evidence is trustworthy; the import ban proves it can never leak into a product.

probePlacements.probe: P8 — operational scripts against live systems, outside product gates
probePlacements.placement: ops/: audience class 'operational' with its own gate profile — dry-run proof, credential-handling review, no product-suite obligations. Outside the product gates but never gateless: the stage-management book is maintained, not exempted.

probePlacements.probe: P9 — deployed product app vs near-identical demo app
probePlacements.placement: apps/<name> vs demos/<name>. Identical internal scaffolding is encouraged; the support promise lives in the top-level path and manifest audience field, and the gate runner differs only in deploy and support obligations. Structural similarity never merges across an audience boundary.

probePlacements.probe: P10 — generic machinery embedded in a product-specific pipeline
probePlacements.placement: Extract to packages/datastore-machinery at S0; the pipeline keeps a thin S1/S2 binding that injects the vendor specifics. The graph lint holds the extracted unit vendor-clean thereafter — S0 must survive extraction to any other estate unchanged.

probePlacements.probe: P11 — widget whose built output is embedded and served by a different unit
probePlacements.placement: Source at apps/widget (S2, hand-written, full gates); built output at artefacts/widget-dist (trigger: widget release, ~18x/yr) because the cross-toolchain handoff decouples regeneration from consuming commits. The serving unit depends on the artefact unit, giving a pinned, provenance-stamped, inspectable boundary.

probePlacements.probe: P12 — commit-hook guards and repo-state validators, same rhythm
probePlacements.placement: Two units: tools/guards and tools/validators. Same change rhythm, but different consumers and failure modes (a guard failure blocks a commit; a validator failure reports estate state) — and rhythm alone never merges units across a failure-mode boundary.

probePlacements.probe: S1 — tiny zero-dependency error primitive imported nearly everywhere
probePlacements.placement: packages/errors, S0, its own unit despite its size: ubiquity gives it the largest blast radius in the estate, so its changes must be individually visible in the dependency graph. Folding it into a grab-bag utils unit is forbidden.

packages/path-safety, S0, own unit with a security flag in the manifest raising its gate profile (mandatory second review on every change). Never merged into errors despite both being tiny S0: their assurance profiles differ, and the flag's blast radius must be exact.

probePlacements.probe: S3 — large graph-data library, ~74 public symbols
probePlacements.placement: packages/graph, one S0 unit. Size is acceptable while trigger, licence, and audience are single; 74 symbols is an API-surface concern managed with an explicit export barrel and an API-report gate. Split only if the dependency graph shows disjoint consumer sets, not because of bulk.

probePlacements.probe: S4 — typed client for the external curriculum service, published publicly
probePlacements.placement: packages/curriculum-client, S1 adapter (its one named vendor), MIT, private:false. The only unit permitted to hold the vendor credential contract and import the vendor's wire types; publication adds an API-stability gate to its profile.

probePlacements.probe: S5 — design-token pipeline emitting generated CSS for several surfaces
probePlacements.placement: design/tokens, S1 (estate-aware, zero vendors). The CSS regenerates in the same commit that edits token source, so it is a turbo build product flowing to consumers through the build graph — never a committed artefact unit. This is the boundary case that defines the committed-artefact law.

probePlacements.probe: S6 — search-retrieval library over a commodity datastore
probePlacements.placement: packages/search-retrieval, S1 adapter with the commodity datastore as its one named vendor; the datastore SDK is importable nowhere else. If it sheds its estate knowledge it graduates to S0 alongside datastore-machinery.

probePlacements.probe: S7 — largest unit: codegen pipeline mixing spec-fetch, generated types, corpus mining, hand curation
probePlacements.placement: Deliberately decomposed — the design refuses it a single home. Spec-fetch and mining harnesses go to tools/jobs (S2, calling the S1 curriculum-client); generated types to artefacts/spec-types; mined corpus to artefacts/corpus; hand-curated material to content/ under OGL. 'Largest unit' is the symptom; three authorship classes and at least three triggers in one unit is the disease.

probePlacements.probe: S8 — observability adapter for a commodity vendor
probePlacements.placement: packages/observability-adapter, S1 adapter, one named vendor. Surfaces import the adapter, never the vendor SDK directly — the graph lint confines each vendor SDK to the single adapter that names it.

result.notes:
Repository files read: zero. I read nothing from the repository or filesystem; the task statement was my entire world, and the design is derived from it plus the repertory-house frame.

Questions the task statement should have asked but did not:

1. Are the generated artefact classes committed to the repository at all, or rebuilt on demand? The refresh-rate framing (29/19/18/16/7 per year) strongly implies committed snapshots, and my whole artefacts/ doctrine — including the law that an artefact is committed iff its regeneration event is decoupled from consuming commits — rests on that inference. If they are build-on-demand, artefacts/ collapses into the turbo graph and the trigger axis becomes a scheduling concern instead of a layout one.

2. What is the composition of the 308 multi-unit commits — which unit pairs actually co-change? The count alone says boundaries are mostly respected; the co-change matrix is the only empirical validator of where the boundaries should sit, and any real reorganisation should be checked against it before adoption.

3. Who holds the single upstream credential and where do refresh jobs execute (CI, a scheduled host, an interactive agent session)? I placed the credential contract in the S1 client and the jobs in tools/jobs, but the operational topology could overturn that placement.

4. What is the publishing and versioning policy — which units are published publicly besides the typed client, and how are versions cut? Publication forces API-stability and changelog gates that change a unit's assurance profile, and the task named only one published unit.

5. What is the agent-concurrency model — how many agents write in parallel? Unit granularity trades merge-conflict cost against dependency-graph complexity; with a primarily-AI workforce the sweet spot depends on how many seats hold overlapping claims at once, and the answer would tune how aggressively I split (e.g. whether tools/ needs four units or two).

One assumption worth surfacing: I treated "estate" as a single monorepo throughout; the task never asked whether any unit class (the published client, the brand assets) should live outside the repo entirely, and I did not propose extraction.

walkers.constraint: Directory depth at most 1 below the repository root, AND every organising rule must be enforceable by a machine check you name.

result.design:
Questions answered: What is an independently governed unit? Which differences require separation? Where does each unit live? How is it named? Who owns it? What may depend on it? What is shipped, published, generated, fetched, vendored, researched, or operated? Which licence, editability, support, failure, and assurance rules apply? Who owns generated output? How are shared credentials referenced? How are all rules checked?

A unit is the smallest payload with one coherent capability and exactly one value for each of five independent classifications: (1) rights: MIT, OGL, Brand-Reserved, or an identified upstream licence; (2) provenance/lifecycle: authored, fetched snapshot, regenerated, byte-vendored, or built output, with one trigger and production mechanism; (3) operational contract: library, deployed app, demo, interactive tool, commit guard, scheduled job, research, live operations, data, asset, or generated output, including audience, shipping status, support promise, and failure mode; (4) semantic scope: domain, capability, and generic-versus-product-specific status; (5) assurance profile: standard product, public API, security-critical, research-product, live-operations, generated, vendor-integrity, or brand-controlled. A difference in any classification requires separate units. Matching classifications permit, but do not require, combination; the payload must also expose one cohesive capability. File count, symbol count, common origin, and frequent co-change are not boundaries.

Every unit is a direct child of the repository root and contains only files, never subdirectories. The tracked layout therefore has maximum directory depth one. Root files are an allowlisted set of workspace coordination files. Each unit contains unit.json and package.json directly beside flat source, tests, data, or assets. Tests use filename suffixes such as .test.ts. Unit directories use <role>-<scope>[-<capability>], for example lib-curriculum-client; workspace packages use @estate/<unit-id>. Public packages may additionally declare a stable publishName. There are no apps/, packages/, tools/, generated/, or domain bucket directories.

The five classifications are carried by unit.json fields rights, provenance, contract, scope, and assurance. Other required fields are id, owner, exports, dependencies, artifactInputs, artifactOutputs, secretRefs, and publishName where applicable. Payload files inherit the unit classification; authored management manifests are the only non-payload exception in generated, fetched, or vendored units.

The dependency graph is constructed from TypeScript imports, package dependencies, Turbo task inputs and outputs, manifest generator/input relationships, and served-artifact relationships. Cross-unit relative imports and undeclared deep imports are forbidden; consumers use declared package exports or artifact edges. Strongly connected components must contain one unit. Topological rank, reverse fan-in, affected-build closure, runtime roots, shared capabilities, and composition roots are derived rather than manually classified. Generic units cannot depend on product-specific units. Apps, demos, research, operations, guards, jobs, and tools are graph roots and cannot become runtime dependencies of libraries or other products. Generated output depends by provenance on its producer and inputs; a serving unit consumes that output without thereby owning it.

The implied known-estate layout includes app-curriculum-mcp, tool-search-cli, two demo-curriculum-<purpose> units, lib-design-system, data-design-tokens, tool-design-token-build, gen-design-token-css, tool-agent-interactive, guard-agent-commit, job-agent-scheduled, lib-curriculum-client, data-curriculum-interface-spec, data-curriculum-bulk, tool-curriculum-spec-fetch, tool-curriculum-bulk-fetch, tool-curriculum-spec-codegen, gen-curriculum-spec-types, tool-search-contract-codegen, gen-search-contracts, tool-curriculum-bulk-codegen, gen-curriculum-bulk-schemas, tool-curriculum-corpus-miner, gen-curriculum-corpus, lib-browser-widget, gen-browser-widget-embed, lib-search-retrieval, lib-observability-adapter, lib-auth-adapter, ops-deploy, lib-errors, lib-path-safety, and lib-graph. Demo names must use their actual purpose rather than ordinal names once known. The single curriculum-platform credential is an injected logical secret referenced by eligible units, never copied into a unit. Multi-unit commits remain valid atomic changes; co-change never erases legal, lifecycle, contract, scope, or assurance boundaries.

organisingRules.name: Direct-root unit shape
organisingRules.rule: Every tracked payload belongs to exactly one direct-child unit directory; no tracked directory may exist beneath a unit, and non-unit root files must be explicitly allowlisted.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory path /<unit-id>/<file>; enforced by check-unit-shape, which scans tracked paths, rejects depth greater than one, rejects root payloads, and verifies unit.json and package.json.

organisingRules.name: Canonical identity and naming
organisingRules.rule: Each unit has one stable id matching <role>-<scope>[-<capability>], its directory name and internal package name must derive from that id, and role must agree with its operational contract.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory name plus unit.json.id and package.json.name; enforced by check-unit-id.

organisingRules.name: Rights homogeneity
organisingRules.rule: A unit has one payload rights class. MIT code, OGL content, reserved brand assets, and differently licensed upstream material may never share a unit.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.rights plus per-file licence headers, binary rights declarations, and a root rights-policy.json; enforced by check-unit-rights.

organisingRules.name: Single provenance and change trigger
organisingRules.rule: A unit has one provenance kind, editability policy, triggering event class, and production mechanism. Different refresh schedules or generators require separate units even when inputs come from the same service.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.provenance with kind, editable, trigger, producer, inputs, and expectedRefreshClass; enforced by check-unit-lifecycle.

organisingRules.name: Single operational contract
organisingRules.rule: A unit has one invocation model, audience, shipping status, support promise, and failure mode. Interactive commands, commit guards, scheduled jobs, demos, deployed products, research, and live operations therefore remain distinct.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.contract and declared package entrypoints or Turbo tasks; enforced by check-unit-contract.

organisingRules.name: Single semantic scope
organisingRules.rule: A unit represents one named capability in one domain and declares whether it is generic or product-specific. Generic commodity machinery must be extracted from product orchestration and may not import product-specific code.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.scope with domain, capability, and generality; directory name; declared exports; enforced by check-unit-scope using the dependency graph.

organisingRules.name: Assurance isolation
organisingRules.rule: Each unit has one gate profile. Research may use product-grade gates without shipping; live operations use a separate safety profile; security, public API, generated, vendor, and brand units receive their specialised checks.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.assurance mapped to mandatory Turbo tasks in assurance-policy.json; enforced by check-unit-assurance and check-affected-gates.

organisingRules.name: Explicit acyclic dependencies
organisingRules.rule: All code and artifact dependencies must be declared, cross-unit deep imports are forbidden, cycles are forbidden, and contract/scope-specific forbidden edges are rejected.
organisingRules.carrier: package.json dependencies, unit.json dependencies and artifact edges, parsed TypeScript imports, and Turbo inputs/outputs; enforced by check-unit-graph. Topological rank, reverse fan-in, shared-capability status, roots, and affected closure are derived from this graph.

organisingRules.name: Immutable generated and vendor payloads
organisingRules.rule: Fetched, generated, built-output, and byte-vendored payloads cannot be hand-edited. Generated output must reproduce from its declared producer and inputs; vendor bytes must match the recorded upstream digest.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.provenance, artifact lock digests, generator task identity, and byte manifests; enforced by check-immutable-payloads and check-reproducible-artifacts.

organisingRules.name: Explicit public surface
organisingRules.rule: Consumers may access only declared exports or artifact outputs. A large coherent library is not split merely because it exposes many symbols, but all public symbols and compatibility promises must be explicit.
organisingRules.carrier: package.json.exports, unit.json.exports, publishName, and contract.support; enforced by check-public-surface and check-no-deep-imports.

organisingRules.name: Human ownership
organisingRules.rule: Every unit has an accountable human owner; specialised assurance classes require the corresponding approval authority despite implementation being primarily agent-produced.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.owner and root owners.json; enforced by check-unit-ownership and check-required-approvals.

organisingRules.name: Credential references, not credential ownership
organisingRules.rule: Units may declare logical secret requirements but may not store credentials. Sharing the curriculum-platform credential does not merge otherwise independent units.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.secretRefs and an external injection policy; enforced by check-secret-boundaries, which validates permitted references and scans tracked payloads for secret material.

probePlacements.placement: Place the interface snapshot in /data-curriculum-interface-spec and the bulk dataset in /data-curriculum-bulk. Use separate /tool-curriculum-spec-fetch and /tool-curriculum-bulk-fetch producers. Their common external origin and credential do not override their distinct triggers, mechanisms, and artifact contracts.

Use /gen-curriculum-spec-types, /gen-search-contracts, /gen-curriculum-bulk-schemas, and /gen-curriculum-corpus, each with its own producer tool and trigger corresponding respectively to spec refresh, search-contract change, bulk refresh, and corpus-mining change.

Put byte-preserved files in /vendor-widget-upstream with vendor-integrity assurance and digest locking; put authored styling in /lib-widget-styles with authored provenance. A wrapper may depend on both.
Split into /tool-agent-interactive, /guard-agent-commit, and /job-agent-scheduled. Extract only genuinely shared, contract-neutral implementation into a /lib-agent-<capability> unit.
Place the curated reference payload in /data-curriculum-reference with rights OGL and authored provenance; MIT loaders, validators, and APIs live in separate library or tool units.
Place trademark images in /asset-brand with Brand-Reserved rights and brand-controlled assurance; no code, OGL content, or generally reusable design-system assets share the unit.
Place it in /research-<study>-evidence with contract ships=false and assurance research-product, which runs the product-quality gate set without making the unit a production dependency.

Use one live-operations unit per target and failure domain, such as /ops-curriculum-maintenance, /ops-search-maintenance, and /ops-deploy. They use the live-operations assurance profile and are excluded from product runtime and product-gate dependency closures.

Keep /app-<scope>-<purpose> and /demo-<scope>-<purpose> separate because audience, shipping, support, and failure contracts differ. Extract structurally shared code only when it is a coherent contract-neutral library.

Extract the commodity datastore machinery into /lib-datastore-core with generality=generic; leave product semantics and orchestration in /job-curriculum-indexing or the relevant product unit, which depends on the generic library.

Keep authored browser source in /lib-browser-widget, built bytes in /gen-browser-widget-embed, and the serving application in its own /app-* or /demo-* unit. The generated unit declares its producer; the host consumes its artifact output.

Place commit-hook enforcement in /guard-commit-policy and repository-state validation in /tool-repo-validator. Their matching change rhythm does not merge their consumers, invocation contracts, or failure modes.
Place it in /lib-errors as a foundation unit with explicit exports and no internal runtime dependencies. High reverse fan-in is derived from the graph and triggers stricter compatibility checks.
Place it in /lib-path-safety with assurance=security-critical, a narrow explicit API, mandatory security-owner approval, and no product-specific dependencies.

Place it in /lib-graph. Approximately 74 public symbols are acceptable when they form one coherent graph capability; declare every symbol through exports and split only if scope, contract, lifecycle, rights, or assurance diverges.
Place it in /lib-curriculum-client with contract=public-library, public-api assurance, publishName, semantic versioning policy, and dependency only on lower-level protocol or generated-type units.
Place authored tokens in /data-design-tokens, build machinery in /tool-design-token-build, and generated CSS in /gen-design-token-css. Consumer surfaces depend on the CSS artifact unit.
Place generic retrieval mechanics in /lib-search-retrieval. Curriculum-specific query construction or ranking policy belongs in a separate curriculum-scoped library or product composition unit.

Dissolve the mixed unit into /tool-curriculum-spec-fetch, /data-curriculum-interface-spec, /tool-curriculum-spec-codegen, /gen-curriculum-spec-types, /tool-curriculum-corpus-miner, /gen-curriculum-corpus, and /data-curriculum-reference. Add separate event-specific job units only where orchestration is needed. This separates fetch, generation, mining, curation, triggers, and rights.

Place it in /lib-observability-adapter with MIT rights, authored provenance, commodity scope, and a vendor-facing adapter contract. Product units depend on the adapter interface rather than vendor SDK details.

result.design: Use Flat Contract Units. The design answers: (1) what is the independently changeable contract; (2) which consumers and gates are affected by changing it; (3) who controls each byte and what event may replace it; (4) what execution, distribution, audience, support, and failure promises apply; (5) what legal terms constrain it; and (6) what a proposed split, merge, or reclassification will cost. It rests on four independent classifications only: contract-unit identity, byte controller, obligation vector, and rights regime. Dependency relations are derived facts, not another placement taxonomy. A unit is the smallest collection presenting one versioned contract and having one controller tuple, obligation vector, and rights regime. A difference in any of those values forces separation. Internal file structure, size, technology, vendor, team, and historical origin do not force separation. Each payload unit occupies one top-level directory named u<stable-id>-<display-slug>, for example /u0042-error. Files are directly inside it; no tracked subdirectory is permitted. Local structure is expressed with descriptive flat filenames such as parser.tokenise.ts and parser.tokenise.test.ts. Stable IDs, import aliases, published package names, and deployable names are independent of the editable display slug. The root contains estate.units.json, generated import maps, and unavoidable repository-level configuration. Those exact root files form reserved unit u0000-repo-control; no other root payload files are allowed. estate.units.json explicitly enumerates every tracked file and, per unit, records stable ID, directory, human owner, controller tuple, rights ID, contract kind, public entrypoints, obligation vector, gates, and declared non-code relations. Controller kinds are human-authored, generated, external-mirror, vendor-byte-preserved, and build-output; machine-controlled kinds additionally declare producer identity, input units, command, refresh trigger, and receipt or digest. The obligation vector independently records contract kind, execution context, distribution mode, audience, support promise, live-system capability, invocation mode, failure semantics, and gate set. Contract kinds are library, executable, application, dataset, asset, generated-artifact, and repository-control. Cross-unit source imports must use stable aliases and public entrypoints. A generated dependency graph combines TypeScript imports, package exports, build configuration, and declared generates, embeds, deploys-with, and operates-on relations. org-impact computes the reverse transitive closure using an edge-type propagation table, so a change reports affected units, stale generated outputs, public contracts, deployables, and required gates. The flat layout deliberately does not encode apps, packages, tools, generated material, ownership, vendors, or legal status as directory hierarchy; changing any such classification normally changes one manifest field rather than paths. Splits and merges allocate or retire stable IDs, while compatibility facades may retain old aliases. org-reorg-report reports the exact files moved, incoming and outgoing edges, affected public or deployed contracts, controller changes, and gates before a reorganisation can land.

organisingRules.name: Flat unit carrier and naming
organisingRules.rule: Every tracked payload file belongs to exactly one u<stable-id>-<display-slug> directory directly below the root, and no tracked directory may exist beneath a unit. Only the exact manifest-declared u0000 repository-control files may live at root.
organisingRules.carrier: Top-level directory plus estate.units.json unit.dir and unit.files; enforced by org-check layout.

organisingRules.name: Stable identity
organisingRules.rule: A unit ID is unique, never reused, and remains stable when its slug, owner, obligations, or implementation changes. Cross-unit aliases use the ID rather than the directory slug.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.units.json unit.id and generated TypeScript/package-manager import maps; enforced against the merge base by org-check identities.

organisingRules.name: Mechanical separation test
organisingRules.rule: Files may share a unit only when their controller tuple, obligation vector, and rights ID are identical and they contribute to one declared contract. Any difference forces separate units; libraries shared by several executable surfaces are separate dependency units.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.units.json unit.controller, unit.obligations, unit.rightsId, and unit.contract; enforced by org-check unit-homogeneity and org-check contract-shape.

organisingRules.name: Single contract shape
organisingRules.rule: Each unit declares exactly one contract kind. A library has one version/support promise and declared entrypoints; an executable has one invocation and failure contract; an application has one deployable and support promise; a dataset has one schema and refresh promise; an asset has one reuse promise; and a generated artefact has one producer and trigger.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.units.json unit.contract discriminated union; enforced by org-check contract-shape.

organisingRules.name: Byte authority
organisingRules.rule: Every unit has one controller kind and one accountable human owner. Human-authored bytes may be edited through normal review. Generated, mirrored, vendor-preserved, and build-output bytes may change only through their declared controller and must carry a matching refresh receipt or digest.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.units.json unit.owner and unit.controller; enforced on changed files by org-check authority.

organisingRules.name: Generated and mirrored freshness
organisingRules.rule: Every machine-controlled unit declares exact inputs, producer, command or fetch mechanism, trigger class, and output digest. Input changes invalidate the output; deterministic producers must reproduce it, while external fetches must supply a controller-issued receipt binding source revision and digest.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.units.json controller inputs and receipts plus generated digest records; enforced by org-check freshness.

organisingRules.name: Independent obligations
organisingRules.rule: Execution context, distribution, audience, support promise, live-system access, invocation, failure semantics, and gate set are explicit fields rather than directory categories. Differing obligation vectors require separate units.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.units.json unit.obligations; enforced by org-check obligations and org-check unit-homogeneity.

organisingRules.name: Rights isolation
organisingRules.rule: Every unit has exactly one rights regime. Files with different licences, trademark restrictions, preservation requirements, or redistribution permissions must occupy separate units, and distribution edges must be compatible with the source rights regime.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.units.json unit.rightsId and a root-level machine-readable rights table; enforced by org-check rights.

organisingRules.name: Public boundary
organisingRules.rule: A unit may be consumed only through declared public entrypoints. Relative imports crossing unit directories, undeclared package imports, and access to another unit's internal files are forbidden.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.units.json contract.entrypoints and generated import maps; enforced through TypeScript AST and package-resolution analysis by org-check boundaries.

organisingRules.name: Complete dependency graph
organisingRules.rule: All statically discoverable code and build edges must appear in the generated graph, while non-static generates, embeds, deploys-with, and operates-on edges must be declared. Cross-unit cycles are forbidden unless the participating units are merged.
organisingRules.carrier: Generated estate.graph.json plus estate.units.json declaredRelations; enforced by org-check graph-completeness and org-check graph-cycles.

organisingRules.name: Change impact and gates
organisingRules.rule: For every change, reverse dependency closure determines affected contracts, required regenerations, deployables, and gate sets. CI may pass only when all required gates and freshness checks for that closure have recorded success.
organisingRules.carrier: estate.graph.json, the edge propagation table, unit gate declarations, and CI attestations; enforced by org-check impact.

organisingRules.name: Reorganisation cost control
organisingRules.rule: A split, merge, ID retirement, contract-kind change, or public-edge change must include a generated impact report. Landing is blocked if the report omits moved files, affected edges, managed-byte controllers, public contracts, deployables, compatibility aliases, or required gates.
organisingRules.carrier: A machine-generated reorg report referenced from estate.units.json change metadata; enforced by org-check reorganisation.

One question the task statement should also have asked is: which root-level filenames and generated-directory shapes are unavoidably required by the chosen package manager, compiler, test runner, and deployment systems, and may those tools be configured to obey the one-level depth limit? walkers.constraint: Directories may not carry ANY classification — a flat namespace of units; classifications live in manifest fields or a name grammar you define; machine-regenerated artefacts may not live in version control at all.

result.design: The design answers: what the atomic unit is; when mixed concerns must split; when small or large code should remain together; where units live; how they are named; how licence, provenance, audience, support, execution rhythm, generation and ownership are recorded; which dependencies are permitted; how generated material moves between producers and consumers without entering version control; and how violations are stopped. A unit is the smallest independently reviewable, quality-gated and dependency-addressable body with one legal regime, one source authority and one operational contract. Size, file count and public-symbol count alone never create a boundary. The minimal independent classification tuple is: form, subject domain, legal regime, source authority, delivery contract and primary change trigger. Consumer interface and failure ownership are boundary facts rather than classifications; dependency role is computed rather than declared. The repository layout is one structural root, units/<unit-name>, containing every unit at the same depth. There are no apps, packages, tooling, generated, research or domain parent directories. Directory placement has zero organisational meaning, and internal directories may be used only as implementation details from which no estate rule is inferred. The name grammar is <form>--<domain>--<capability>[--<variant>], using lowercase registered terms; examples are lib--neutral--errors and app--curriculum--mcp-server. Every unit has unit.json; importable or executable TypeScript units additionally have package.json. Generated payloads are represented by manifest-only artifact units and stored in an immutable external artifact store or ephemeral build location. Their changing payloads, digests and run records are never tracked. A tracked generator unit produces an artifact unit through an explicit graph edge, and a consumer names the artifact unit through another edge. This permits generator code and generated content to have different licences without mixing them. Mandatory splits occur across licence regimes, source authorities, delivery/support promises, independently triggered regeneration, deployment boundaries, separately invocable consumer contracts, or independently owned failure modes. A shared library is extracted only when it presents a consumer-neutral API or deserves its own assurance boundary; otherwise sharing alone does not justify a unit. Domain-neutral machinery must point inward from product policy: product-specific units may depend on neutral units, never the reverse.

organisingRules.name: Flat unit identity
organisingRules.rule: Every unit occupies exactly one member of the flat units/* namespace. Units cannot contain units, and no organisational decision may be inferred from a path above or below the unit root.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory level units/<name>; unit.json#id must exactly equal the directory name.

organisingRules.name: Form and subject
organisingRules.rule: Form identifies app, lib, tool, data, asset or artifact; domain identifies the subject such as neutral, curriculum, search, design, widget, estate, research, operations, brand or observability. Capability is a stable singular identity, not a team or temporary project name.
organisingRules.carrier: Name grammar <form>--<domain>--<capability>[--<variant>], schema-checked against controlled form and domain vocabularies.

organisingRules.name: Legal regime
organisingRules.rule: A unit has exactly one substantive licence regime. MIT code, OGL curriculum material, reserved brand material and third-party terms must never coexist in one unit. Distribution closure checks must account for every data, asset and artifact dependency as well as code dependencies.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json#legal with exactly one SPDX identifier or LicenseRef; policy rejects mixed file declarations and incompatible publish or deploy closures.

organisingRules.name: Source authority
organisingRules.rule: Each unit is authored, hand-curated, vendor-byte-preserved or generated-contract. Different authorities require separate units. Vendor material is immutable except through an explicit vendor-import operation. Generated-contract units contain only stable metadata; their payloads remain outside version control.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json#authority; vendor units additionally carry upstream identity and approved byte hashes, while artifact units carry producer and external coordinate templates but no changing digest.

organisingRules.name: Delivery contract
organisingRules.rule: Each unit declares one promise: deployed-supported, public-api, internal-supported, demonstration, research-evidence, live-operations, build-only, content-distribution or restricted-distribution. Product and public units receive product gates; research-evidence receives the same gates but is forbidden from ship closures; demonstration and live-operations receive their own profiles.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json#delivery; gate selection and deploy, publish and embed eligibility are derived from this value.

organisingRules.name: Primary change trigger
organisingRules.rule: Every executable producer and artifact contract declares one primary event class. Independently triggered refreshes are separate units even when they use the same service and credential. Libraries use consumer-driven as their trigger. Measured frequency is telemetry, not a directory or name.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json#trigger with values such as interactive, commit, scheduled:<job>, upstream-spec, upstream-bulk, search-contract, corpus-refresh, source-build, manual-curation or consumer-driven.

organisingRules.name: Consumer and failure boundary
organisingRules.rule: Separately invocable interfaces or failures requiring different containment, rollback or human ownership are separate units even when their change cadence matches. Pure shared implementation may be extracted behind a consumer-neutral library API.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json#interfaces entries declaring consumer, invocation mode, failure owner and failure policy; policy rejects one executable exposing incompatible interface contracts.

organisingRules.name: Artifact lineage
organisingRules.rule: Every regenerated collection has its own artifact unit and exactly one producing edge. Consumers depend on immutable artifact coordinates, never repository paths. Built output may be served by a different unit without transferring source ownership.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json#produces and unit.json#consumesArtifact; Turbo build edges and external artifact-store attestations implement the lineage.

organisingRules.name: Dependency architecture
organisingRules.rule: Cross-unit relative imports are forbidden; every code dependency must use the unit package identity and be declared. The graph must be acyclic. Demo, research and operations units cannot enter supported product deployment closures. Neutral units cannot depend on product-domain units.
organisingRules.carrier: package.json dependencies plus unit.json artifact edges; graph validation derives foundation, adapter, product, deploy-root, fan-in and fan-out roles rather than storing layer labels.

organisingRules.name: Cohesion and extraction
organisingRules.rule: A cohesive library remains one unit regardless of size or export count. A tiny primitive may be a unit when graph centrality, stability or assurance makes it independently governed. Product-neutral mechanisms are extracted from product policy only when they compile and test through a domain-free interface.
organisingRules.carrier: Enforcement combines dependency-graph facts with manifest domain checks; review policy requires a boundary rationale for new units but stores no directory taxonomy.

organisingRules.name: Human accountability
organisingRules.rule: Every unit has one accountable human owner even when agents perform most changes. Generated artifacts inherit operational accountability from their producer but retain their own legal and authority declarations.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json#owner containing a registered human-owned group; commit and CI policy reject missing or inactive ownership.

organisingRules.name: Generated-material exclusion

walkers.constraint: At most ONE of your classifications may be expressed by directory position; every other classification must live in machine-readable metadata.

result.design:
Use a flat, capability-centred unit estate. A unit is the smallest coherent capability that can be owned, understood, verified, versioned or regenerated as one change surface. Two things are separate units when they can change independently and differ in regeneration event or producer, delivery or support contract, legal reuse terms, assurance or operational profile, or accountable ownership. Things remain together when they implement one capability, share those contracts, and normally require atomic change. Authored generator code and its deterministic output may share a unit when they form one release; independently refreshed outputs do not. High co-change is evidence for colocation, but a legally or operationally necessary separation instead creates an enforced coordination relationship.

The design answers: What capability does this belong to? Who owns it? May a human edit it? Where did it come from and how is it reproduced? Who consumes it, how is it delivered, and what support is promised? What may be copied or redistributed? Which checks and operational controls apply? What is its public interface? Which other units would be affected by changing it? What should a newcomer or machine collaborator read first? How can it be split, combined or renamed without an estate-wide move?

There are five independent classifications: unit membership, artifact custody, delivery contract, rights, and assurance profile. Only unit membership is expressed by directory position. All other classifications are required machine-readable metadata in unit.json, with path-specific entries where files within one unit differ. Ownership, public interfaces, guidance, and coordination are relationship or governance facts rather than extra directory taxonomies.

The physical layout is: estate.json at the repository root as a compact generated catalogue; units/<stable-capability-id>/unit.json for every unit; and arbitrary implementation files below that unit root. Internal directory names have no estate-wide meaning. There are no apps, packages, tools, generated, vendor, research, or data directory tiers. Root files required by package managers or CI are explicitly claimed by the estate-governance unit through unit.json rootClaims. Every other tracked path must be beneath exactly one unit root. estate.json contains unit IDs, paths, one-line summaries, owners, authoritative entrypoints, logical import aliases, delivery summaries, and a compact dependency neighbourhood, allowing discovery with one file read.

Unit IDs are stable kebab-case capability names. They must not encode team, maturity, licence, generatedness, runtime tier, support level, or current technology. Those facts change in metadata without moving files. Logical TypeScript imports use stable aliases such as @estate/<unit-id>, never cross-unit relative paths. Published package names are delivery aliases declared in metadata and need not equal physical paths. Renames preserve an alias map until consumers migrate.

Each unit.json includes schemaVersion, id, summary, owners, interfaces, workingSets, guidance, artifacts, delivery, rights, assurance, outputs, coordination, and any rootClaims. Artifact records cover non-overlapping path patterns and declare custody, source, producer, trigger, reproduction command, tool version, input digest, output digest, freshness expectation, and whether bytes are checked in. Guidance records identify exactly one authoritative first-read entrypoint per audience. Working sets identify the smallest entrypoint, public interface, relevant tests, and verification commands for common tasks.

The dependency graph is generated from TypeScript imports, package resolution, build inputs and outputs, generator relationships, embedded artifacts, deployment composition, and script invocation. Architecture labels such as foundation, adapter, application, pipeline, high-fan-in, and leaf are derived views, not directory or name classifications. Cross-unit edges must target a declared public interface or output. Private cross-unit imports, undeclared output copying, and dependency cycles fail CI. Impacted-unit checks are selected from the reverse graph, keeping verification proportional as the estate grows.

A path-change matrix supplies a separate cohesion signal. Persistently high co-change across units requires either consolidation or a metadata coordination contract explaining the necessary separation and naming the atomic consumer checks. A unit with several weakly connected graph clusters, unrelated working sets, or multiple independent regeneration events is flagged for decomposition. Size alone is not decisive, but size combined with independent graph clusters or contracts is.

Machine-owned artifacts are protected by reproduction checks: generated bytes must match deterministic regeneration from pinned inputs, fetched or vendored bytes must match recorded upstream digests, and changes require an updated machine-produced provenance receipt. Human edits to such paths therefore fail before merge rather than disappearing at the next rebuild. Copy and export tooling consults rights metadata; unknown rights deny copying, restricted or trademarked material requires an explicitly permitted destination and retained attribution, and CI rejects duplicate or moved assets without a provenance link.

Rules are valid only when represented in the unit.json schema, implemented as executable policy, and covered by positive and negative fixtures. The same policy runs in editor or commit-time checks and in CI; CI is authoritative. Documentation may explain a rule but cannot create one. Reorganisation is performed by an AST-aware unit move or split command that updates manifests, aliases, public imports, coordination records, and the generated catalogue atomically. Because changing delivery, licence, assurance, ownership, or lifecycle metadata causes no directory move, most future reclassification is cheap.

organisingRules.name: Unit membership — classification 1 of 5
organisingRules.rule: Place a path in the unit representing its coherent capability. Split independently ownable or independently changing capabilities; colocate implementation and deterministic outputs only when they share one atomic contract. This is the sole classification conveyed by directory position.
organisingRules.carrier: The single semantic directory level units/<stable-capability-id>/. Every tracked path is covered exactly once; unavoidable root control files use unit.json rootClaims. Internal subdirectories carry no estate meaning. CI rejects gaps, overlaps, and cross-unit relative imports.

organisingRules.name: Artifact custody — classification 2 of 5
organisingRules.rule: Classify every artifact pattern as authored, generated, fetched-snapshot, vendored-byte-preserved, or built-output. Independently triggered or independently sourced machine outputs become separate units; a generator and its atomic output may remain together.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json artifacts[] fields: match, custody, producerUnit, source, trigger, reproduce, toolVersion, inputDigest, outputDigest, freshness, checkedIn, and provenanceReceipt. Regeneration and digest checks reject hand edits or untraceable refreshes.

organisingRules.name: Delivery contract — classification 3 of 5
organisingRules.rule: State who consumes the capability, through which interface, at what runtime or event, with what distribution and support promise. Different audiences, release rhythms, failure modes, or support promises normally require separate units with a shared core extracted only when genuine reuse exists.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json delivery[] and interfaces[] fields: mode, audience, runtime, distribution, support, schedule, portability, stability, entrypoint, and publishedAlias. Contract tests and release policy are selected from these fields.

organisingRules.name: Rights and reuse — classification 4 of 5
organisingRules.rule: Every code, data, image, or vendor-byte pattern has explicit reuse terms. The most restrictive applicable record wins; missing rights metadata denies copying or publication.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json rights[] fields: match, SPDX expression or controlled rights code, holder, source, copyPolicy, redistribution, attribution, trademark, and approvedDestinations. Copy/export commands and CI provenance scanning enforce the decision at the point of reuse.

organisingRules.name: Assurance and execution — classification 5 of 5
organisingRules.rule: Declare the evidence and controls required before the unit can change or run. Product-quality evidence code may be non-shipping; live operational code uses an operations-specific profile rather than inheriting product gates; security-critical primitives receive stronger review regardless of size.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json assurance fields: profile, criticality, liveAccess, dataSensitivity, requiredChecks, requiredReviewers, dryRun, confirmation, auditTrail, and rollback. CI and runtime wrappers materialise these controls.

organisingRules.name: Stable identity and naming

Questions answered: What may share a unit? Where does it live? What is its public contract? Who owns and ships it? What may be generated or edited? Which rights apply? What dependency directions are legal?

A unit is the smallest independently owned, versioned, tested, and releasable (or explicitly non-releasable) boundary with one runtime/support promise, one rights class, one source-of-truth/provenance policy, and one dominant change trigger. Split when any of those differs; do not split merely for size, naming aesthetics, or implementation language.

Layout:
- apps/<surface>: deployable/supported user or agent surfaces; demos are separately named apps.
- packages/<domain-or-capability>: reusable runtime libraries, clients, adapters, primitives, and pipelines.
- tools/<consumer>/<tool>: command-, hook-, CI-, or scheduled-job entrypoints; shared logic remains in packages.
- operations/<system>/<operation>: live-system automation, separately controlled from product release gates.
- experiments/<study>: non-shipping research evidence code.
- assets/<rights-class>/<asset-family>: non-code assets isolated by licence/brand terms.
- data/<rights-class>/<source-or-collection>: curated data isolated from code and assets.
- generated/<producer>/<event-class>: committed generated outputs, grouped by producer and regeneration event—not by a broad generic 'generated' bucket.
- vendor/<vendor>/<artifact>: byte-preserved third-party material, immutable except replacement from its declared source.

Each unit has a manifest declaring kind, owner, stability, consumers, rightsClass, sourcePolicy, generation/refresh trigger where applicable, support tier, publication/deployment target, and allowed dependency classes. The graph is derived continuously from imports, workspace dependencies, build inputs, and deployment edges; it audits the manifest claims rather than defining them.

Dependency shape: primitives point inward only; capabilities may depend on primitives and declared adapters; product/domain packages may depend on capabilities; entrypoints/apps depend inward; generated and vendor material are leaves consumed through a typed boundary; data/assets are not imported as arbitrary package internals. No unit may cross rights classes. External-service code is separated into public client, provider-specific acquisition, and product pipeline layers.

walkers.constraint: At most ONE of your classifications may be expressed by directory position; every other classification must live in machine-readable metadata.

result.design:
Use one flat physical estate: `units/<unit-id>/`. The sole fact encoded by directory position is that the subtree is one managed unit; `unit-id` is stable kebab case. Do not use `apps/`, `packages/core/`, `libs/`, `sdks/`, `demos/`, `generated/`, or `research/` as organisational classifications.

A unit is separate when it has an independently reviewable contract or any independently changing boundary in delivery promise, provenance/editability, licence/policy, or allowed dependency surface. It is not separate merely because it is large, uses a different language/tool, or has a different maintainer. Small shared primitives remain units when their blast radius or security contract warrants an explicit public boundary. Conversely, a large coherent library can remain one unit with explicit subpath APIs.

Each `units/<unit-id>/package.json` carries an `oak` object, validated by JSON Schema. Proposed shape:

```json
{
  "name": "@oaknational/curriculum-sdk",
  "oak": {
    "unit": { "id": "curriculum-sdk", "kind": "library", "domain": "curriculum" },
    "contract": { "exports": [".", "./client", "./types"], "stability": "public" },
    "delivery": { "audience": "external-developers", "support": "versioned", "publish": "npm" },
    "policy": { "qualityProfile": "product", "licence": "MIT", "securityTier": "standard" },
    "artifacts": [],
    "architecture": { "mayDependOn": ["result", "type-helpers"], "mayBeDependedOnBy": ["application", "library"] }
  }
}
```

`artifacts` is an array of records, not a directory convention: `{id, role, provenance, editability, licence, producer, refreshTrigger, checksum, consumers, servedBy?}`. `kind` is a bounded vocabulary (`library`, `application`, `tool`, `data-product`, `asset-bundle`, `evidence`, `widget`, `adapter`); it describes responsibility, not a folder. `qualityProfile` selects the gate set (`product`, `research`, `operational`, `generated`), while `delivery` records audience, support commitment, and publication/hosting channel. Licence and security tier are policy metadata, not inferred from neighbours.

Generate `unit-dependency-graph.json` from workspace dependencies and TypeScript imports. It derives graph measures (in/out-degree, cycles, SCCs, forbidden edges) and checks each edge against the two unit manifests; it is derived evidence, never a hand-maintained classification. A validator enforces the schema, package-name/id agreement, declared exports, no undeclared cross-unit source import, producer-to-artifact completeness, pinned external checksums, generated-file ownership, licence compatibility, and quality-profile task selection. Turbo consumes task declarations generated from the same metadata, so an operational unit is deliberately outside product gates while research remains inside its declared research gates.

This matches live evidence without treating current folder names as architecture: manifests already distinguish private/public packages, exports, publish configuration, scripts and licences; the root workspace currently has separate `apps`, `demos`, and several package strata; source confirms a tiny result primitive, a path-containment guard, a graph library with subpath exports, a mixed code-generation unit, generated design-token CSS, and an embedded widget build. The proposal replaces positional meaning with explicit metadata rather than renaming folders cosmetically.

result.design:
Use a flat, unit-first workspace: each independently versioned/buildable/reviewable unit is one package directory under `units/<unit-id>/`. Directory position expresses only unit membership. Every other concern is declared in each unit's `unit.json` and validated centrally. A unit boundary exists when change authority, released contract, licence, deployment/support promise, regeneration authority, or consumer failure mode differs; size, language, and apparent similarity do not create a boundary alone.

Questions answered: what may change together; who owns and approves it; what may depend on it; whether it ships, deploys, publishes, or only supports operations; which licence governs it; whether it is authored, fetched, generated, or byte-preserved; which trigger may replace it; and which consumers receive its contract.

Layout:
`units/<unit-id>/package.json`
`units/<unit-id>/unit.json`
`units/<unit-id>/src/`
`units/<unit-id>/generated/` (only when `provenance=generated`)
`units/<unit-id>/vendor/` (only when `provenance=byte-preserved`)
`units/<unit-id>/assets/` (only when the entire unit has one asset licence)

Examples: `units/curriculum-client`, `units/curriculum-spec-snapshot`, `units/curriculum-bulk-data`, `units/search-core`, `units/mcp-server`, `units/search-cli`, `units/demo-curriculum`, `units/design-tokens`, `units/widget-source`, `units/widget-delivery`, `units/ops-live`, `units/research-evidence`. No nesting conveys product, layer, team, runtime, generated state, licence, or audience.

`unit.json` is schema-validated and contains: `id`, `kind`, `owners`, `licence`, `provenance`, `refresh`, `distribution`, `audience`, `supportTier`, `qualityProfile`, `consumers`, `provides`, `dependencyPolicy`, and optional `deliveryOf`. `package.json` remains the pnpm/turbo integration carrier; it repeats only package name and scripts, not organisational truth.

A graph compiler reads package imports, declared runtime/service edges, and `consumers`; it produces dependency policy checks, public-API reports, impact sets, forbidden licence edges, cycle checks, and ownership-review requirements. Turbo tasks use metadata-derived tags rather than path globs. Generated content is replaced only by declared generators; vendor content is hash-locked; licence policy rejects mixed licence classes inside a unit and rejects prohibited dependency/distribution combinations.

result.design:
Six independent classifications: (1) unit contract, (2) lifecycle/provenance, (3) licence, (4) surface promise, (5) dependency role, and (6) ownership/risk. A unit is a direct child directory of the repository root, containing only flat files; there are no nested directories. Each unit has `package.json` and `unit.json`. Filenames encode their role, for example `client.source.ts`, `tokens.generated.css`, `snapshot.external.json`, and `logo.brand.svg`. Root files include `unit-registry.json`, `unit-policy.ts`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and `turbo.json`.

A unit exists when any one of its public contract, lifecycle trigger, licence class, deployment/support promise, dependency role, or accountable owner/risk policy differs. Mere implementation size, language, or topic does not create a unit. Package names use `@estate/<root-directory-name>`; direct-root directory names are singular responsibility names in kebab case.

Representative layout: `mcp-curriculum-server/`, `search-cli/`, `demo-curriculum/`, `demo-search/`, `curriculum-client/`, `curriculum-spec-snapshot/`, `curriculum-bulk-data/`, `curriculum-spec-types/`, `bulk-schemas/`, `corpus-miner/`, `curriculum-curated-reference/`, `search-contracts/`, `search-retrieval/`, `search-pipeline-product/`, `foundation-errors/`, `security-path-safety/`, `graph-data/`, `design-system/`, `design-tokens/`, `embedded-widget-source/`, `vendor-widget-files/`, `brand-assets/`, `observability-adapter/`, `agent-tooling-core/`, `agent-cli/`, `commit-guards/`, `repo-state-validator/`, `scheduled-agent-jobs/`, `research-evidence/`, and `live-operations/`.

Generated outputs belong to the unit owning the published or deployed output contract, never to a generic catch-all. The widget source is separate from its served output: `embedded-widget-source/` produces a declared generated artifact in `mcp-curriculum-server/`.

The design answers: what is independently releasable or supportable; what can legally coexist; what refresh/generation event owns an artifact; what may depend on what; what is shipped versus demonstrative, research-only, or operational; and who owns high-risk change decisions.

result.design:
Use a strictly flat physical estate: the repository root contains only root files and one directory per deployable or independently versioned/owned unit. No directory may exist inside a unit. A unit's files are flat and role-prefixed (for example `src-client.ts`, `src-query.ts`, `test-client.ts`, `generated-types.ts`, `asset-logo.svg`). Every unit has a machine-readable `unit.json`; the root has generated `ESTATE.json` and `DEPENDENCY-GRAPH.json`.

A unit is separate only when it has a different public contract, consumer/audience promise, legal reuse condition, execution authority, release/deployment lifecycle, or independently enforceable change boundary. Mere implementation size, language, team, or current folder history never creates a unit. If none differs, keep it together. If two units repeatedly require atomic changes, consolidate them unless an explicit, expiring machine-readable boundary exception records why.

Root layout example: `app-curriculum/`, `app-demo/`, `lib-errors/`, `lib-curriculum-client/`, `lib-graph/`, `lib-search/`, `integration-observability/`, `pipeline-codegen/`, `tool-hooks/`, `tool-operations/`, `data-reference/`, `vendor-brand/`, `evidence-study/`, `generated-tokens/`, `artifact-widget/`, plus root `ESTATE.json`, `DEPENDENCY-GRAPH.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and check configuration files. All source, tests, metadata, assets, and generated files belonging to a unit are direct children of that unit directory.

`unit.json` declares: `kind`, `contract`, `consumers`, `audience`, `supportTier`, `shipClass`, `authority`, `generator` (when applicable), `legalClass`, `publication`, `riskClass`, `qualityProfile`, and `allowedDependencies`. The root index is generated exclusively from these manifests and the import/dependency graph; it is the first machine-readable entry point for people and agents. A `locate` command answers a capability query from that index before opening implementation files.

Naming is semantic and stable: root directory names use `<kind>-<contract>`; files use `<role>-<subject>.<ext>`. `kind` is one of `app`, `lib`, `integration`, `pipeline`, `tool`, `data`, `vendor`, `evidence`, `generated`, or `artifact`. Generated or preserved external files must also begin `generated-`, `snapshot-`, `bulk-`, or `vendor-`, making authority visible at the copy/edit point.

This makes generation authority, legal restrictions, consumer promises, and dependency direction queryable rather than prose-only. It also makes reorganisations inexpensive: imports address declared contracts, not incidental paths; physical moves update the generated graph and import map mechanically; co-change evidence identifies candidate mergers before the layout becomes an obstacle.
