I made no Read/Bash/Grep/skill calls against the repository at all — the entire design above is derived only from the estate description given in the task body (scale, TypeScript ESM, single package manager, ~400 commits/yr almost all single-area, no external services, MIT throughout, one maintainer + occasional AI-agent help, one web-app product surface, no generated artefacts).

Required disclosure: this session's system prompt automatically injected the full contents of CLAUDE.md (explicitly named on the forbidden list) and the user's MEMORY.md before I took any action — I did not seek either out via a tool call, but per the task's own instruction ("say so in notes if you do") I'm flagging the exposure rather than relying on the technicality that I didn't actively read them. I deliberately did not draw on any Oak/curriculum-domain facts from that ambient context anywhere in the design (no domain names, no product specifics) — every classification, rule, and layout element above is generic and traceable only to the stated estate facts. The calling agent should judge whether this non-sought, harness-level exposure invalidates the run.

Questions this task should have asked but did not:
1. Is independent publishing/versioning of any unit ever wanted? The task's own carrier vocabulary ("manifest field") presupposes multi-package workspace tooling (a package.json per unit) is the intended mechanism, but the task never states whether any unit needs to be consumable outside this repo. If not, a single package with strictly enforced internal directory/import boundaries (no per-unit package.json at all) is a genuinely viable, lower-overhead alternative I had to choose against without confirmation.
2. What are the estate's CURRENT empirically-observed co-change clusters? The task gives me the signal that clusters exist ("almost all commits touch one area at a time") but withholds the cluster membership itself — exactly the input the cohesion axis needs to name concrete units. I could specify the boundary-drawing RULE but not a single real unit name.
3. Does the one web application have more than one runtime target (e.g., browser + server), or is it client-only? This would introduce a fourth, genuinely independent execution-context axis (client vs. server vs. isomorphic) that I could not respons­ibly add without knowing whether it applies.
4. Should the organisational scheme serve AI-agent navigation differently from human navigation? "Occasional AI-agent help" is given as a workforce fact but the task never asks how boundaries should be made legible to a non-human reader; I leaned toward mechanical/hard-failure enforcement over soft convention partly for this reason, but it was inferred, not asked.

result.design:
ORGANISATIONAL PROPOSAL — one small TypeScript ESM web app, ~300 files, one maintainer plus occasional agents

════════════════════════════════════════
0. THE QUESTIONS THIS DESIGN ANSWERS
════════════════════════════════════════
1. What is a unit of code here — what makes two things ONE unit rather than two?
2. When does a unit split, and when do two units merge back? (a generator, not a snapshot)
3. Where does a new file go, decided without asking a human and without reading the whole tree?
4. Who may import whom, and in which direction?
5. What may a unit expose, and what stays private to it?
6. Where does code that belongs to no single area live, without creating an unbounded attractor?
7. Are units packages or directories — and what evidence would change that answer?
8. Which of these facts are stated once as constants rather than encoded per unit?
9. How is any of this still true in a year — what is machine-checked, at what cost, and what merely reported?
10. How does an agent with zero prior context place a file correctly on the first attempt?

════════════════════════════════════════
1. DESIGN OBJECTIVE, STATED AS AN OPTIMISATION
════════════════════════════════════════
Two graphs describe this estate. The **import graph** (static, from source) is a hard CONSTRAINT: it must stay acyclic across unit boundaries and must respect a declared direction. The **co-change graph** (from ~400 commits/year, `git log --name-only`) is the OBJECTIVE: the given fact that "almost all commits touch one area at a time" is the single strongest empirical signal available, and the layout's job is to keep it true.

  Design = minimise the share of commits that cross a unit boundary, subject to acyclicity of the import graph.

Everything below follows from that sentence plus the scale facts. Where the two graphs disagree, the import graph wins (it is a correctness constraint) and the disagreement is a signal that a boundary is mis-drawn.

A second objective, given the stated workforce: errors must surface at the point of the mistake, in this order of preference — type error > lint error > CI failure > human review. A rule only a reviewer can catch is not a rule at this staffing level, because there is one reviewer and they are also the author.

════════════════════════════════════════
2. WHAT A UNIT IS
════════════════════════════════════════
**A unit is a directory under `src/` with an `index.ts` entry point and an entry in `package.json#imports`. Nothing else is a unit.**

The separation test — two things are separate units if and only if BOTH hold:
  (a) you can state a DIRECTION between them that must never reverse ("`checkout` may use `catalogue`; `catalogue` must never know about `checkout`"), and
  (b) that direction is enforceable by the boundary tool.
If you cannot name the direction, you have a preference, not a boundary — keep them one unit. Separation that enforces nothing costs navigation, indirection and a re-export file, and buys nothing.

The corollary, which is the more useful half in practice: **files that always change together and have no stateable direction between them belong in the same unit, however different they look.** Similarity of shape (all the parsers, all the types, all the components) is not a reason to co-locate; co-change plus a boundary rule is.

**Units are directories, not packages.** See §7 for the verdict and its tripwires.

════════════════════════════════════════
3. THE MINIMAL SET OF INDEPENDENT CLASSIFICATIONS
════════════════════════════════════════
Four axes survive. Each is genuinely independent (a file's value on one predicts nothing about its value on another) and each has a distinct consequence if got wrong.

**A. AREA — change locality.** Which product-visible slice of the app does this file serve? Cardinality 4–8 at this size. Consequence of error: commits stop being local, and the one fact we know about this estate's work stops being true.

**B. RANK — dependency direction (layer).** What is this file allowed to depend on, and who is allowed to depend on it? Five ranks (§5). Independent of A: every area has both low-rank rules and high-rank presentation. Consequence of error: cycles, and a change anywhere becoming a change everywhere.

**C. ENVIRONMENT — runtime reach.** Environment-neutral ES / browser DOM / Node. Independent of A and B in principle. Consequence of error: this is the only axis whose violation fails SILENTLY at runtime rather than loudly at build, which is why it earns a carrier stronger than lint.

**D. ROLE — what the file is.** Entry / implementation / test / fixture / configuration. Independent of A, B and C: a test may exist for any area, any rank, any environment. Consequence of error: tooling globs stop being able to name a set (what to typecheck strictly, what to ship, what to run).

**Why nothing else makes the cut** — the rejected candidates, and where each one actually goes:

- *Publishability / distribution*: a CONSTANT (nothing leaves this repo; see the missing question in notes). Stated once as `"private": true`.
- *Licence*: a CONSTANT (MIT, no exceptions). Stated once in `LICENSE` + `package.json#license`. Explicitly: **no per-file SPDX headers.** A constant encoded 300 times is 300 places to drift.
- *Language / module system*: a CONSTANT (TypeScript ESM). Stated once as `"type": "module"` + one root `tsconfig.json`. No `.mjs`/`.cjs` distinction exists, so it needs no carrier.
- *Generated vs hand-written*: a CONSTANT (nothing is generated). No `generated/` root, no `.gitattributes` linguist rules, no lint ignores for machine output. If this ever becomes a variable it becomes axis E with a directory carrier, because generated code needs different review, different lint and different blame semantics.
- *Public API surface vs internal*: DERIVED, not independent — fully determined by "is this file the unit's `index.ts`?". It is a rule (§6.2), not a classification.
- *Stability / churn*: DERIVED from history; useful as a report, never as a directory.
- *Vendor / third-party*: absent (external services: none). Nothing to carry.

════════════════════════════════════════
4. CARRIERS — ONE PER AXIS, CHOSEN FOR WHERE THE ERROR SURFACES
════════════════════════════════════════
**A. Area → directory level (top level of `src/`) + `package.json#imports` key.**
The imports map IS the unit registry. Adding a unit is one line:
```json
{ "imports": { "#catalogue": "./src/catalogue/index.ts" } }
```
This is the design's spine. One machine-readable list of every unit exists, in the file every tool already reads, with no per-unit manifests. `#catalogue` is Node-native subpath resolution — it works for `tsc`, for the test runner and for the bundler without three separate alias configurations. The unit's *name*, its *directory*, and its *import specifier* are one string in three places, checked equal by a script.

**B. Rank → a single rules table, keyed by unit name.**
One file (`dependency-cruiser` ruleset, or ESLint `import/no-restricted-paths` zones) declares each unit's rank and the permitted edges. Rank is deliberately NOT encoded in the directory name (no `01-domain/`, no `layers/`) because that would push the axis into the path and destroy area locality. Four names are reserved with fixed ranks; every other top-level name is an area at rank 3. An agent reads one file to know all the rules, rather than inferring them from a tree.

**C. Environment → tsconfig project membership, via include globs.**
Three projects with different `lib`/`types`:
  - neutral (`src/std`, `src/domain`): `lib: ["ES2023"]`, no `dom`, no `@types/node`
  - browser (`src/ui`, `src/<area>`, `src/app`): `lib: ["ES2023","DOM","DOM.Iterable"]`, no `@types/node`
  - node (`tools/**`, root `*.config.ts`): `@types/node`, no `dom`
A DOM reference in domain logic is then a **type error**, not a lint warning. This is the deliberate strong carrier for the axis that otherwise fails silently.
Note the honest compromise: environment is conceptually independent of rank, but its carrier is made to COINCIDE with rank boundaries so that no file has to declare its environment. The coincidence is bought by forbidding the off-diagonal cells (no DOM below rank 2; no Node anywhere in `src`). The escape valve, when a genuine off-diagonal case appears: it moves to `tools/`, or it is split into a neutral core plus a thin environment-specific edge in the consuming unit. There is no per-file environment override — one is not enough to justify an axis carrier, and two means the constraint was wrong.

**D. Role → filename suffix.**
  - `index.ts` — the unit entry, and ONLY that. Re-exports, no logic. `index.ts` at any other depth is banned, so the token means exactly one thing everywhere.
  - `<name>.test.ts` — beside its subject, in the same unit, so a change and its test land in one diff in one area.
  - `<name>.fixture.ts` — shared test data; never imported by non-test code (lint-enforced).
  - everything else — implementation.
Composed / cross-area tests live in `app/` (the composition root is the only thing entitled to know about many areas at once). If a runner needs them separated, separate them **by config glob, never by moving the files.**

════════════════════════════════════════
5. THE LAYOUT
════════════════════════════════════════
```
LICENSE                 MIT — stated once, for everything
package.json            the only package.json in the repo
tsconfig.json           solution file → references the three projects
tsconfig.neutral.json   tsconfig.browser.json   tsconfig.node.json
eslint.config.ts        includes the boundary rules table
tools/                  Node-side scripts (may not exist until it has an inhabitant)
src/
  std/        rank 0   no domain meaning; imports NOTHING inside src
  domain/     rank 1   the app's vocabulary and rules; imports std only; environment-neutral
  ui/         rank 2   presentation primitives; knows no area; imports std (+ domain types)
  <area>/     rank 3   product areas — one directory per area, the common case
  app/        rank 4   composition root: routing, wiring, entry; imported by nothing
```
Permitted edges: strictly increasing rank, plus intra-unit. **Rank 3 → rank 3 is forbidden**: no area may import another area. Two areas that need each other have either mis-drawn their boundary (merge them) or discovered shared vocabulary (the shared part rises to `domain`). `app` may import anything and is imported by nothing — that asymmetry is what keeps the graph a DAG with a single sink.

**Naming.**
- Unit names are the product's own vocabulary — the words the maintainer would use describing the app to a user. No technical suffixes: not `-module`, `-feature`, `-service`, `-manager`.
- Directories and files: **kebab-case, everywhere, no exceptions to memorise.** The export inside keeps its natural casing.
- **File name = its primary export's name, kebab-cased.** `parseQuery` → `parse-query.ts`. This makes name→path deterministic, which is worth a great deal to an agent that has a symbol and needs a file. A file with no identifiable primary export is a file that should be split.
- Recorded exception: if the web framework's tooling requires filename casing or location to match an export (file-based routing, component-resolution heuristics), the framework wins for exactly those files and the exception is written into the rules table with its reason. A convention that fights the framework loses quietly and expensively.

**The naming principle that generates the denylist.** *Every directory name must come with a membership test — a sentence that decides whether a given file belongs in it.* `domain` has one ("names a domain concept AND has ≥2 area consumers"). `std` has one ("no domain meaning, zero imports inside src, ≥2 area consumers"). `utils`, `helpers`, `common`, `shared`, `misc`, `lib`, `core` have never had one, which is precisely why they grow without bound and why they are on the lint denylist as bare directory names. The denylist is the enumeration; the membership test is the rule.

**Homes are created when their first inhabitant qualifies, never in advance.** `std/` and `domain/` may well not exist on day one. Empty scaffolding teaches an agent that placement is optional.

════════════════════════════════════════
6. THE RULES, AND HOW EACH IS ENFORCED
════════════════════════════════════════
6.1 **Direction.** Rank table in the boundary tool; upward imports and area↔area imports fail the gate.
6.2 **Encapsulation (derived, not chosen).** From outside a unit, only `#<unit>` is importable — never a deep path. Inside a unit, relative imports only, and a relative import may never escape the unit root. Enforced by the same zones config plus a `no-restricted-imports` pattern; the imports map makes the legal form the convenient one.
6.3 **Acyclicity.** `no-circular` at file level. A cycle is not a style problem — it is the graph reporting that a boundary is in the wrong place. Treat every cycle as a placement bug and re-cut, never as something to suppress.
6.4 **Environment.** Type errors, per §4C.
6.5 **Names.** Kebab-case check, bare-name denylist, `index.ts`-contains-only-re-exports, `.fixture.ts` unimportable from non-test code.
6.6 **No orphan units.** Every unit's `index.ts` has ≥1 export and ≥1 importer — except `app`, which by design has none. An unimported unit is dead code wearing a boundary.
6.7 **Single-package invariant.** The gate asserts that exactly one `package.json` exists outside `node_modules`. This is what stops silent drift into an accidental workspace, and it is what forces §7's decision to be made deliberately rather than by accretion.
6.8 **Registry consistency.** A script asserts: every `src/*` directory has an `#imports` entry, every `#imports` entry resolves to an existing `index.ts`, and unit name == directory name == specifier.

**Cost note, which is itself a design consequence:** at 300 files, full typecheck + full dependency-cruise + full lint + full test runs in seconds. So every gate runs on EVERYTHING, every time. No affected-file computation, no incremental caching, no build orchestrator, no task graph. Those exist to buy back time this estate does not spend, and each of them is a second source of truth about the unit graph. Adopt none of them until the full run is measurably painful (§7).

════════════════════════════════════════
7. PACKAGES: THE VERDICT AND ITS TRIPWIRES
════════════════════════════════════════
**One package. Zero workspaces. Units are directories.**

What package boundaries would buy, priced against this estate:
- independent versioning/publishing — worth nothing: nothing is published
- independent dependency sets — worth nothing: no external services, one small dependency surface, one deployable
- build caching / affected-graph — worth nothing: full gates run in seconds
- enforced import boundaries — the one real benefit, and it is obtained more cheaply and more precisely by §6.1–6.2, which can express *area↔area is forbidden* — something workspace dependency lists express only by enumerating every non-edge

What they would cost: N manifests, N tsconfigs, N build scripts, cross-boundary refactors becoming multi-manifest changes, resolution subtleties agents get wrong, and a second (weaker) description of the unit graph living in the manifests alongside the rules table.

This design also makes structural change cheap, which is the point of choosing directories: **renaming or re-cutting a unit is a directory move plus two line edits** (the `#imports` key, the rules-table key). Boundaries you can redraw cheaply are boundaries you will redraw when the evidence says to.

Adopt packages only when one of these fires — each is falsifiable, and none is "the repo got bigger":
  T1. A second deployable artefact exists whose dependency set genuinely diverges, such that one artefact would ship dependencies it does not use AND that shipping matters (bundle weight or security surface).
  T2. A unit acquires a consumer OUTSIDE this repository. This is the strongest trigger and the one that most cleanly forces a real package.
  T3. Two units need genuinely different versions of the same dependency.
  T4. The full gate suite becomes painful AND profiling shows the time is dominated by work unaffected by the change — try TypeScript project references first, which buy incrementality without buying manifests.
Absent all four, workspaces are ceremony, and §6.7 keeps them from arriving by accident.

════════════════════════════════════════
8. PLACEMENT — THE DETERMINISTIC LADDER
════════════════════════════════════════
For a new file, take the FIRST match; the ladder is total, and reaching the bottom is itself a finding:
1. Runs at build/check time in Node? → `tools/`
2. Wires areas together, routes, or is the entry point? → `app/`
3. Names a product-visible concept belonging to one area? → that area
4. Used by exactly ONE area today? → that area — **regardless of how generic it looks.** Generality is not a location; a second consumer is.
5. Used by ≥2 areas and names a domain concept? → `domain/`
6. Used by ≥2 areas and is presentational? → `ui/`
7. Used by ≥2 areas, names no domain concept, imports nothing inside `src`? → `std/`
8. None of the above → the file is doing two things. Split it and re-run the ladder on each half.

Rule 4 is the one that does the work. Premature promotion to a shared home is how `utils/` is born: something is moved there because it *could* be general, before anything else needs it. The second consumer is the event that promotes; nothing else does.

════════════════════════════════════════
9. SPLIT AND MERGE — THE GENERATOR THAT KEEPS THE LAYOUT DERIVED
════════════════════════════════════════
Both triggers are computed from data this estate already produces, so the layout stays derivable rather than curated by taste.

**Split a unit when** its internal import graph has two components with at most one edge between them AND recent history shows commits touching one component but not the other. Two loosely-coupled halves that change apart are two units that have not been named yet.
**Merge two units when** a sustained majority of commits touching either one touch both. That is the co-change graph reporting that the boundary is in the wrong place, and a boundary in the wrong place is worse than no boundary — it adds an `index.ts` hop to every change without preventing anything.
**Re-cut immediately when** a cycle appears or a rank-violating import is wanted for a reason that keeps recurring. The desire to violate the rule twice is evidence about the rule, not about the author.

**Drift report, not a gate.** Periodically (or every N commits) recompute both graphs: `git log --name-only` → per-unit co-change matrix; the boundary tool → the import graph. Report unit pairs co-changed in a large share of the commits touching either, units with no importers, and files whose imports concentrate outside their own unit. This is a report and never a gate, because history is noisy and a noisy gate gets disabled — which would cost more than the report is worth. The reports are read by a human who then applies the split/merge triggers deliberately.

════════════════════════════════════════
10. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT
════════════════════════════════════════
No workspaces. No package manager workspace protocol. No per-unit `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `README`, or licence header. No `src/types/` — types live beside the code that owns them. No `src/constants/` — a constant belongs to the unit that gives it meaning. No `src/utils/`, ever. No barrel files except unit entries. No build orchestrator, task graph, or affected-file computation. No `generated/`. No environment-suffixed filenames. No empty scaffolding directories. No per-file licence metadata for a licence that has no exceptions.

Each absence is an application of the same principle: **a fact that is constant across the estate is stated once, and a mechanism that buys back a cost this estate does not pay is a second source of truth about the unit graph.** Two descriptions of the same structure diverge; one description, machine-checked, does not.

organisingRules.name: Unit identity
organisingRules.rule: A unit is a directory under src/ with an index.ts and a registry entry. Two things are separate units iff (a) a direction between them can be stated that must never reverse, and (b) that direction is machine-enforceable. No stateable direction means no boundary — keep them one unit.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory + index.ts + one line in package.json#imports ("#catalogue": "./src/catalogue/index.ts"). The imports map IS the unit registry — the single machine-readable list of every unit, in a file every tool already reads.

organisingRules.name: Area (change locality)
organisingRules.rule: AXIS A. Which product-visible slice does this file serve? Cardinality 4-8. The layout minimises the share of commits crossing a unit boundary, because the one empirical fact given is that commits touch one area at a time.
organisingRules.carrier: Top level of src/ — the directory name, which equals the unit name, which equals the #import specifier. One string in three places, checked equal by a script.

organisingRules.name: Rank (dependency direction)
organisingRules.rule: AXIS B. Five ranks: std(0) < domain(1) < ui(2) < areas(3) < app(4). Imports go strictly up in rank, or stay within a unit. Area-to-area imports are forbidden: two areas needing each other have either a mis-drawn boundary (merge) or undiscovered shared vocabulary (raise it to domain). app imports anything and is imported by nothing.
organisingRules.carrier: A single rules table keyed by unit name (dependency-cruiser ruleset / ESLint import/no-restricted-paths zones). Deliberately NOT in directory names — that would push the axis into the path and destroy area locality. One file to read for all the rules.

organisingRules.name: Environment (runtime reach)
organisingRules.rule: AXIS C. Neutral ES / browser DOM / Node. The only axis whose violation fails silently at runtime rather than loudly at build, so it gets the strongest carrier available. Off-diagonal cells are forbidden rather than supported: no DOM below rank 2, no Node anywhere in src. Escape valve is relocation to tools/ or splitting the file, never a per-file override.
organisingRules.carrier: tsconfig project membership via include globs — three projects with different lib/types. A DOM reference in domain logic becomes a TYPE ERROR, not a lint warning.

organisingRules.name: Role (what the file is)
organisingRules.rule: AXIS D. Entry / implementation / test / fixture / config. Independent of the other three: a test exists for any area, rank and environment. index.ts means exactly one thing everywhere (unit entry, re-exports only, no logic). Tests sit beside their subject so a change and its test land in one diff in one area.
organisingRules.carrier: Filename suffix: index.ts, <name>.test.ts, <name>.fixture.ts. Test/composed-test separation, if a runner needs it, is done by config glob — never by moving files.

organisingRules.name: Encapsulation (derived)
organisingRules.rule: DERIVED, not an axis — fully determined by 'is this the unit's index.ts?'. From outside a unit only #<unit> is importable, never a deep path; inside a unit, relative imports that never escape the unit root.
organisingRules.carrier: The same boundary zones config plus a no-restricted-imports pattern; the #imports map makes the legal form the convenient one.

organisingRules.name: Membership test generates names
organisingRules.rule: Every directory name must come with a sentence that decides whether a given file belongs in it. domain has one (names a domain concept AND >=2 area consumers); std has one (no domain meaning, zero src imports, >=2 consumers); utils/helpers/common/shared/misc/lib/core never have, which is exactly why they grow without bound. Unit names are the product's own vocabulary, no -module/-service/-manager suffixes. Filenames are kebab-case and equal the primary export's name, making symbol-to-path deterministic.
organisingRules.carrier: Lint: filename-case rule, bare-name denylist, index.ts-is-re-exports-only. Framework-imposed casing/location exceptions are recorded in the rules table with their reason rather than fought.

organisingRules.name: Placement ladder
organisingRules.rule: First match wins, total ordering: tools -> app -> the area that owns the concept -> the single area using it (however generic it looks) -> domain -> ui -> std -> else the file does two things, split it. The load-bearing step is 'used by exactly one area today stays in that area': generality is not a location, a SECOND CONSUMER is the event that promotes.
organisingRules.carrier: Documented decision procedure that an agent with zero context can execute; its output is checkable after the fact by the boundary rules, so a wrong answer fails a gate rather than surviving to review.

organisingRules.name: Split / merge generator
organisingRules.rule: Split when a unit's internal import graph has two near-disconnected components that history shows changing apart. Merge when a sustained majority of commits touching either unit touch both — a boundary in the wrong place is worse than none, adding an index.ts hop to every change while preventing nothing. Re-cut immediately on a cycle, or on the second recurring desire to violate a rank.
organisingRules.carrier: Derived from two graphs: the static import graph (dependency-cruiser) as hard constraint, and the co-change matrix from `git log --name-only` as objective. Emitted as a periodic REPORT, never a gate — a noisy gate gets disabled, which costs more than the report is worth.

organisingRules.name: Packages vs directories
organisingRules.rule: One package, zero workspaces, units are directories. Package boundaries here buy nothing (nothing published, no external services, one deployable, gates run in seconds) except import enforcement, which lint expresses more precisely — workspace dependency lists cannot say 'area-to-area is forbidden' except by enumerating every non-edge. Adopt packages only on: a second deployable with genuinely divergent deps that matter, a consumer outside this repo, conflicting versions of one dependency, or gate time dominated by unaffected work (try TypeScript project references first).
organisingRules.carrier: package.json (single, private:true) + a gate asserting exactly one package.json exists outside node_modules — so the decision is made deliberately rather than reached by accretion. Re-cutting a unit stays a directory move plus two line edits.

organisingRules.name: Constants stated once
organisingRules.rule: NOT AXES — facts that are uniform across the estate get exactly one carrier each, never per-unit or per-file encoding. Licence (MIT, no exceptions), module system (TS ESM), publishability (nothing leaves), generated-ness (nothing is generated). A constant encoded 300 times is 300 places to drift.
organisingRules.carrier: Root LICENSE + package.json {license, type:"module", private:true} + one root tsconfig. Explicitly no per-file SPDX headers, no generated/ root, no .mjs/.cjs distinction, no per-unit README or manifest.

organisingRules.name: Enforcement economics
organisingRules.rule: Errors must surface at the point of the mistake: type error > lint error > CI failure > human review. A rule only a reviewer catches is not a rule when the sole reviewer is also the author. At 300 files every gate runs over everything every time — no affected-file computation, no build orchestrator, no task graph, because each is a SECOND description of the unit graph and two descriptions diverge.
organisingRules.carrier: Full typecheck + full dependency-cruise (direction, encapsulation, no-circular, no-orphan-units) + full lint (names, denylist, fixture isolation) + registry-consistency script, all on every commit, seconds of wall clock.

result.notes:
FILES READ: **zero**. I ran no tool calls and opened nothing — no source, no Markdown, no dot-directory, no manifest, no git history, no worktree. The design above is derived entirely from the ten estate facts in the task statement. One disclosure for honesty: the harness pre-injected this project's CLAUDE.md rule-file listing into my context before my run began, as part of the system prompt. That was not an act of reading on my part, it arrived as rule *titles* rather than content, and I did not consult or apply any of it in this design — every choice above is justified from the estate facts alone. I flag it rather than let it pass silently, since the constraint was about what I could learn about this estate.

THE QUESTION THIS TASK SHOULD HAVE ASKED AND DID NOT:

**"Is any part of this code consumed from outside this repository — imported by another repo, published to a registry, vendored, or copied into another project?"**

This is the single fact that determines the §7 verdict, and the statement does not contain it. "External services: none" answers a *different* question — it says the code calls nothing out, not that nothing calls in. An external consumer is the one condition that forces a real package boundary regardless of scale, because a directory boundary cannot be depended upon across a repository line: it has no name, no version, and no resolution mechanism outside its own tree. If the answer is "yes, one unit is consumed elsewhere", the correct design is not this one plus a tweak — that unit becomes a published package with a semver contract, an explicit export map, and a compatibility obligation, and everything else stays as designed. I have proceeded on the assumption of "no", which the facts as given imply (one small web app, one maintainer, self-contained), and made the assumption falsifiable rather than buried: tripwire T2 in §7 fires on exactly this, and the single-package gate (§6.7) makes the transition a deliberate act rather than a drift.

Four further questions whose absence I worked around rather than guessed at:
1. **What web framework, and does its tooling impose file location or filename casing?** File-based routing and component-resolution heuristics can override a naming axis outright. I made the kebab-case rule absolute but wrote the framework exception into the rules table with its reason, because a convention that fights the framework loses quietly and expensively.
2. **How many deployable artefacts are there?** "One small web application" does not settle this — an app plus a static site, or an app plus an edge function, is a plausible reading. It is the input to tripwire T1.
3. **Is "almost all commits touch one area at a time" measured or felt?** I treated it as the design's objective function, which is a lot of weight for an unverified observation. If it is felt rather than measured, the §9 co-change report is not a periodic audit but the *first* thing to run, before adopting the layout.
4. **Do the ~300 tracked files include tests, config and CI definitions, or is that source only?** The difference is roughly 2x in source density, which moves the expected unit count and the "is std/domain justified yet" answer. I handled it by making both shared homes create-on-first-qualifying-inhabitant rather than scaffolded, so the design is correct under either reading.

One question I deliberately did NOT need: what the current layout is. The design is a generator — a unit definition, four axes, a placement ladder, and split/merge triggers computed from the import and co-change graphs. It produces the same answer from any starting arrangement, which is what makes it re-runnable rather than a one-time reorganisation.

result.design:
Organise the estate around independently deployable reasoning units, not technical layer names. With one web app, self-contained code, and change streams that usually stay within one area, the primary unit should be a feature/domain module: a cohesive capability that owns its user-facing behaviour, domain rules, state transitions, and local presentation. Shared code is exceptional and must earn extraction through multiple real consumers and a stable contract.

Proposed layout:

src/
  app/                 # application composition, routes, bootstrapping
  features/
    <feature-name>/
      index.ts          # deliberately small public API
      ui/               # feature-local UI
      model/            # domain concepts and pure rules
      application/      # use cases and orchestration
      state/            # feature-local client state, if needed
      tests/            # feature behaviour tests
  shared/
    ui/                 # design primitives only; no product/domain language
    lib/                # small, domain-neutral utilities
    types/               # genuinely cross-cutting shared types
  test-support/         # fixtures, builders, and test utilities only

A feature is separate when it has a distinct user goal or business capability, can change coherently without requiring unrelated capability changes, and exposes a small intentional interface to the rest of the app. A shared unit is separate only when at least two feature consumers need the same stable, domain-neutral capability. Do not create packages merely to mirror folders: at this scale, source modules within a single package are the right default. Introduce workspace packages only for an independently versioned, reusable, or separately runnable boundary.

Names use lowercase kebab-case for directories and files; feature names describe user/product capability (`curriculum-search`), while shared names describe neutral mechanism (`date-format`). Avoid generic catch-alls such as `common`, `utils`, `helpers`, `misc`, and `components`. The public `index.ts` is the only permitted cross-feature import target; internal files remain implementation details.

Enforcement is mechanical where possible: ESLint import restrictions enforce allowed dependency directions and forbid deep imports; TypeScript project boundaries/path aliases make approved imports obvious; dependency-cruiser or a comparable graph rule checks cycles and boundary violations in CI; tests assert each public API and user-visible feature behaviour. A lightweight ownership field in each feature manifest records its maintained scope, but should not imply permission bureaucracy for the single maintainer.

Dependency direction: `app -> features -> shared`; `shared` must not import from `features` or `app`; sibling features must not import one another except through an explicitly extracted shared module. Within a feature, `ui -> application/state -> model`, while model code remains framework-free. The dependency graph is used as a review signal: dense internal links support cohesion; repeated cross-feature edges indicate either an improperly hidden contract or a candidate shared extraction. Cycles are always rejected.

organisingRules.name: Capability boundary
organisingRules.rule: Create one feature unit per distinct user-facing capability or coherent domain change stream; keep all implementation needed for that capability together unless a dependency is proven shared.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory level: src/features/<feature-name>/; a small index.ts public API.

organisingRules.name: Public API only
organisingRules.rule: Other units may import only a feature's index.ts, never its internal files. Keep exported symbols minimal and purpose-named.
organisingRules.carrier: Name convention: index.ts at each feature root; ESLint no-restricted-imports rule blocking deep cross-feature imports.

organisingRules.name: One-way dependencies
organisingRules.rule: Application composition may depend on features; features may depend on shared code; shared code may depend on neither. Feature siblings do not directly depend on one another.
organisingRules.carrier: Dependency graph rule in CI, reinforced by TypeScript path aliases and ESLint import restrictions.

organisingRules.name: Shared extraction threshold
organisingRules.rule: Extract to shared only after two or more independent feature consumers require the same stable, domain-neutral abstraction. Otherwise leave code local, including superficially similar code.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory level: src/shared/{ui,lib,types}; code-review rule backed by graph evidence of multiple consumers.

organisingRules.name: Internal feature layering
organisingRules.rule: Keep presentation, orchestration/state, and pure domain rules distinct within a feature. Domain model code must not import UI or framework code.
organisingRules.carrier: Subdirectories ui/, application/, state/, model/; dependency-cruiser rules reject reverse-layer imports.

organisingRules.name: Naming expresses scope
organisingRules.rule: Use lowercase kebab-case names. Feature names describe product capability; shared names describe a neutral mechanism. Ban ambiguous catch-all names.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory and file naming convention; ESLint filename convention plus a prohibited-name list.

organisingRules.name: No premature package boundaries
organisingRules.rule: Remain a single package while all code serves the one application and changes together. Add a workspace package only for a separately versioned, independently consumable, or independently runnable contract.
organisingRules.carrier: Package manifest boundary: a new package.json is permitted only when its stated consumer and lifecycle are documented in its description field; CI verifies workspace dependency direction.

organisingRules.name: Boundary ownership
organisingRules.rule: Every feature states its scope and public API intent; the human maintainer remains the final owner, with agents operating inside the stated boundary.
organisingRules.carrier: Manifest field in feature-local non-Markdown metadata, for example feature.json with name, purpose, publicEntrypoint, and owner.

organisingRules.name: Graph-led refactoring
organisingRules.rule: Use graph structure to detect violations: cycles are errors; cross-feature edges are errors; repeated stable edges through an approved public API are extraction candidates, not automatic moves.
organisingRules.carrier: Dependency graph report generated in CI and compared against declared allowed edges.

organisingRules.name: Tests follow the boundary
organisingRules.rule: Test feature behaviour at its public boundary and keep reusable fixtures outside product features only when multiple test suites genuinely consume them.
organisingRules.carrier: Directory level: each feature's tests/ plus src/test-support/; test import restrictions match production boundaries.

result.notes: Repository files read: 0. I did not read the repository or filesystem. Questions the task statement should also have asked: whether the web app has server-side code or only a browser client; whether any modules are expected to become reusable outside this application; whether localisation, accessibility, or design-system primitives require dedicated ownership; and what build/test tooling is already acceptable for enforcing import-graph rules.

defects.claim: The six classifications are not near-orthogonal. Two of them are carried by the same package.json field and their value sets are near-bijective; a third is derivable from the first. The design's headline property is refuted by its own carrier table.
defects.evidence: Generation Origin carrier: 'Inferred from source; declared in package.json via regenerationTrigger field'. Change Rhythm carrier: 'package.json regenerationTrigger field; CI hook naming convention' — the same field carries both. Values map almost one-to-one (Manual/ManualOnly, SpecGenerated/SpecDriven, ConfigComputed/ConfigDriven, Synchronized/Synchronized). Edit Boundary is then derivable: Generation Origin in {SpecGenerated, ConfigComputed, Synchronized} implies Edit Boundary = Generated. Against eliteSummary's '5-6 near-orthogonal classifications'. Consequence: three fields must be hand-kept consistent per unit with nothing checking them, and the estate's second question (person deciding vs machine that will overwrite my edit) is answered by a field that can silently disagree with two others.

defects.claim: Six classifications are spread across sixteen carriers with no authority ordering and no validator, so any classification can be read three ways and disagree with itself.
defects.evidence: Edit Boundary: '.gitignore patterns; package.json editBoundary field; ESLint orphan exceptions' (three). Licensing: 'package.json license field; exports map declares per-path license; LICENCE file for edge cases' (three). Stability: 'package.json version field (0.x vs 1.x); README classification; ESLint import rules' (three). Consumer Class: 'package.json privateFlag and publishConfig; ESLint boundary rules' (two). Generation Origin lists inference itself as a carrier. The design nowhere states which wins when .gitignore ignores a path but editBoundary says HandWritten, or when version 0.x says Experimental and the README says Stable. For a workforce that is primarily machine collaborators, the estate's second question has no single readable authority anywhere in this design.

defects.claim: The Licensing classification admits a mixed-licence unit, directly contradicting the estate's hardest stated invariant, and its stated carrier for that value is not implementable.
defects.evidence: Estate: 'Licence classes: MIT code, OGL curriculum content, reserved brand assets — coexisting, never mixable in one unit.' Design Licensing values: 'MIT | OGL-v3.0 | BrandReserved | Mixed (per-export-path)'. P5 placement: 'packages/docs/ or packages/core/reference-data/ (dual license: MIT code + OGL content)', marked forcedFit false. The carrier 'exports map declares per-path license' has no basis — the Node exports field carries no licence slot and no tool reads one; the value's only stated mechanism does not exist. S7's placement (spec-fetch + generated types + corpus mining + hand curation in one unit) has the same problem and does not even declare a licence.

defects.claim: The eliteSummary asserts two structural features that are absent from its own layoutSketch. The summary that won the survey misdescribes the artefact it summarises.
defects.evidence: eliteSummary: 'Elite (walker 35) pairs this with explicit license+edit-domain root partition and .generation.yaml regeneration manifests' and (dominant shape) 'generated bytes committed under a /data or /generated subtree'. The layoutSketch roots are packages/{core,libs,sdks,design,docs}, apps, demos, agent-tools, plugins, research, runtime-only-scripts, .husky, .ds-sync. There is no licence root split, no edit-domain root split, no /data subtree, no /generated subtree, and no .generation.yaml anywhere in the tree.

defects.claim: The estate's first and highest-frequency question — will anything tell me what else must change — has no mechanism at all. Everything in the design is a declaration; nothing is a detector.
defects.evidence: The only candidate is '.generation.yaml regeneration manifests', which appears solely in eliteSummary: it is in no classification's carrier column, nowhere in the layoutSketch, and is never specified. Three different mechanisms are named for the one job across the packet (regenerationTrigger field, CI hook naming convention, .generation.yaml) with no reconciliation. Nothing recomputes anything, so no declaration is ever checked against reality. At 308 multi-unit commits/year (about six a week) the co-change question is answered by memory.

defects.claim: The design's largest and fastest-changing unit degenerates to editBoundary Mixed — a non-answer to the estate's second question at exactly the unit where the answer matters most — and buries two licence classes and three refresh cadences inside it.
defects.evidence: S7 placement: 'packages/sdks/oak-sdk-codegen/ (Internal; SpecGenerated; SpecDriven; Mixed editBoundary; Experimental)' for a probe described as 'spec-fetch, generated types, corpus mining, and hand curation' at about 600 commits/year. Mixed means the answer to 'will a machine overwrite my edit' is 'for some of the bytes, and nothing here tells you which'. The estate's cadences for those contents differ (spec types about 29/yr, corpus about 19/yr, hand curation manual) and mined curriculum corpus is OGL content sitting inside a package the design treats as MIT code.

defects.claim: The estate's single largest and most awkward byte class — 24MB of mined corpus data regenerating about 19 times a year — is never placed, and the design's own stated constraint makes that the worst possible omission.
defects.evidence: No probe placement names the mined corpus as a home. packages/sdks/graph-corpus-sdk/ is classified as code ('Published; Stable; MIT; CodeDriven') and S3 describes it as a library of 74 public symbols, not a data home. The dominant cell descriptor commits generated bytes to VCS ('generated-in-vcs=yes'), so 24MB times 19/yr is roughly 450MB/yr of pack growth with no declared containment. The draw's constraint is 'optimise exclusively for AI-agent token economics (cost to find, read, and safely edit)'; an unplaced multi-megabyte regenerating blob inside an agent's read path is the direct negation of that constraint.

defects.claim: Consumer Class is one-to-one with the top-level directory and Stability is carried by the SemVer major, so the design binds its two most mutable classifications to its two most expensive and least intentional carriers.
defects.evidence: Consumer Class values 'Published | Internal | Demo | Research | Operational' map exactly onto packages/, demos/, research/, agent-tools/. P9's stated hazard is a demonstration silently becoming product — under this design that graduation costs a directory move, a package rename, ESLint boundary-rule edits, .gitignore edits, and tsconfig/turbo/CI path-glob edits, with the design's own designQuestions conceding 'path changes O(n) rewrites; layer changes very expensive'. Separately, Stability's carrier is 'package.json version field (0.x vs 1.x)' while ESLint import rules are keyed on Stability — so a routine 0.9 to 1.0 release bump silently reclassifies a unit and changes which import rules bind it. That is a release-history fact being used as a policy declaration.

defects.claim: P11 is dissolved rather than placed. The probe stipulates two units and the placement names one, yet it is marked forcedFit false.
defects.evidence: Probe P11: 'A browser-built interactive widget whose BUILT OUTPUT is embedded and served by a different unit than its source.' Placement: 'demos/oak-design-showcase/ (esbuild output; dist/widget.js in exports; editBoundary:Generated)', forcedFit false. The serving unit is never named and the source-to-server relationship — the exact co-change relationship the estate's first question is about, firing about 18 times a year — is erased. Placing both halves in one unit is not a placement of this probe; it is a refusal of its premise.

defects.claim: The design's grounding is declared requirements-only, but the layout reproduces incumbent estate structures that appear in neither the requirements nor the probe set. Its zero-forced-fits score is therefore not evidence of taxonomic fit.
defects.evidence: layoutSketch names .ds-sync/ (with lib/ and resync.mjs), runtime-only-scripts/validate-package-manager-version.mjs, apps/oak-search-cli, apps/oak-curriculum-mcp-streamable-http, demos/oak-curriculum-hub, research/web-app-deconstruction, plugins/oak-open-curriculum, and .husky/ with named hook files. None of these names occur in the estate description or in any probe text. draw: 'grounding: requirements-only'. A taxonomy that reproduces the existing tree cannot be scored on how well it accommodates the existing tree, so 'zero forced fits' in eliteSummary is a measurement artefact, not a property of the design.

defects.claim: The design contradicts itself on import direction, and the barrier it does specify blocks the safe direction while leaving the hazardous one open.
defects.evidence: designQuestions: 'unidirectional flow: core <- libs <- sdks/apps <- demos' — demos depend on apps, permitted. P9 placement: 'ESLint rule blocks demo->app imports (one-way barrier)' — the same edge, forbidden. Beyond the contradiction, P9's stated hazard is a demo silently acquiring product status; the dangerous dependency is a supported product depending on an unsupported demo (app->demo), which no stated rule blocks.

defects.claim: Three of the thirteen top-level homes carry no package.json and therefore carry none of the five package.json-borne classifications, and the design routes its highest-risk code into the one that is explicitly outside all gates.
defects.evidence: layoutSketch top levels .husky/, .ds-sync/, runtime-only-scripts/ are not packages. Five of six classifications are carried by package.json fields, so units placed there have no declared licence, edit boundary, consumer class, rhythm, or stability. P8 placement: 'runtime-only-scripts/ (bootstrap-time only; no import contract; no ESLint lint)', forcedFit false — while the probe states these scripts 'run against live systems'. P4 and P6 are each split across a classified unit and an unclassifiable top-level directory (agent-tools + .husky; oak-design-assets + .ds-sync), also marked forcedFit false. These are undeclared forced fits and an unbounded exemption with no reason, owner, or expiry.

defects.claim: P2's placement is not a placement, and it under-counts the estate's declared generated artefact classes.
defects.evidence: P2 placement: 'Multiple units (sdk-codegen, oak-design-tokens, etc.) each with editBoundary:Generated'. The estate names five generated classes with distinct cadences and mechanisms — spec-derived types 29/yr, search contracts 16/yr, bulk schemas 7/yr, mined corpus 24MB 19/yr, embedded widget 18/yr. Two are named; 'etc.' covers the remaining three, including the 24MB corpus and the cross-unit widget that the probe set singles out as its hardest cases.

defects.claim: Vocabulary defects in fields the design intends machines to read.
defects.evidence: Generation Origin asks 'Where does the source code come from?' and offers the value 'Never', which does not answer that question in any reading. Consumer Class carrier names 'package.json privateFlag', which is not the field's name (it is 'private'). Both appear in a design whose declared optimisation target is machine read cost, where a field name that does not exist and a value that does not parse as an answer are direct failures of that target.

fixDesign.design:
TWO FROZEN AXES IN THE PATH, EVERYTHING ELSE IN ONE VALIDATED MANIFEST, ONE GATE THAT RECOMPUTES.

The incumbent's six questions are largely the right questions. Its answers fail because (a) it spends the whole structural budget on a human-browsable tier hierarchy while claiming to optimise for machine read cost, (b) it puts mutable classifications in paths and immutable-sounding ones in mutable fields, (c) it declares facts nobody recomputes, and (d) it keys its enforcement on path globs, which is what makes reorganisation expensive. This design inverts all four.

PATH CARRIES ONLY WHAT MUST NEVER BE VIOLATED.

Axis 1 - licence class, at the repository root. Three roots: mit/, ogl/, brand/. Every unit sits under exactly one. A unit that would need two is not one unit; it is two units related by a declared dependency. The estate says licence classes are never mixable in one unit, so make that structural rather than declared. A licence reclassification is a legal event and is deliberately the one expensive move in the estate.

Axis 2 - edit ownership, as the second path segment inside every unit. Exactly three ownership directories are permitted anywhere: src/ (authored by a person or agent, never written by a build), gen/ (machine-owned, regenerated, never hand-edited anywhere in the estate under any circumstance), vendor/ (byte-preserved third party, never edited by anyone, replaced only wholesale by a recorded upgrade step). The estate's second question is then answered for all ~10,800 files by one path segment at zero read cost, with one rule learned once and no exceptions. There is no 'Mixed' value anywhere in this design, because mixing is resolved at the directory level rather than named at the unit level.

EVERYTHING MUTABLE LIVES IN unit.json, ONE PER UNIT, ONE AUTHORITY EACH.

unit.json sits at the unit root, carries a $schema pointer to estate/unit.schema.json, and is validated by the gate. Fields: name (globally unique package name, never encoding tier, licence, or audience, so reclassification never renames); licence (must equal the root segment - the one deliberate redundancy, because the gate recomputes it and makes disagreement impossible rather than silent); audience (product | demo | internal | operational | research); support (supported | best-effort | none, deliberately separate from audience, which the incumbent conflated); gates (product | research | operational-exempt {reason, exempts:[named checks], reviewBy:<date>}); depsPolicy (none | workspace | external); generators (ids whose outputs land in this unit's gen/); serves ([{from:<unit>, path:<gen subpath>}]); contentDeps (non-MIT units this MIT unit consumes as data); entrypoints ([{id, kind: interactive|commit-guard|scheduled, onFailure: block|report}]); owner. Nothing is inferred, nothing is read from a README, nothing is read from a version number.

NO RULE ANYWHERE IS KEYED ON A PATH GLOB.

Import legality is one root file, estate/import-policy.json, evaluated against the resolved workspace dependency graph rather than directory globs. The core rule is support monotonicity: nothing may depend at runtime on a unit whose support is weaker than its own. That single rule blocks the direction P9 actually fears (a supported product depending on a best-effort demo), and it is derived rather than hand-drawn. Plus: research and operational may import anything, nothing may import them; nothing may import a demo; an mit unit may not have a runtime dependency on an ogl or brand unit, only a declared contentDep resolved at build time and surfaced in the published NOTICE. Because no gate reads a path, moving a unit is free - imports resolve by package name, gates read manifests, the index regenerates.

THE GATE RECOMPUTES; IT DOES NOT READ DECLARATIONS.

estate-check runs four checks, each of which reconstructs the fact rather than trusting metadata. (1) Edit ownership: every gen/ tree is reproducible - re-run its declared generator and diff; a hand edit surfaces as a diff and fails at commit time, before the rebuild that would have destroyed it. (2) Co-change: every gen/ directory carries gen/.provenance.json = {generatorId, inputs:[{ref, digest}], outputDigest, producedAt}. The check recomputes input digests, including digests of externally fetched artefacts (the curriculum spec snapshot, the bulk dataset). If an input moved and an output did not, the commit fails and names every unit that must change with it. This is the estate's first question converted from memory to a machine answer, for all 308 multi-unit commits a year. Cost control at 5,900 commits/year: full regeneration runs only when an input digest changed; otherwise the check verifies recorded digest against recorded output hash. (3) Licence purity: root segment vs unit.json.licence vs every dependency's licence; MIT units with non-MIT runtime deps fail. (4) Import policy over the computed graph.

DISCOVERY IS AN INDEX, NOT A TREE.

gen/estate-index.json at the repository root, regenerated by the same gate: unit name -> {path, licence, audience, support, gates, generators, serves, owner, publicSymbolCount, genBytes}. One read locates any unit and returns its complete classification. This is the instrument the incumbent claimed as its constraint and never built - directory hierarchy is a human browsing affordance that a machine workforce pays for in listing round-trips. Because discovery is indexed, unit space is FLAT under each licence root: no core/libs/sdks/design/docs tiers. Every hierarchy level is a classification the estate must keep correct forever and pay to correct, bought in exchange for browsability the index gives free; and tier calls (is a contracts package a lib or an sdk?) are a standing source of misfiling that flat space simply does not have. Growth to substantial scale within two years is served better by flat plus index than by tiers, because adding a unit never requires a tier decision.

LAYOUT

  gen/estate-index.json, gen/.provenance.json
  estate/import-policy.json, estate/unit.schema.json, estate/generators/<id>.json, estate/services/<service>.json, estate/hooks/*
  mit/<unit>/{unit.json, package.json, src/|gen/|vendor/}
  ogl/<unit>/{...}
  brand/<unit>/{...}

estate/generators/<id>.json is where refresh rhythm lives - trigger, inputs, outputs, observed cadence. Rhythm is a property of the generator, not of the unit, which is why the incumbent needed three fields to express it: the estate's five generated classes do not align with unit boundaries. estate/services/<service>.json holds the shared external-service facts (endpoint, credential reference, rate limits) that P1's two units both need and neither owns.

organisingRules.name: Licence class is the only path-carried classification
organisingRules.rule: Three repository roots - mit/, ogl/, brand/. Every unit is under exactly one. A unit that would span two is split into two units with a declared dependency. Mixing is structurally impossible rather than declared, because the estate states licence classes are never mixable in one unit.
organisingRules.carrier: Repository root path segment, recomputed against unit.json.licence by estate-check

organisingRules.name: Edit ownership is the second path segment, with exactly three values and no exceptions
organisingRules.rule: src/ is authored and never written by a build. gen/ is machine-owned and never hand-edited anywhere in the estate. vendor/ is byte-preserved and replaced only wholesale by a recorded upgrade. There is no Mixed value; a unit needing both simply has both directories.
organisingRules.carrier: Path segment inside every unit, enforced by regeneration-diff in estate-check

organisingRules.name: One fact, one carrier
organisingRules.rule: Every classification that is not licence or edit ownership is declared exactly once, in unit.json, validated against a published schema. No inference, no README semantics, no SemVer-major-as-policy, no .gitignore as a second opinion. Where a fact is deliberately duplicated (licence), the gate recomputes it so disagreement is impossible rather than silent.
organisingRules.carrier: <unit>/unit.json validated against estate/unit.schema.json

organisingRules.name: No rule is keyed on a path glob
organisingRules.rule: Import policy, gate profiles, ownership, and licence checks all read manifests and the resolved workspace dependency graph. Consequence: moving or renaming a directory changes no rule, no config, and no import specifier. Reorganisation is cheap by construction, which is the estate's third question answered mechanically rather than in prose.
organisingRules.carrier: estate/import-policy.json plus the pnpm workspace dependency graph

organisingRules.name: Generated bytes carry provenance and the gate recomputes it
organisingRules.rule: Every gen/ directory carries .provenance.json recording generator id, each input with its digest, and the output digest. estate-check recomputes input digests including externally fetched artefacts; an input that moved without its output moving fails the commit and names every unit that must change with it.
organisingRules.carrier: <unit>/gen/.provenance.json plus estate/generators/<id>.json

organisingRules.name: Refresh rhythm belongs to the generator, not the unit
organisingRules.rule: Trigger, inputs, outputs, and cadence are declared once per generator. Units reference generator ids. This is why one field suffices where the incumbent needed three: the estate's five generated classes cross unit boundaries and a unit may host outputs of several generators.
organisingRules.carrier: estate/generators/<id>.json, referenced by unit.json.generators

organisingRules.name: Audience and support are separate, both one line, and import legality is derived from support monotonicity
organisingRules.rule: Nothing may depend at runtime on a unit whose support is weaker than its own; nothing may import a demo, research, or operational unit. A demo graduating to product costs one manifest line and a gate re-run - no move, no rename, no rule edit.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.audience and unit.json.support, evaluated against estate/import-policy.json

organisingRules.name: Gate profile is independent of audience; exemptions are named, reasoned, and dated
organisingRules.rule: Research code can be fully quality-gated while shipping to nobody; operational code can be exempt from named checks only via operational-exempt with a reason, an explicit list of exempted checks, and a review date. There is no directory that is silently outside the gates.
organisingRules.carrier: unit.json.gates

organisingRules.name: Discovery is an index, not a tree; unit space is flat under each licence root
organisingRules.rule: gen/estate-index.json maps unit name to path and full classification, regenerated by the same gate that validates the manifests, so it cannot drift. No tier hierarchy exists, so no unit ever has to be filed into or refiled between tiers.
organisingRules.carrier: gen/estate-index.json

organisingRules.name: Structural wrongness is reported, not remembered
organisingRules.rule: estate-check emits a non-failing report of extraction candidates - internal directories with no unit-specific dependency and a single ingress - and of units whose gen/ byte volume or symbol count crosses a read-cost threshold. The estate's admission that it will turn out to be wrong somewhere gets a detector rather than a note.
organisingRules.carrier: estate-check report output, computed from the module graph and the index

probePlacements.probe: P1: spec snapshot plus bulk dataset from the same service, different schedules and mechanisms
probePlacements.placement: Two units, because generator identity rather than service identity is the unit boundary. Spec snapshot: mit/curriculum-api-spec/gen/ (generator spec-fetch, about 29/yr). Bulk dataset: ogl/curriculum-bulk/gen/ (generator bulk-fetch, about 7/yr) - separate root because the bulk payload is curriculum content, not code. The shared credential and endpoint live once in estate/services/curriculum-platform.json, referenced by both generators.

probePlacements.probe: P2: four collections of machine-regenerated artefacts, each on a different event class
probePlacements.placement: One generator id per event class in estate/generators/, each writing into exactly one gen/ tree with its own .provenance.json. The estate's five classes: spec-types (29/yr) into mit/curriculum-sdk/gen/; search-contracts (16/yr) into mit/search-contracts/gen/; bulk-schemas (7/yr) into ogl/curriculum-bulk/gen/; corpus-mine (19/yr, 24MB) into ogl/curriculum-corpus/gen/; widget-bundle (18/yr) into the serving unit, see P11.

probePlacements.probe: P3: byte-preserved third-party vendor files alongside freely-changing hand-written styling
probePlacements.placement: One unit, mit/design-system/, with vendor/ (never edited by anyone; replaced wholesale by the vendor-refresh generator, which records the upstream digest) and src/styles/ (freely authored). The distinction is readable from the path segment with no metadata lookup and no .gitignore consultation.

probePlacements.probe: P4: one tooling area serving several consumers on different rhythms
probePlacements.placement: mit/agent-tools/, audience operational, gates product (it is real code and is gated as such). Consumer rhythm is a property of the invocation surface, not the unit: unit.json.entrypoints declares [{id, kind: interactive|commit-guard|scheduled, onFailure}]. Git hooks are shims under estate/hooks/ that only exec an entrypoint id and hold no logic, so the same code has no second home.

probePlacements.probe: P5: hand-curated reference data carrying a content licence different from surrounding code
probePlacements.placement: ogl/curriculum-reference/src/ - its own unit under the OGL root, human-owned bytes. MIT consumers declare it in unit.json.contentDeps and resolve it at build time; the licence-purity check fails any MIT unit that takes it as a runtime dependency. This is where the incumbent placed a dual-licence unit and violated the estate's stated invariant.

probePlacements.probe: P6: trademark image assets with reuse terms unlike anything else
probePlacements.placement: brand/oak-brand-assets/, its own licence root and its own unit. The synchronisation machinery is a generator (brand-sync) declared in estate/generators/ writing to brand/oak-brand-assets/gen/, not an unclassifiable top-level directory. Every consuming unit reaches it through contentDeps, so brand bytes never travel inside an MIT tarball.

probePlacements.probe: P7: research-study evidence code, quality-gated but never shipped
probePlacements.placement: mit/research-web-app-deconstruction/, audience research, support none, gates product. Gate profile is deliberately independent of audience, so this unit is held to full product quality while the support-monotonicity rule forbids anything depending on it. The incumbent could not express this pair because its Consumer Class and gate posture were the same axis.

probePlacements.probe: P8: operational scripts running against live systems, outside product quality gates
probePlacements.placement: mit/ops-scripts/, audience operational, gates operational-exempt {reason, exempts:[named checks], reviewBy:<date>}. It is a unit, not a hole: licence, edit ownership, import policy, and ownership all still bind, and the exemption names exactly which checks are skipped, why, and when it expires.

probePlacements.probe: P9: deployed product application and demonstration application, near-identical structure, different audiences and support promises
probePlacements.placement: mit/curriculum-mcp-server/ (audience product, support supported) and mit/curriculum-hub-demo/ (audience demo, support best-effort). Identical structure is correct and desirable; the entire difference is two manifest lines. Support monotonicity blocks the product depending on the demo - the direction that is actually hazardous. Graduation costs one line plus a gate run: no move, no rename, no ESLint edit.

probePlacements.probe: P10: generic machinery reusable against any similar datastore, currently embedded in a product-specific pipeline
probePlacements.placement: Extracted as mit/datastore-kit/, with mit/search-cli/ depending on it. The extraction is also detected rather than remembered: estate-check reports any internal directory with a single ingress and no unit-specific dependency as an extraction candidate. This is a placement plus a detector, where the incumbent offered a status-quo description plus an aspiration.

probePlacements.probe: P11: browser-built widget whose built output is embedded and served by a different unit than its source
probePlacements.placement: Two units, as stipulated. Source: mit/curriculum-widget/src/. Output: generator widget-bundle (about 18/yr) writes into the SERVING unit's tree at mit/curriculum-mcp-server/gen/widget/. The serving unit's unit.json.serves records {from: curriculum-widget, path: gen/widget}, and gen/widget/.provenance.json records the source unit's tree digest as an input - so changing the widget source without rebuilding fails the co-change check and names the serving unit by name.

probePlacements.probe: P12: commit-hook guard code and repo-state validator code - same rhythm, different consumers and failure modes
probePlacements.placement: Both in mit/agent-tools/src/, as two entrypoints differing in kind (commit-guard vs interactive) and in onFailure (block vs report). Honest strain: same rhythm argues for one unit, but a bad commit-guard release blocks every commit estate-wide while a bad validator only misreports - one unit means one version and one blast radius. The rhythm rule wins and the blast radius is accepted, mitigated by hooks executing a pinned committed build rather than the working tree. Marked forced because the failure-mode difference is real and the design subordinates it.

probePlacements.probe: S1: error-handling primitive, tiny, zero dependencies, imported nearly everywhere
probePlacements.placement: mit/result/, audience internal, support supported, depsPolicy none. Zero-dependency is a checked property (estate-check asserts an empty dependencies map) rather than a directory convention that merely suggests it. No tier home is needed or wanted.

probePlacements.probe: S2: path-safety utility born from a security incident, small and security-critical
probePlacements.placement: mit/safe-path/, depsPolicy none, plus unit.json.owner and a review requirement that generates its CODEOWNERS entry. Structurally identical to S1 - criticality is a declared property with a mechanical consequence, not a special place in the tree.

probePlacements.probe: S3: large graph-data library exposing about 74 public symbols
probePlacements.placement: mit/graph-corpus/, audience internal, published. Its data arrives via contentDeps on ogl/curriculum-corpus, so the code stays MIT and the corpus bytes stay OGL in separate units. gen/estate-index.json records publicSymbolCount so an agent knows the read cost before opening it.

probePlacements.probe: S4: typed client for the external curriculum service, published publicly
probePlacements.placement: mit/curriculum-sdk/, audience product, support supported. src/ holds the hand-written surface; gen/ holds spec-derived types from generator spec-types (29/yr) whose provenance records the digest of mit/curriculum-api-spec/gen/. A spec refresh that lands without regeneration fails the co-change check.

probePlacements.probe: S5: design-token pipeline whose generated CSS is consumed by several surfaces
probePlacements.placement: mit/design-tokens/ with src/tokens/ (authored) and gen/css/ (generator tokens-css). Consumers depend on the unit and never copy the CSS into their own gen/, so there is exactly one home for the generated bytes and one provenance record.

probePlacements.probe: S6: search-retrieval library over a commodity datastore
probePlacements.placement: mit/search-sdk/, audience internal, depending on mit/datastore-kit/ from P10. Nothing distinguishes it structurally, which is the point - ordinary units need no ceremony.

probePlacements.probe: S7: the estate's largest unit - codegen pipeline mixing spec-fetch, generated types, corpus mining, and hand curation
probePlacements.placement: Split into four units, because keeping it whole is what forces the unanswerable Mixed value. mit/spec-fetch/ (audience operational, the fetcher); mit/curriculum-sdk/gen/ (spec-derived types, 29/yr - see S4); ogl/curriculum-corpus/gen/ (24MB mined data, 19/yr); ogl/curriculum-reference/src/ (hand curation - see P5). Justified by the estate's own numbers: four parts, two licence classes, cadences of 29 / n-a / 19 / manual. Bonus that the incumbent forfeits - because the corpus is its own unit, moving 24MB times 19/yr out of git to release assets later touches zero imports and zero rules.

probePlacements.probe: S8: observability adapter for a commodity vendor
probePlacements.placement: mit/sentry-adapter/, audience internal, support supported, depsPolicy external. One unit per vendor; nothing special.

fixDesign.notes:
WHAT SURVIVES FROM THE AUDITED DESIGN. Four of its six questions are the right questions and I have kept them: who may edit these bytes, who may import whom, under what licence a unit travels, and what changing the organisation costs. Its instinct to isolate research and operational code from product, and to hold demos apart from products, is correct and is preserved. What does not survive is every carrier choice, the tier hierarchy, and the claim of orthogonality - three of its six classifications collapse into one fact expressed three ways, and its enforcement is keyed on the paths it also admits are expensive to change.

TWO HONEST FORCED FITS IN MY DESIGN. P8: operational-exempt is an escape hatch by construction. I can make it visible, reasoned, scoped to named checks, and time-boxed, but I cannot eliminate it while scripts must run against live systems outside product gates - so I declare it rather than hiding it in an unclassified directory. P12: I subordinate a real failure-mode difference (a bad commit-guard blocks the whole workforce; a bad validator misreports) to the rhythm rule, and accept a shared blast radius mitigated by running hooks from a pinned committed build.

RESIDUAL RISKS I WOULD FALSIFY FIRST. (1) Regeneration-diff cost at 5,900 commits/year - the digest short-circuit is load-bearing; if input digests are expensive to compute for the 24MB corpus, check 1 becomes a pre-push rather than a pre-commit gate and the design's headline promise weakens to next-push detection. Measure before committing to commit-time. (2) The index is a single point of failure for discovery - it is generated by the gate that validates manifests, so it cannot drift silently, but a broken gate blinds the estate; the index must therefore be committed and diffable, never build-time-only. (3) The three-root licence split raises the cost of a licence reclassification to a physical move. I accept this deliberately - a licence change is a legal event and should be expensive and visible - but if the estate discovers that units routinely change licence class, the correct response is to demote licence to a manifest field with a per-file purity check, not to add a Mixed value. (4) Flat unit space assumes tens of units, not hundreds. If unit count passes roughly 150 the index remains fine but human navigation degrades; the cure is index tooling, never a reintroduced tier hierarchy, because tiers reintroduce filing decisions and path-bound cost.

WHAT I DID NOT VERIFY. I read nothing from the repository, as instructed. Unit counts, actual dependency shapes, whether imports really resolve by package name in this workspace, and the true cost of the incumbent's path moves are all inferred from the estate description and the design's own text. The defect findings above rest only on the packet and the estate paragraph; the fix design's cost claims rest on standard pnpm workspace semantics and should be checked against the real workspace before adoption.

defects.claim: The Licensing classification violates the estate's hard constraint that licence classes are never mixable in one unit, and its carrier is a mechanism that does not exist.
defects.evidence: Estate: 'MIT code, OGL curriculum content, reserved brand assets — coexisting, never mixable in one unit.' Design: Licensing values include 'Mixed (per-export-path)' and the P5 placement reads 'packages/docs/ or packages/core/reference-data/ (dual license: MIT code + OGL content)' — a single unit carrying two licence classes, marked forcedFit:false. The carrier, 'exports map declares per-path license', names an npm mechanism that does not exist: the exports map carries no licence metadata and no tool reads one, so even the illegal mixing is unenforced prose.

defects.claim: Question 2 (who may edit these bytes) is answered at package granularity with a 'Mixed' escape value precisely at the units where it matters most; the file-level mechanism the summary advertises appears nowhere in the design body.
defects.evidence: Edit Boundary's carrier is 'package.json editBoundary field' — one value per package.
